promise: Pass a Zero Carbon Act and establish an independent Climate Commission.
keyNumber: Zero Carbon Act promised -> passed 13 Nov 2019, net zero (excl. biogenic methane) by 2050
statusReason: The Act passed within the term. It created both the 2050 target and the independent Commission exactly as promised.
whatHappened: The Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Act 2019 received royal assent on 13 November 2019 with cross-party support. It set a target of net zero for all greenhouse gases other than biogenic methane by 2050. It also set a separate biogenic methane target of 10 percent below 2017 levels by 2030 and 24-47 percent by 2050. It established He Pou a Rangi / the Climate Change Commission as an independent Crown entity. The first three emissions budgets, covering 2022-2035, were set in 2022, and the first emissions reduction plan followed the same year.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, item 40 (also a Labour-Greens confidence and supply commitment)

promise: Deliver a Zero Carbon Act, set up an independent Climate Change Commission and establish a Green Investment Fund. These were the Greens' price for confidence and supply.
keyNumber: 3 institutions promised -> Zero Carbon Act, Climate Change Commission and Green Investment Fund all established
statusReason: All three named institutions were created within the 2017-2020 term.
whatHappened: Green co-leader James Shaw held the Climate Change portfolio outside Cabinet from 2017 and inside it from 2020. The Zero Carbon Act passed on 13 November 2019 and the Climate Change Commission was established under it. New Zealand Green Investment Finance was capitalised as a Crown-owned green investment bank. The Greens describe all three as fulfilling the confidence and supply agreement.
sourceDoc: Labour-Greens Confidence and Supply Agreement 2017 (climate commitments)

promise: Require a climate change lens (a climate impact assessment) on major government decisions and legislation.
statusReason: The climate lens was implemented. It came as Cabinet-office guidance on qualifying proposals, not the statutory across-the-board requirement the Greens originally sought.
whatHappened: The Government issued new Cabinet guidance requiring a climate implications of policy assessment (CIPA) for policy proposals with significant emissions implications. The Greens state this fulfilled the confidence and supply commitment. It built on a Green member's bill that would have required climate change impact statements on all legislation. The requirement is administrative Cabinet guidance rather than a statutory duty on all bills, which is narrower than the member's bill sought.
sourceDoc: Labour-Greens Confidence and Supply Agreement 2017 (climate lens on government decisions)

promise: If the Climate Commission decides agriculture should be included in the Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS), free allocation to agriculture on entry will be 95 percent. All revenue will be recycled back into agriculture for innovation, mitigation and additional forestry planting.
keyNumber: 95 percent free allocation on ETS entry promised -> agriculture never entered the ETS
statusReason: Agriculture never entered the ETS during the term. The 95 percent free allocation and revenue recycling arrangement never took effect.
whatHappened: On 24 October 2019 the Government decided agriculture would not enter the reformed ETS. Instead it set up a sector partnership, He Waka Eke Noa, to design a farm-level pricing system. A legislated backstop would bring agricultural processors into the ETS from 2025 if no alternative was agreed. He Waka Eke Noa reported in 2022 and the Government proposed a farm-level system in October 2022. No pricing system was in force when Labour left office in October 2023. The incoming coalition disbanded He Waka Eke Noa and removed agriculture from the ETS entirely in 2024.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, item 41

promise: Plant 100 million trees a year under a One Billion Trees programme, reaching one billion trees by 2028.
keyNumber: 1,000,000,000 trees by 2028 (100m/yr) -> approx 149.4 million recorded planted by May 2020
statusReason: A programme was established and large-scale planting occurred, but the run rate was roughly half what a billion trees by 2028 required.
whatHappened: The One Billion Trees Programme was launched in 2018 with a grants fund, and a new forestry agency, Te Uru Rākau, was established on 11 May 2018. About 149.4 million trees had been recorded as planted by May 2020, well behind the 100 million per year run rate needed. The grant fund closed to new applications in 2021 and the programme wound down. Forestry planting still became a large part of New Zealand's projected emissions reductions, with the Climate Change Commission noting in 2025 that 46 percent of planned third-budget reductions rely on forest removals.
contestedNote: Supporters point out the target date is 2028, and that seedling supply rather than policy constrained early planting. Critics note the programme was wound down years before 2028 with no plausible path to a billion trees, and that the Ministry counted trees planted commercially anyway.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, item 1b: "Planting 100 million trees per year in a Billion Trees Planting Programme"

promise: Make the Government's vehicle fleet, where practicable, emissions-free by 2025/26.
keyNumber: Emissions-free fleet by 2025/26 -> 78 of 15,473 government vehicles electric at Oct 2019, target later redefined
statusReason: Some electrification occurred and a programme was created, but the target was redefined from an emissions-free fleet to emissions-free new purchases.
whatHappened: By October 2019 only 78 of 15,473 government vehicles were electric. The Government then restated the commitment as a requirement that all new vehicles entering the fleet be emissions-free after mid-2025, rather than the whole fleet being emissions-free by 2025/26. The Carbon Neutral Government Programme, announced in 2020, carried the fleet work forward. The original whole-of-fleet date was not met by the end of Labour's term.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, item 39

promise: Achieve 100 percent renewable electricity generation by 2030, five years earlier than the previous 2035 goal. Support this with pumped hydro at Lake Onslow and a ban on new thermal baseload generation.
keyNumber: 100 percent renewable electricity by 2030 -> 87 percent of generation renewable in 2022
statusReason: Renewable share rose, but the key enabling project was unfinished and the firm 2030 target was softened. The target date itself falls outside the term.
whatHappened: Renewables supplied 87 percent of electricity generated in 2022, up from about 82 percent in 2021. The rise came mainly from favourable hydro conditions rather than new policy. The NZ Battery Project, set up in 2020 to investigate the Lake Onslow pumped-hydro scheme as the enabler of a 100 percent renewable grid, was still in feasibility stage at the 2023 election, and investigations were stopped in late 2023. No ban on new thermal baseload generation was legislated. By the time Labour left office, official documents had recast the 100 percent figure as an aspiration rather than a firm target.
contestedNote: Labour argues the target was always for 2030 and cannot be judged at a 2023 handover. Critics note the flagship enabling project was never committed to, the thermal ban never happened, and the increase that did occur was largely weather-driven.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 election energy policy announcement (10 September 2020)

promise: Run the Emissions Trading Scheme in line with the Zero Carbon Act's emissions budgets, including setting auction volumes and price controls in line with Climate Change Commission advice.
keyNumber: ETS settings aligned with budgets -> approx 35 million extra units released Dec 2022, all 4 auctions in 2023 failed, settings remade by Sept 2023
statusReason: The settings were eventually aligned with Commission advice. That came only after a Cabinet decision that a court required to be remade, and a year of failed auctions.
whatHappened: In December 2022 Cabinet rejected the Commission's advice. It released about 35 million more units over five years than recommended and held the cost containment trigger price well below the recommended level, reportedly because of cost-of-living concerns. The secondary carbon price fell sharply and all four 2023 ETS auctions failed to clear. Lawyers for Climate Action NZ sought judicial review. In 2023 the High Court required the Minister to reconsider the settings by 30 September 2023, and the Government remade the regulations adopting the Commission's recommendations before the election.
contestedNote: The Government's position was that Ministers are entitled to weigh household cost impacts alongside Commission advice, and that it corrected the settings within the same year. The successful judicial review found the December 2022 decision was not lawfully made.
sourceDoc: Labour-Greens Cooperation Agreement 2020: "achieving the purpose and goals of the Zero Carbon Act"

promise: Increase uptake of zero-emission vehicles and introduce clean car standards as part of achieving the goals of the Zero Carbon Act.
keyNumber: Clean car standard + ZEV uptake promised -> feebate live 1 Jul 2021, Clean Car Standard in force 2023
statusReason: Both a feebate and a clean car standard were legislated and in force before the end of the term. That is what the agreement committed to.
whatHappened: The Clean Car Discount (a feebate) began paying rebates from 1 July 2021 and charging fees on high-emitting vehicles from 1 April 2022. Rebates ran to about $7,500 for zero-emission vehicles and $5,000 for hybrids. The Clean Car Standard, a CO2 standard on vehicle importers, was legislated in the Land Transport (Clean Vehicles) Amendment Act 2022 and took effect from 2023. EV registrations rose sharply over 2021-2023. Both policies were reversed or weakened after the change of government: the discount ended on 31 December 2023 and the standard's 2025-2029 CO2 targets were eased in July 2024.
sourceDoc: Labour-Greens Cooperation Agreement 2020, decarbonising public transport, increasing uptake of zero-emission vehicles, introducing clean car standards

promise: Support the switch of industrial process heat from coal and gas to renewable energy.
keyNumber: Renewable process heat support promised -> GIDI Partnerships $230m public + $860m private, approx 9.3 Mt lifetime abatement; coal boiler phase-out set for 2037
statusReason: Both a large co-funding scheme and a regulatory phase-out were in place before the end of the term. The later reversal is outside the promising party's term.
whatHappened: The Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry (GIDI) fund began in 2020 and was expanded from the Climate Emergency Response Fund in Budget 2022. It co-funded boiler conversions across dairy, meat, timber and steel. EECA's GIDI Partnerships stream alone involved $230 million of EECA co-investment alongside $860 million of private capital, with lifetime abatement of about 9.3 million tonnes of CO2 from the NZ Steel and Fonterra projects. In June 2023 the Government banned new low-to-medium temperature coal boilers from 27 July 2023 and required existing ones to be phased out by 2037. GIDI later closed to new applications. In June 2026 the National-led government scrapped the 2037 coal boiler phase-out without replacing it.
sourceDoc: Labour-Greens Cooperation Agreement 2020, supporting the use of renewable energy for industrial heat

promise: Deliver net zero by 2050, including by doubling New Zealand's renewable electricity generation.
keyNumber: Net zero 2050 + double renewables -> EB1 284.1/290 Mt and EB2 303.1/305 Mt projected met, EB3 projected 249.2 Mt vs 240 Mt budget
statusReason: The 2050 target is intact and the first two budgets are on track. The third budget is projected to be missed, and the term is not finished.
whatHappened: The 2050 target in the Zero Carbon Act was retained. The second emissions reduction plan, published in December 2024 and amended in January 2026, projects the first emissions budget (290 Mt) will be met at 284.1 Mt and the second (305 Mt) narrowly met at 303.1 Mt. It claims net zero could be reached as early as 2044. The Climate Change Commission's 2025 monitoring report agrees budgets one and two are achievable, but finds the third budget (2031-2035) is projected to be exceeded by about 9.2 Mt, with 46 percent of planned reductions relying on forest removals. Consenting was streamlined for renewables through the fast-track regime and RMA changes. The Commission still singled out electricity generation in 2025 as an area of increased risk, and the total renewable share of primary energy was 45.4 percent in 2024.
contestedNote: The Government points to official projections showing the first two budgets met and net zero reachable by 2044. The Climate Change Commission and critics point to a 9.2 Mt shortfall against the third budget, heavy reliance on forestry, and the November 2025 decision to de-couple ETS settings from the Paris target.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023: "Deliver Net Zero by 2050 including by doubling New Zealand's renewable electricity"

promise: Scrap the Clean Car Discount, including the fee on higher-emitting vehicles that National labelled the "ute tax".
keyNumber: Clean Car Discount scrapped -> ended 31 Dec 2023 after approx $579m rebates paid vs approx $290m fees collected
statusReason: Repealed by legislation within the first month of government, exactly as promised.
whatHappened: The Land Transport (Clean Vehicle Discount Scheme Repeal) Amendment Act 2023 passed on 14 December 2023 and received royal assent on 19 December 2023. Both the rebates and the fees ended for vehicles registered after 31 December 2023. Over its life the scheme paid out about $579 million in rebates and $13.5 million in administration, against about $290 million collected in fees. EV registrations fell steeply in early 2024 after the rebates ended.
sourceDoc: National 2023 campaign commitment to scrap the Clean Car Discount / "ute tax"

promise: Deliver 10,000 public EV chargers by 2030, backed by $257 million over four years using a co-investment model modelled on Ultra-Fast Broadband.
keyNumber: 10,000 public chargers by 2030 ($257m) -> 0 delivered under the programme and 0 contracts signed as at March 2026
statusReason: No chargers had been delivered and no contracts signed at 30 months. The required build rate is now far above the current national rate.
whatHappened: The programme was restructured from grants to concessionary loans. A request for proposals closed in July 2025 and attracted only six compliant submissions. As at March 2026 the Minister for Climate Change and Energy said the Government was in the final stages of contracting, but no contracts had been signed and no chargers had been delivered under the programme, 30 months after the commitment. Industry analysis put the required pace at about 174 new charging points a month to reach 10,000 by 2030, more than were built in all of 2025. The second emissions reduction plan attributes only about 0.01 Mt of emissions budget 2 reductions to EV charging.
contestedNote: The Government argues the 2030 deadline is still four years away and that contracts are imminent, so the promise remains live. On the evidence to date nothing has been built under the programme, and the required monthly build rate now exceeds anything achieved.
sourceDoc: National 2023 policy. Supercharging EV Infrastructure

promise: Keep agriculture out of the Emissions Trading Scheme and remove the legislated 2025 backstop that would have brought farm emissions into it.
keyNumber: Agriculture out of the ETS -> legislated before 1 Jan 2025; $400m over 4 years for mitigation technology
statusReason: Agriculture was legislated out of the ETS within the promised timeframe and the backstop removed.
whatHappened: On 11 June 2024 Ministers announced agriculture would be permanently removed from the ETS before 1 January 2025. The Climate Change Response Act was amended to strip out the processor-level backstop for farmers, meat and dairy processors and fertiliser companies. He Waka Eke Noa was disbanded and replaced with a Pastoral Sector Group, alongside $400 million over four years for emissions-reduction technology and $50.5 million over five years for the Agricultural Greenhouse Gas Research Centre. The January 2026 amendment to the second emissions reduction plan then confirmed the Government would not proceed with an on-farm agricultural emissions pricing system by 2030 at all.
sourceDoc: National 2023 election commitment to keep agriculture out of the ETS

promise: Stop the previous government's review of the Emissions Trading Scheme, to restore confidence and certainty to the carbon market.
keyNumber: Stop ETS review to restore certainty -> review stopped; all 4 auctions in 2025 failed to sell a single unit
statusReason: The review was stopped as promised. On the auction evidence, the stated purpose of restoring carbon-market confidence and certainty has not been achieved.
whatHappened: The ETS review begun under Labour was halted early in the term, and the Government stated the ETS would remain its main emissions-reduction tool. Market confidence did not follow. All four quarterly auctions failed to attract a single bid in 2025, the second calendar year of complete auction failure after 2023, with secondary-market units trading around $40 against a $68 auction reserve. Brokers attributed the collapse in participation to policy signals. These included the November 2025 decision to de-couple ETS settings from New Zealand's Paris commitments, the lowered methane target and weakened reporting requirements.
contestedNote: The Government's reading is that the commitment was simply to end the review, which it did. Critics measure it against the agreement's own stated purpose of restoring market confidence, which the failed auctions suggest has not happened.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023: "Stop the current review of the ETS system to restore confidence and certainty"

promise: Encourage the uptake of on-farm emissions reduction mitigations, such as low-methane genetics and low-methane animal feed, rather than pricing farm emissions.
keyNumber: Incentivise low-methane technology -> $400m over 4 years plus $50.5m over 5 years committed
statusReason: Substantial research and commercialisation funding was delivered, but uptake incentives have not yet produced measurable on-farm methane reductions.
whatHappened: Alongside removing agriculture from the ETS in June 2024, the Government committed $400 million over four years to speed up commercialisation of emissions-reduction tools, including methane inhibitors, vaccines and low-methane breeding. It added $50.5 million over five years for the Agricultural Greenhouse Gas Research Centre. In October 2025 it confirmed there would be no methane tax and a technology-and-partnership approach instead. As at 2026 no methane inhibitor or vaccine is in widespread commercial on-farm use in New Zealand pasture systems, and the Climate Change Commission's 2025 monitoring report lists agriculture among the areas needing additional policy.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023, incentivise uptake of emissions reduction mitigations such as low methane genetics and low methane feed

promise: Keep a split-gas approach to methane and carbon dioxide through to 2050. Review the methane science and targets in 2024 for consistency with no additional warming from agricultural methane emissions.
keyNumber: Methane target reviewed for no additional warming -> target cut from 24-47% to 14-24% below 2017 levels by 2050
statusReason: The split-gas approach was maintained, and the review was carried out and acted on. The decision came in October 2025 rather than in 2024.
whatHappened: An independent methane science and target review panel was appointed in 2024. It reported that a 14-24 percent reduction below 2017 levels by 2050 would be consistent with no additional warming from agricultural methane. On 13 October 2025 the Government announced it would adopt that range. That lowered the Zero Carbon Act target from 24-47 percent to 14-24 percent by 2050, left the 2030 target unchanged and ruled out a methane tax. The Climate Change Commission's own 2024 review of the 2050 target had recommended a different basis, advising that New Zealand should aim to be carbon negative by 2050 to be consistent with the Paris 1.5C goal. The split-gas structure was retained throughout.
contestedNote: The Government and farm sector groups say the new range implements the agreement's "no additional warming" test using independent science. The Climate Change Commission and climate scientists argue "no additional warming" locks in existing warming and is not aligned with the Paris temperature goal, making the change a weakening of the 2050 target.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023, maintain a split-gas approach and review the methane science and targets in 2024 for consistency with no additional warming

promise: Repeal the ban on offshore oil and gas exploration.
keyNumber: Repeal 2018 offshore exploration ban -> repealed by Crown Minerals Amendment Act 2025, royal assent 5 Aug 2025
statusReason: The ban was repealed by Act of Parliament within the term.
whatHappened: The Labour Government announced on 12 April 2018 that it would grant no new offshore oil and gas exploration permits, leaving 30 existing permits untouched. The Crown Minerals Amendment Bill was introduced on 24 September 2024 and passed its third reading on 31 July 2025, receiving royal assent on 5 August 2025. The Act removed the offshore exploration ban and changed the purpose of the Crown Minerals Act 1991 from managing to promoting the use of Crown minerals. It also created a Tier 3 permit regime for small-scale gold mining and replaced the trailing decommissioning liability model with ministerial discretion. Of 5,524 select committee submissions, 94.5 percent opposed the bill. A first offshore exploration permit off Taranaki followed the repeal.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023: "Repeal the ban on offshore oil and gas exploration"

promise: Let farmers and landowners offset on-farm sequestration (such as riparian planting, shelter belts and scattered vegetation) against their on-farm emissions.
keyNumber: On-farm sequestration offsetting -> no mechanism in place; on-farm pricing abandoned in Jan 2026
statusReason: No on-farm offsetting mechanism was created. The decision not to price farm emissions removed the framework it would have operated in.
whatHappened: Agriculture was removed from the ETS in 2024 and no farm-level pricing system was created, so there is no compliance obligation for on-farm sequestration to be offset against. The January 2026 amendment to the second emissions reduction plan confirmed the Government would not implement an on-farm agricultural emissions pricing system by 2030. That ended the pathway that would have required recognising on-farm sequestration. Work continued on recognising additional sequestration categories such as blue carbon under the separate NZ First commitment, but no offsetting mechanism for farm emissions exists.
contestedNote: The Government's view is that the commitment is moot and satisfied in practice, because farmers now face no pricing obligation at all. On a literal reading, the specific mechanism ACT negotiated, recognising on-farm sequestration against on-farm emissions, was never built.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023: "Enable farmers and landowners to offset sequestration against their on-farm emissions"

promise: Set up a Tax Working Group in the first term to design a fairer tax system, including consideration of a capital gains tax. Take its recommendations to voters at the 2020 election.
keyNumber: Tax Working Group's central recommendation (broad capital gains tax) -> ruled out April 2019, none legislated
statusReason: The working group was set up and reported as promised. The government then dropped its central recommendation, and Labour later ruled the policy out entirely.
whatHappened: The Tax Working Group, chaired by Sir Michael Cullen, was established in December 2017. It delivered its final report in February 2019, recommending a broad capital gains tax that excluded the family home. On 17 April 2019 the government announced it would not proceed. Jacinda Ardern said no capital gains tax would be introduced while she led the Labour Party, telling RNZ she 'just couldn't get the numbers'. Coalition partner NZ First had refused to support it, with Winston Peters saying there was no compelling evidence it would improve equality. In July 2023 Chris Hipkins went further and ruled out both a capital gains tax and a wealth tax under his leadership. He also shelved a Treasury/IRD high-wealth study commissioned by Revenue Minister David Parker.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 manifesto / 2017 campaign tax policy

promise: Introduce a new top personal income tax rate of 39 percent on income above $180,000, affecting roughly the top 2 percent of earners.
keyNumber: 39% on income over $180,000 promised -> legislated December 2020, in force 1 April 2021
statusReason: Legislated within four months of the election at the promised rate, threshold and start date.
whatHappened: The Taxation (Income Tax Rate and Other Amendments) Bill was introduced on 2 December 2020 and passed under urgency. The 39 percent rate took effect on 1 April 2021 exactly as promised. The same Act introduced new trust disclosure rules to police avoidance of the new rate. Inland Revenue reported the rate captured tens of thousands more taxpayers than originally estimated, as wages rose.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 manifesto / 2020 campaign tax policy

promise: The 39 percent top rate would be the only tax change in the 2020-23 term: no wealth tax, no capital gains tax and no change to GST.
keyNumber: 1 promised new tax (39% rate) -> 39% rate plus removal of landlord interest deductibility, a 10-year bright-line test and GST on online platforms
statusReason: The specific taxes Labour ruled out were not introduced. Two large revenue-raising changes outside the stated plan were legislated during the term.
whatHappened: Labour did not introduce a wealth tax, a capital gains tax or any GST rate change, and in 2023 Chris Hipkins publicly ruled the first two out. In March 2021, however, the government removed interest deductibility for residential landlords and extended the bright-line test on investment property to ten years. In 2022-23 it legislated GST on services sold through online platforms such as Uber and Airbnb (the 'app tax'), to take effect from 1 April 2024. Opposition parties and property groups described these as new taxes. Labour said they were changes to existing rules rather than new taxes.
contestedNote: Labour argued that the bright-line extension and the removal of interest deductibility were adjustments to existing income tax rules, and that the platform rules extended existing GST rather than creating a new tax, so the pledge was kept. National, ACT and property investor groups argued they were new taxes in substance and that the pledge was broken. Both readings rest on the same undisputed policy changes.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 manifesto / 2020 campaign tax policy

promise: Cancel National's legislated April 2018 income tax threshold cuts and replace them with a Families Package worth $890 million in 2018/19. The package includes a Winter Energy Payment of $450 a year for single superannuitants and beneficiaries and $700 for couples, a Best Start payment of $60 a week per child, a higher Family Tax Credit and an increased Working for Families abatement threshold of $42,700.
keyNumber: Winter Energy Payment $450 single / $700 couple and Best Start $60 a week promised -> both legislated December 2017 and paid from 2018
statusReason: Legislated within the first three months of the term at the promised payment rates and thresholds.
whatHappened: The Families Package (Income Tax and Benefits) Act 2017 passed in December 2017. It repealed National's planned threshold changes and legislated the package. Accommodation Supplement increases began on 1 April 2018, and the Winter Energy Payment and Best Start payments began in 2018. The Winter Energy Payment has been paid every winter since. A 2022 Motu evaluation found the payment had a weakly positive effect on recipients' energy spending and hardship assistance needs, though most estimated effects were not statistically significant.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 manifesto / Families Package campaign policy

promise: Remove GST from fresh and frozen fruit and vegetables from 1 April 2024. Raise the Working for Families in-work tax credit by $25 a week from the same date, and lift the Working for Families abatement threshold to $50,000 from 1 April 2026.
keyNumber: GST off fresh and frozen fruit and vegetables from 1 April 2024 -> not legislated; GST still applies to all food in August 2026
statusReason: GST was not removed from fruit and vegetables. Labour left office three weeks after making the promise and never had the numbers to legislate it.
whatHappened: Labour lost the October 2023 election and the policy was never introduced as legislation. GST still applies to all food as at August 2026. Economists including Infometrics' Brad Olsen and Deloitte publicly questioned how much of the saving would reach consumers. The incoming National government later legislated the $25 a week in-work tax credit increase in Budget 2024, taking effect on 31 July 2024.
sourceDoc: Labour 2023 campaign policy announcement, 13 August 2023

promise: From 1 July 2024, lift income tax thresholds to compensate for inflation: the 10.5 percent bracket from $14,000 to $15,600, the 17.5 percent bracket from $48,000 to $53,500 and the 30 percent bracket from $70,000 to $78,100. The cost is about $8.9 billion over four years.
keyNumber: Thresholds $15,600 / $53,500 / $78,100 from 1 July 2024 -> legislated in Budget 2024, effective 31 July 2024
statusReason: The promised bracket thresholds were legislated in the first Budget of the term, four weeks later than the promised start date.
whatHappened: Budget 2024, delivered on 30 May 2024, legislated exactly those thresholds, effective 31 July 2024 rather than 1 July. The package also expanded the Independent Earner Tax Credit and raised the in-work tax credit by $25 a week. Finance Minister Nicola Willis said 3.5 million New Zealanders would benefit, at a cost of $3.7 billion a year including the restoration of interest deductibility. No further threshold changes were made in Budget 2025 or Budget 2026, and the thresholds are not indexed.
sourceDoc: National 2023 manifesto / 'Back Pocket Boost' tax plan, 30 August 2023

promise: Deliver up to $250 a fortnight in extra income to an average-income household with children (household income around $120,000). This would come from threshold changes, FamilyBoost and Working for Families increases together.
keyNumber: Up to $250 a fortnight for an average family -> $78 a fortnight average for households with children; about 3,000 households qualified for the full amount
statusReason: Real tax relief was delivered. The typical gain for households with children was under a third of the headline figure, and only a very small number of households received the advertised maximum.
whatHappened: Budget 2024 delivered up to $102 a fortnight for average-income households. The Beehive's own figures put the average gain at $78 a fortnight ($2,028 a year) for households with children and $32 a fortnight ($832 a year) for working-age New Zealanders. A single person on $55,000 gained about $51 a fortnight. During the 2023 campaign the Council of Trade Unions calculated that only about 3,000 households out of 1.63 million (under 0.2 percent) met all the conditions needed to receive the full $252. It required a couple with children both earning between $53,500 and $66,000 and spending at least $300 a week on early childhood education.
contestedNote: National says the figure was always presented as an 'up to' maximum for a specific household type using full-time childcare, and that the components were delivered as designed. Critics say the $250 figure was used throughout the campaign as the benefit to an 'average household', and that the delivered average of $78 a fortnight for families with children shows the headline was not representative. Both sides agree on the underlying payment figures.
sourceDoc: National 2023 manifesto / 'Back Pocket Boost' tax plan, 30 August 2023

promise: Introduce FamilyBoost, a childcare tax rebate of up to $150 a fortnight (25 percent of early childhood fees). It would abate from a household income of $140,000 and cut out at $180,000, benefiting an extra 130,000 households at a cost of $996 million over four years.
keyNumber: Up to $150 a fortnight for an extra 130,000 households -> about 60,000 families claiming by mid-2025, 249 receiving the full amount
statusReason: The rebate exists and pays at the promised headline rate. Take-up fell far short of the 130,000 households promised, and almost no families received the advertised maximum until the scheme was redesigned a year in.
whatHappened: FamilyBoost began on 1 July 2024 and is administered by Inland Revenue on a claim-back basis. Uptake was well below forecast. About 60,000 families had claimed by mid-2025, and only 249 families consistently received the maximum payment. In May 2025 it was reported that close to a quarter of the money spent on the scheme to that point had gone on administration. In July 2025 the government raised the rebate from 25 percent to 40 percent of fees and lifted the income cap from $180,000 to $229,000, with IRD projecting about 16,000 additional claimants and roughly 92,000 in total.
sourceDoc: National 2023 manifesto / 'Back Pocket Boost' tax plan, 30 August 2023

promise: Increase the Working for Families in-work tax credit by $25 a week for low and middle income working families.
keyNumber: In-work tax credit +$25 a week -> $72.50 raised to $97.50 from 31 July 2024
statusReason: The promised $25 a week increase was legislated in the first Budget of the term.
whatHappened: Budget 2024 legislated a $25 a week increase to the in-work tax credit, taking it from $72.50 to $97.50 a week, effective 31 July 2024. Budget 2026 added a further temporary $50 a week in-work tax credit for around 157,000 working families as a cost-of-living measure.
sourceDoc: National 2023 manifesto / 'Back Pocket Boost' tax plan, 30 August 2023

promise: Allow foreign buyers to purchase homes worth over $2 million, subject to a 15 percent foreign buyer tax. This would raise about $740 million a year ($2.9 billion over four years) to help fund the income tax package.
keyNumber: $740 million a year from a 15% foreign buyer tax -> policy dropped in coalition talks, $0 raised
statusReason: National's own manifesto revenue measure was struck out in coalition negotiations before the government took office. No foreign buyer tax was ever introduced.
whatHappened: The policy was dropped in the National-NZ First coalition agreement signed on 24 November 2023. That agreement states that tax relief 'will be progressed as set out in National's Tax Plan, but will not include a repeal of the foreign buyer's residential property ban'. NZ First had opposed the tax throughout negotiations. Independent modelling during the campaign had already suggested the revenue forecast was around $2 billion too high over four years. The revenue gap was covered from other sources, including cancelling the Climate Emergency Response Fund and commercial building depreciation in the December 2023 mini-budget.
sourceDoc: National 2023 manifesto / 'Back Pocket Boost' tax plan, 30 August 2023

promise: Reverse Labour's 'app tax', the GST rules requiring platforms such as Uber and Airbnb to charge GST on services provided through them. On 3 March 2023 finance spokesperson Nicola Willis said the change would 'increase prices in the middle of a cost of living crisis', and that National would repeal it.
keyNumber: Promised repeal of GST on platform services -> rules took effect 1 April 2024 and remain in force
statusReason: An explicit campaign commitment to reverse a tax was dropped in office and the tax took effect unchanged.
whatHappened: After taking office the coalition indicated in late 2023 that it would not repeal the rules. The platform GST rules took effect on 1 April 2024 as Labour had legislated, and remain in force in August 2026. The retained revenue helped offset the loss of the foreign buyer tax in funding the income tax package.
sourceDoc: National 2023 campaign commitment / National's economic plan

promise: Abolish the Auckland regional fuel tax introduced in 2018.
keyNumber: Auckland regional fuel tax (introduced 2018) -> repealed in 2024
statusReason: The tax was repealed within the first year of the term as set out in the 100-day plan.
whatHappened: Legislation repealing the Auckland regional fuel tax was passed in 2024 and collection ceased during that year. For context on the other side of the ledger, Labour's separate temporary relief package ended on 30 June 2023 at a total cost of roughly $2 billion. That package was a 25 cents a litre cut to fuel excise duty and half-price public transport fares, introduced in March 2022 and extended four times. Budget 2026 added $150 million for strategic fuel reserves and a $450 million contingency for fuel-related pressures.
sourceDoc: National's 100-day plan, November 2023

promise: Move to a flatter, lower income tax scale: 17.5 percent under $60,000, 30 percent from $60,000 to $70,000, 33 percent from $70,000 to $180,000 and 39 percent above that. Extend the 30 percent bracket to $180,000 in 2025/26, and cut the top rate from 39 percent to 33 percent in 2026/27. Pay a carbon tax refund of about $243 per person in 2023/24.
keyNumber: Top rate cut from 39% to 33% by 2026/27 and a $243 per person carbon tax refund -> neither delivered; 39% rate still in force in August 2026
statusReason: ACT's rate structure and carbon dividend were both dropped in favour of National's tax plan in the coalition agreement, and none of the promised rate changes were legislated.
whatHappened: The coalition agreements committed the government to National's tax plan, not ACT's. The 2024 changes lifted thresholds but kept all five rates, and the 39 percent top rate remains in force in August 2026. No carbon tax refund was paid. The Climate Emergency Response Fund, which ACT and National both proposed to redirect, was cancelled in the December 2023 mini-budget and its $2 billion used to help fund National's tax package. ACT's longer-standing goal of a two-rate or single-rate income tax scale was not adopted at any point in the term.
sourceDoc: ACT 2023 alternative budget and tax policy

promise: Make the lowest income tax bracket (the first $14,000 of income) tax free no later than 1 April 2027, worth $28.27 a week to workers. Adjust tax brackets for inflation, with the first adjustment in 2027 and reviews every three years.
keyNumber: $14,000 tax-free bracket worth $28.27 a week by 1 April 2027 -> not legislated as at August 2026
statusReason: As at August 2026 no tax-free bracket or bracket indexation regime has been legislated, and the policy was not picked up in the coalition agreement.
whatHappened: The National-NZ First coalition agreement committed the government to National's tax plan. Thresholds were lifted once, on 31 July 2024, and the bottom $15,600 of income is still taxed at 10.5 percent. No automatic inflation indexation of brackets has been legislated, and neither Budget 2025 nor Budget 2026 made further threshold changes. Budget 2026 instead introduced a new prudential levy on financial institutions and a cap on charitable donation tax credits.
contestedNote: One reading is that the promise was superseded, because it was not written into the National-NZ First coalition agreement, which adopted National's tax plan instead. Another is that the promise is not yet due, because NZ First set a deadline of 1 April 2027 that falls after the current parliamentary term ends. On either reading, nothing had been legislated by August 2026.
sourceDoc: New Zealand First 2023 Policy Manifesto

promise: Give SuperGold cardholders a 50 percent local authority rates rebate of up to $1,600 a year, costed in the manifesto at about $480 million for couples.
keyNumber: 50% rates rebate up to $1,600 a year for SuperGold cardholders -> not implemented as at August 2026
statusReason: The rebate was not adopted in the coalition agreement, and no SuperGold rates rebate has been legislated as at August 2026.
whatHappened: The rebate was not included in the National-NZ First coalition agreement and has not been introduced. Rates relief for superannuitants is still delivered through the pre-existing means-tested Rates Rebate Scheme rather than a SuperGold entitlement. Budget 2026's cost-of-living measures were a temporary in-work tax credit top-up and fuel-related contingencies rather than rates relief.
sourceDoc: New Zealand First 2023 Policy Manifesto

promise: Ask the Commerce Commission to conduct market studies on supermarkets and building supplies to ensure everyone is getting a fair deal.
keyNumber: 2 market studies promised -> both completed; grocery study reported March 2022 with 14 recommendations, 12 accepted
statusReason: Both market studies were carried out as promised. The grocery study was followed by a regulator and two Acts before the end of the term.
whatHappened: The Commerce Commission launched its market study into the retail grocery sector in November 2020 and published its final report in March 2022. The report concluded that competition was not working well for consumers and made 14 recommendations, of which the Government accepted 12. The Commerce (Grocery Sector Covenants) Amendment Act 2022 banned restrictive land covenants and exclusive leases used to block competing grocery retailers. The Grocery Industry Competition Act 2023 created a Grocery Commissioner within the Commerce Commission, a wholesale supply regime with a regulatory backstop, and supplier protections, with the Grocery Supply Code taking effect on 28 March 2024. A parallel market study into residential building supplies was also completed. The Commission has since reported that competition in groceries remains limited.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 manifesto

promise: Meet five Budget Responsibility Rules. The strictest is to reduce net core Crown debt to below 20 percent of GDP within five years of taking office, and to keep core Crown spending at or around 30 percent of GDP, while running sustainable operating surpluses across the economic cycle.
keyNumber: Net core Crown debt below 20% of GDP within 5 years -> on track pre-COVID, target dropped in 2020; operating deficits every year from 2019/20 to 2022/23
statusReason: The rules were met in the first term and abandoned in the second. The debt and surplus targets were not in place at the end of the era.
whatHappened: Labour ran operating surpluses in its first two full years and was on track against the debt rule before the COVID-19 pandemic. From 2020 the rules were set aside. The government borrowed heavily for the wage subsidy and other pandemic support, the 20 percent debt ceiling was replaced with a looser range, and the books were in operating deficit every year from 2019/20 through to the October 2023 handover. The Greens, who had co-signed the rules in 2017, formally abandoned them in December 2019, before the pandemic.
contestedNote: Labour argues the rules were explicitly conditional on there being no major economic shock, and that abandoning them in 2020 was the intended response to a once-in-a-century pandemic, which the Treasury and Reserve Bank supported. Critics argue the deficits and debt continued well beyond the pandemic emergency, with the books still in deficit at the 2023 handover, and that no replacement debt anchor of comparable strictness was adopted. The underlying fiscal record is not disputed.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 fiscal plan / Budget Responsibility Rules (agreed with the Greens, March 2017)

promise: Sign up to and govern by Labour's Budget Responsibility Rules. These include reducing net core Crown debt to less than 20 percent of GDP within five years and keeping government spending at or below 30 percent of GDP.
keyNumber: Debt below 20% of GDP and spending at or below 30% of GDP -> rules formally scrapped by the Greens in December 2019
statusReason: The Greens explicitly and publicly dropped a fiscal commitment they had campaigned on, part-way through the term.
whatHappened: In December 2019, after an internal policy review, the Green Party's policy group voted to scrap the Budget Responsibility Rules and replace them with an economic policy allowing higher public spending. Co-leader James Shaw said the rules had limited the government's scope for change, and that the party would instead focus on wellbeing measures beyond GDP and a stronger public sector. The rules did not appear in the Greens' 2020 platform.
sourceDoc: Green Party 2017 election commitment (Budget Responsibility Rules co-signed with Labour, March 2017)

promise: Introduce Fair Pay Agreements, allowing unions and employers to bargain sector-wide minimum terms and conditions binding on all employers in an occupation or industry.
keyNumber: Fair Pay Agreements promised in 2017 -> Act passed October 2022; 0 agreements concluded before repeal in December 2023
statusReason: The system was legislated as promised, but only in the final year of the second term, and no agreement was ever concluded under it.
whatHappened: A Fair Pay Agreements Working Group was set up in June 2018. The Fair Pay Agreements Bill passed its third reading on 25 October 2022 by 76 votes to 43 and received royal assent on 1 November 2022, five years after the promise was first made. Bargaining was initiated in a small number of sectors. No fair pay agreement had been concluded when the incoming government repealed the Act on 20 December 2023.
contestedNote: One reading is that the promise was to legislate the framework, which happened in full, so this is close to delivered. The other is that the point of the policy was agreements covering workers, of which there were none, so it is closer to partly delivered. The five-year delay and the zero-agreement outcome are both undisputed.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 and 2020 manifestos / workplace relations policy

promise: Raise the adult minimum wage from $15.75 to $20 an hour by 2021, starting with $16.50 from 1 April 2018. Workplace Relations Minister Iain Lees-Galloway said on 22 December 2017: 'we are committed to increasing the minimum wage to $20 by 2021'.
keyNumber: $15.75 in 2017 -> $20.00 on 1 April 2021 as promised, and $22.70 by April 2023
statusReason: The exact rate was reached on the exact promised date.
whatHappened: The adult minimum wage rose to $16.50 on 1 April 2018, $17.70 in 2019, $18.90 in 2020 and $20.00 on 1 April 2021, hitting the target on schedule. It kept rising to $21.20 in 2022 and $22.70 in 2023, a cumulative increase of 44 percent over the six years of the Labour government.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 manifesto / workplace relations policy

promise: Abolish 90-day trial periods. They allow an employer to dismiss a new employee within their first 90 days, without the employee being able to bring a personal grievance for unjustified dismissal.
keyNumber: Abolish 90-day trials -> restricted to employers with fewer than 20 staff from 2019, reversed in December 2023
statusReason: Trial periods were narrowed rather than abolished, and the narrowing lasted less than five years.
whatHappened: The Employment Relations Amendment Act 2018 did not abolish trial periods. Instead it restricted them to employers with fewer than 20 employees, with the change taking effect in 2019. Coalition partner NZ First required the carve-out for small business. The incoming government reversed the restriction in December 2023, extending trials back to employers of all sizes.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 manifesto / workplace relations policy

promise: Establish a Regional Development (Provincial Growth) Fund of $1 billion a year to invest in the regions.
keyNumber: $1 billion a year for the regions -> $3 billion Provincial Growth Fund over three years from February 2018
statusReason: A fund of the promised scale was established and spent, but at $3 billion over three years rather than $1 billion every year of the term. It did not survive the change of government arrangements in 2020.
whatHappened: The Provincial Growth Fund was launched in February 2018 with $3 billion allocated over three years. NZ First minister Shane Jones ran it as Regional Economic Development Minister. It included dedicated allocations such as $100 million for Māori economic development. Much of the remaining money was redirected into COVID-19 infrastructure and redeployment packages in 2020, and the fund did not continue in its original form after NZ First left Parliament at the 2020 election. Job-creation claims made for the fund were disputed at the time.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement, 24 October 2017

promise: Reform the Reserve Bank Act so that monetary policy is directed at maximising employment alongside price stability, and move decision-making to a committee.
keyNumber: Employment added to the RBNZ mandate -> legislated in 2018; removed again on 20 December 2023
statusReason: The mandate change and the committee structure were both legislated within the first term, as agreed.
whatHappened: The Policy Targets Agreement signed in 2018 added 'supporting maximum sustainable employment' to the Reserve Bank's objectives. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Monetary Policy) Amendment Act 2018 wrote the dual mandate into legislation and created a statutory Monetary Policy Committee, which began operating in 2019. The dual mandate was carried into the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 2021. The incoming government removed it on 20 December 2023.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement, 24 October 2017

promise: Ban overseas buyers who are not residents from purchasing existing residential homes in New Zealand.
keyNumber: Ban on non-resident foreign buyers of existing homes -> in force from 22 October 2018
statusReason: Legislated within the first year of the term, and still in force in August 2026.
whatHappened: The Overseas Investment Amendment Act 2018 classified residential land as sensitive land requiring consent. That in effect barred most non-resident foreign buyers from purchasing existing homes from 22 October 2018. Australian and Singaporean buyers remained exempt under existing free trade agreements. The ban survived the 2023 change of government. National campaigned on partially lifting it for homes over $2 million, but agreed in the National-NZ First coalition agreement that its tax plan 'will not include a repeal of the foreign buyer's residential property ban'.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 manifesto / Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement, 24 October 2017

promise: Return the government's books to an operating surplus of $2.9 billion in the 2026/27 year. Fund this by spending restraint and reduced growth in new expenditure rather than higher borrowing.
keyNumber: $2.9 billion surplus in 2026/27 -> $11.4 billion deficit forecast for 2026/27; first surplus now forecast for 2028/29
statusReason: The specific surplus year and amount promised in the 2023 fiscal plan will not be met. The 2026/27 year is now forecast to be an $11.4 billion deficit.
whatHappened: The government changed its headline fiscal measure in 2024 to OBEGALx, which excludes ACC. Nicola Willis publicly conceded the 2026/27 surplus was unlikely to be met, saying she 'wouldn't describe myself as optimistic' about it. Budget 2026, delivered on 28 May 2026, forecast OBEGALx deficits of $11.9 billion in 2025/26 and $11.4 billion in 2026/27. The first surplus of $2.6 billion is not due until 2028/29. That is a year earlier than the December 2025 half-year update had projected, but two years later than promised. Net core Crown debt is forecast to peak at 46.1 percent of GDP in 2027/28 before easing to 44.4 percent by 2029/30.
sourceDoc: National 2023 fiscal plan

promise: Fund the $14.6 billion tax package without additional borrowing. Use roughly $800 million a year of public service back-office savings, $2.3 billion from the Climate Emergency Response Fund and new revenue measures.
keyNumber: About $800 million a year of back-office savings -> $7.47 billion of savings over four years identified in the December 2023 mini-budget
statusReason: The savings were found and the tax package was funded without extra borrowing. The mix of measures used differed materially from the one put to voters.
whatHappened: The December 2023 mini-budget identified $7.47 billion of savings over four years. These included cancelling the Climate Emergency Response Fund ($2 billion), removing depreciation deductions for commercial buildings ($2.3 billion), $400 million from reduced consultant spending and $600 million from departmental cost reductions. In January 2024 departments were told to find baseline savings of 6.5 or 7.5 percent towards a $1.5 billion a year target. The package was delivered as fiscally neutral, but two of the three funding legs changed. The promised foreign buyer tax was dropped, and the gap was helped by the commercial building depreciation change and the retained 'app tax', neither of which National had campaigned on as revenue for the package.
sourceDoc: National 2023 manifesto / 'Back Pocket Boost' fiscal plan, 30 August 2023

promise: Remove 'supporting maximum sustainable employment' from the Reserve Bank's remit, so that monetary policy focuses solely on price stability.
keyNumber: Dual mandate removed -> legislated 13 December 2023, in force 20 December 2023
statusReason: Legislated within the first month of the term exactly as set out in the coalition agreement and 100-day plan.
whatHappened: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Economic Objective) Amendment Bill was the first bill passed by the new Parliament. It went through all stages on 13 December 2023 and came into force on 20 December 2023. The accompanying Remit removes the employment objective, but retains employment as one of the variables in which the Monetary Policy Committee should seek to avoid unnecessary volatility. Treasury's regulatory impact statement on the change was published in November 2023.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement and National's 100-day plan, November 2023

promise: Repeal the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022 by Christmas 2023.
keyNumber: Repeal by Christmas 2023 -> repealed 20 December 2023
statusReason: Repealed within the promised timeframe and before Christmas 2023.
whatHappened: The Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill passed its third reading under urgency on 14 December 2023, received royal assent on 19 December and took effect on 20 December 2023. No fair pay agreement had been concluded under the Act, so none were cancelled. Unions, Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori opposed the repeal. Business groups supported it.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement and National's 100-day plan, November 2023

promise: Restore 90-day employment trial periods for businesses of all sizes, reversing Labour's restriction to employers with fewer than 20 staff.
keyNumber: 90-day trials limited to employers with under 20 staff -> extended to all employers from December 2023
statusReason: Legislated within the first month of the term as promised.
whatHappened: Amending legislation passed in December 2023, and 90-day trial periods became available to all employers from 23 December 2023. It was one of the first measures completed under the 100-day plan.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement and National's 100-day plan, November 2023

promise: Establish a Ministry for Regulation to cut red tape, funded by disestablishing the Productivity Commission. Pass a Regulatory Standards Act setting principles for good law-making.
keyNumber: Ministry for Regulation and a Regulatory Standards Act -> ministry established 2024; Act passed November 2025
statusReason: Both the new ministry and the Act were delivered within the term, in the form set out in the coalition agreement.
whatHappened: The Ministry for Regulation was established in 2024 with ACT leader David Seymour as Minister for Regulation, and the New Zealand Productivity Commission was disestablished to fund it. The Regulatory Standards Bill passed its second and third readings in November 2025 and received royal assent, becoming the Regulatory Standards Act 2025. The Act sets principles covering the rule of law, personal liberties, property rights and taxation. It also establishes a Regulatory Standards Board to consider complaints about existing law. ACT had pursued the policy for around 20 years, and Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori strongly opposed it.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement, 24 November 2023

promise: Shrink the public sector back to 2017 levels by reducing non-essential back-office functions.
keyNumber: Public sector back to 2017 levels -> 64,535 public service FTEs at March 2026, versus a December 2023 peak of 65,699 and a June 2017 base roughly a third smaller
statusReason: Public service headcount at March 2026 was only about 1,200 below its December 2023 peak and remained far above 2017 levels. The government's own new target date for a smaller public service is 2029.
whatHappened: Departments were directed in January 2024 to find baseline savings of 6.5 or 7.5 percent, the higher figure applying to agencies that had grown more than 50 percent since 2017. RNZ counted around 9,500 public sector roles going by the end of 2024. Public service full-time-equivalent staffing fell from a peak of 65,699 in the December 2023 quarter to 62,654 in June 2025, but then rose again to 64,535 by March 2026. At June 2024 the public service was still about 34 percent larger than at June 2017. In May 2026 the government announced a further plan to cut about 8,700 roles, setting a target of no more than 55,000 full-time equivalents by July 2029, four years after the end of this parliamentary term.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement, 24 November 2023

promise: Freeze the adult minimum wage for three years.
keyNumber: Three-year minimum wage freeze -> minimum wage rose from $22.70 to $23.95 between April 2023 and April 2026
statusReason: ACT's policy was not written into the coalition agreements, and the minimum wage was increased in each of the three years.
whatHappened: The freeze was not adopted in the coalition agreements. The adult minimum wage rose from $22.70 to $23.15 on 1 April 2024 (2.0 percent), to $23.50 on 1 April 2025 (1.5 percent) and to $23.95 on 1 April 2026 (1.9 percent). The increases were much smaller than the 5.8 to 7.3 percent annual rises under the previous government, but the wage was not frozen in any year of the term.
sourceDoc: ACT 2023 election policy

promise: Lift New Zealand into the top 10 OECD countries for GDP growth. Do this through lower taxes, deep cuts to government spending and the removal of programmes ACT considered wasteful.
keyNumber: Top 10 OECD for GDP growth -> 1.2% annual growth in the year to June 2026 and unemployment at 5.6%, a decade high
statusReason: Growth of 1.2 percent in the year to June 2026, following a recession, is not consistent with a top-10 OECD growth ranking, and unemployment rose over the term.
whatHappened: The economy contracted through much of 2024 and recovered only slowly. Unemployment rose steadily across the term, reaching 5.6 percent in the June 2026 quarter, the highest reading in more than a decade, with 171,000 people unemployed. Underutilisation was 13.8 percent, or about 440,000 people wanting more work. Treasury's Budget 2026 forecasts put annual GDP growth at 1.2 percent for the year to June 2026, rising to 3.2 percent by June 2028, with nominal GDP growth forecasts revised slightly down from earlier updates.
contestedNote: ACT could argue the goal was framed as a medium-term ambition rather than a single-term deliverable, and that the coalition did not adopt most of its spending and tax programme, so the target was never properly tested. Critics point out that the party campaigned on it as the measure of its economic programme, and that on any within-term reading the target was missed. The growth and unemployment figures themselves are not disputed.
sourceDoc: ACT 2023 election policy / alternative budget

promise: Establish a $1.2 billion Regional Infrastructure Fund over three years, reviving the model of the Provincial Growth Fund.
keyNumber: $1.2 billion Regional Infrastructure Fund over three years -> established in Budget 2024
statusReason: A fund of the promised size was established in the first Budget of the term with the promised minister and scope.
whatHappened: The Regional Infrastructure Fund was established with $1.2 billion in Budget 2024. NZ First minister Shane Jones administers it as Minister for Regional Development. Allocations to flood protection, water storage, energy and regional transport projects have continued through the term.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement, 24 November 2023

promise: Return the Budget to surplus in 2024/25. Hold total government expenses to no more than $165 billion and core government expenses to no more than $133 billion for 2024/25.
keyNumber: Budget surplus in 2024/25 -> deficits in every year; first surplus now forecast for 2028/29
statusReason: No surplus was achieved in 2024/25 or any later year of the term, and the forecast surplus is four years later than promised.
whatHappened: The books remained in deficit through 2024/25 and 2025/26. Budget 2026 forecast OBEGALx deficits of $11.9 billion in 2025/26 and $11.4 billion in 2026/27, with the first surplus not expected until 2028/29, four years later than NZ First's target. Budget 2026 held new operating spending to $2.1 billion against a $2.4 billion allowance and cut the bond programme by $6 billion over four years, the first downward revision since 2021.
sourceDoc: New Zealand First 2023 Policy Manifesto ('Back to Black')

promise: Lift the adult minimum wage to at least $25 an hour, offset for employers through business tax concessions.
keyNumber: At least $25 an hour -> $23.95 at 1 April 2026
statusReason: The minimum wage was $23.95 at April 2026, more than a dollar short of the promised floor, and the tax offset mechanism was never introduced.
whatHappened: The minimum wage rose to $23.15 on 1 April 2024, $23.50 on 1 April 2025 and $23.95 on 1 April 2026. The offsetting business tax concessions were not introduced. NZ First's target was not written into the National-NZ First coalition agreement.
sourceDoc: New Zealand First 2023 Policy Manifesto

promise: Rebuild KiwiSaver. Restore the KiwiSaver kickstart with auto-enrolment at birth from July 2024, pay a $250 annual state contribution matched by the individual until age 18, and raise the government contribution to $1,540. Separately, redefine a small or medium enterprise from 19 to 50 full-time equivalent employees, and allow 100 percent depreciation on business equipment worth up to $20,000.
keyNumber: KiwiSaver kickstart from July 2024 and a $1,540 government contribution -> neither introduced as at August 2026
statusReason: No element of the KiwiSaver package or the small business tax changes was adopted in the coalition agreement or legislated during the term.
whatHappened: None of the KiwiSaver commitments were written into the National-NZ First coalition agreement, and none had been legislated as at August 2026. The SME redefinition and the $20,000 full-expensing rule were also not adopted. Regulatory relief for business was pursued instead through ACT's Ministry for Regulation and Regulatory Standards Act.
sourceDoc: New Zealand First 2023 Policy Manifesto

promise: Stimulate up to $1 billion of investment in low carbon industries by 2020, through a proposed Green Investment Fund.
keyNumber: Up to $1b of low carbon investment stimulated by 2020 -> NZGIF capitalised at $100m in 2019, about half committed by 2020; capital reached $700m by May 2023
statusReason: The institution was created and its capital grew, but the $1 billion by 2020 figure in the agreement was not close to being met on that date.
whatHappened: Cabinet agreed to establish New Zealand Green Investment Finance Limited in late 2018. The company was capitalised with $100 million and began investing in 2019. It had committed roughly half its initial capital by 2020, far short of the $1 billion of stimulated investment named for that year. Capital was later increased to $400 million, and on 9 May 2023 Climate Change Minister James Shaw announced a further $300 million, taking total capital to $700 million. NZGIF's investments included EV charging infrastructure, solar on schools and electric buses, with estimated lifetime emissions reductions of 580,000 to 710,000 tonnes CO2e as at June 2022.
contestedNote: The government's reading is that NZGIF mobilises private capital at a multiple of its own balance sheet, so the total investment stimulated exceeds its capitalisation. Critics note that the agreement named a $1 billion figure and a 2020 date, and that on any measure of capital deployed by 2020 the figure was in the tens of millions.
sourceDoc: Labour-Green Confidence and Supply Agreement 2017, policy goal 4, stimulate up to $1 billion of investment in low carbon industries by 2020

promise: Introduce a wealth tax on net assets over $1 million, new top personal income tax rates, and a Guaranteed Minimum Income of at least $325 a week for everyone not in full-time paid work.
keyNumber: Wealth tax over $1m net assets and a $325 a week Guaranteed Minimum Income -> neither included in the 2020 Cooperation Agreement
statusReason: The party's flagship 2020 policy was excluded from the cooperation agreement negotiated after the election and never became government policy.
whatHappened: The Poverty Action Plan was the Greens' central 2020 election policy. Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern publicly ruled out a wealth tax during the campaign, and repeated that position after Labour won an outright majority on 17 October 2020. The 2020 Labour-Greens Cooperation Agreement, signed 1 November 2020, contains no tax or income-support commitments at all. Its cooperation areas are limited to climate, biodiversity and waste, and homelessness, warm homes and child and youth mental health. Neither a wealth tax nor a Guaranteed Minimum Income was introduced during the term.
sourceDoc: Green Party 2020 Poverty Action Plan, wealth tax, new top income tax rates and a Guaranteed Minimum Income

promise: Establish a select committee inquiry into banking competition, focused on how competitive the sector is, customer services and profitability.
keyNumber: Select committee inquiry promised -> held 2024-25; Government agreed or partly agreed to all 19 recommendations on 13 Nov 2025
statusReason: Parliament held the inquiry with the promised focus. It reported, and it drew a full government response.
whatHappened: Parliament's Finance and Expenditure Committee launched an inquiry into banking competition in 2024. It worked alongside the Primary Production Committee on rural banking, and the Reserve Bank and other regulators made submissions from September 2024. The Commerce Commission's separate market study into personal banking reported in August 2024. The Government responded to the Finance and Expenditure Committee's inquiry on 13 November 2025, agreeing or partly agreeing to all 19 of the committee's recommendations. The response focused on standardising bank disclosure to make comparison easier, strengthening Kiwibank's competitive position through more investment, and reducing regulatory barriers to new entrants and non-bank deposit takers.
sourceDoc: National. NZ First Coalition Agreement, 24 November 2023 (Economy)

promise: Increase funding for IRD tax audits to urgently expand Inland Revenue's tax audit capacity.
keyNumber: Increase IRD audit funding -> $116m over four years from Budget 2024; forecast $526m a year in extra revenue
statusReason: Audit and compliance funding rose in the first Budget of the term and again in later Budgets, with published capacity and revenue targets.
whatHappened: Budget 2024 gave Inland Revenue $116 million over four years for compliance and audit work, taking effect from July 2024, and more compliance investment followed in Budgets 2025 and 2026. Inland Revenue's published figures show administration funding rising to $79 million a year from 2026/27, with forecast extra Crown revenue of $526 million a year plus about $18 million a year in student loan repayments. Inland Revenue's performance targets for revenue from compliance interventions rose to $1,228.1 million in 2025/26 and $1,334.1 million in 2026/27. Results are reported quarterly.
sourceDoc: National. NZ First Coalition Agreement, 24 November 2023 (Economy)

promise: Commit to moderate increases to the minimum wage every year.
statusReason: The minimum wage rose in every year of the term, at the modest scale the agreement described.
whatHappened: The adult minimum wage rose in each year of the term: to $23.15 an hour from 1 April 2024, to $23.50 from 1 April 2025, and to $23.95 from 1 April 2026. Workplace Relations and Safety Minister Brooke van Velden announced the 2026 increase on 12 December 2025. She described the 2 per cent rise as a balance between the cost of living and business costs, and said it would benefit about 122,500 workers. The increases were around or slightly below the rate of inflation in each year, which is what the word 'moderate' in the agreement signalled.
sourceDoc: National. NZ First Coalition Agreement, 24 November 2023 (Employment and Immigration)

promise: Make the first year of tertiary study or training fee-free from 2018 (up to about $12,000), then extend free study to two years and then to three years.
keyNumber: 3 years free study promised -> 1 year delivered; extension abandoned in 2020
statusReason: One year of free study was delivered and kept for the whole term. The promised extension to three years was dropped and never happened.
whatHappened: The first year became fee-free from 1 January 2018. There were 47,000 students and trainees in the first year, and student debt fell by $194.2 million between 2017 and 2018. Uptake was lower than forecast. The scheduled extensions to two and then three years were abandoned in 2020. By 2019 the scheme cost $254 million a year, and Budget 2022 allocated $387 million. Later research found the policy did little to widen access, with participation from the wealthiest decile rising 43% between 2017 and 2022.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 election campaign policy on tertiary fees

promise: Scrap National Standards for literacy and numeracy, and primary school league tables.
statusReason: Done in full, immediately and as promised.
whatHappened: The incoming government abolished National Standards and the associated primary school league tables in December 2017, in its first weeks in office. Schools moved to their own assessment and reporting arrangements. Nationally comparable standardised assessment of primary literacy and numeracy did not return until the next government reintroduced twice-yearly assessments and a phonics check from 2026.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 election policy on assessment in schools

promise: End the charter (partnership) school model, stop any new charter schools and bring existing ones into the state system.
keyNumber: 11 partnership schools with 1,441 students -> all converted to state schools by 2019
statusReason: The charter school model was closed within the term, exactly as promised.
whatHappened: Legislation was passed preventing the establishment of new partnership schools. The 11 existing schools were given the option of becoming designated character or special character state schools, which they did over 2018 and 2019. At its peak the partnership school programme had 1,441 students across 11 schools. The next government reinstated the model under the Education and Training Amendment Act 2024.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 election policy on partnership (charter) schools

promise: Introduce and scale up a free healthy school lunch programme for students in the schools with the greatest need.
keyNumber: 2019 pilot -> more than 200,000 students fed daily, at about $8 per student
statusReason: The programme was set up and scaled to more than 200,000 students a day within the term.
whatHappened: A pilot began in 2019 and Ka Ora, Ka Ako was expanded from 2020. It used mostly local suppliers and school-based kitchens, at a cost of roughly $8 per student per day. By the time of the handover the programme was feeding more than 200,000 students a day. The next government kept the programme but redesigned it around a $3 per meal target from the start of the 2025 school year.
sourceDoc: Labour's Ka Ora, Ka Ako Healthy School Lunches programme, piloted 2019 and expanded at Budget 2020

promise: Merge the 16 polytechnics and institutes of technology into a single national institute of skills and technology by April 2020.
keyNumber: 16 polytechnics merged into 1 entity from 1 April 2020 -> 10 re-established as regional institutions from 1 January 2026
statusReason: The merger promised was legislated and the single entity created on schedule. Its later unwinding was the act of a different government.
whatHappened: Te Pūkenga | New Zealand Institute of Skills and Technology was set up on 1 April 2020. The 16 polytechnics and the industry training organisations' training arms were brought into it in stages. The merged entity struggled financially and was never fully unified before the change of government. The incoming coalition began disestablishing it in its 100-day plan. Ten regional polytechnics were re-established as standalone institutions from 1 January 2026, with four remaining inside a transitional federation.
sourceDoc: Labour's Reform of Vocational Education, announced 2019 and carried into the 2020 term

promise: Make tertiary education more affordable for students and reduce the number of students living in financial hardship.
keyNumber: 1 year fee-free delivered from 2018; planned extension to 3 years abandoned in 2020
statusReason: A significant affordability measure was delivered and sustained, but the expansion stopped in 2020. Independent evaluation found little effect on students facing the greatest hardship.
whatHappened: The first year of tertiary study became fee-free from 1 January 2018. In its first year of operation it cut student debt by $194.2 million between 2017 and 2018. The promised extension to two and then three fee-free years was abandoned in 2020, so support stayed capped at one year for the rest of both terms. Later evaluation found the scheme did little to widen access. The share of funding going to students from lower deciles shrank, and participation from the wealthiest decile rose 43% between 2017 and 2022.
sourceDoc: Labour-Green Confidence and Supply Agreement 2017

promise: Ban the use of cellphones in schools.
keyNumber: Phone ban in force from Term 2 2024
statusReason: The ban became a legal requirement for all state schools within the promised 100 days, and took effect in Term 2 2024.
whatHappened: The Government announced the policy on 1 December 2023 as part of its 100-day plan, and confirmed the detail on 19 December 2023. From the start of Term 2 2024, regulations required schools to ensure students do not use phones during the school day, with limited exemptions. The requirement has stayed in force since.
sourceDoc: Coalition 100-day plan, National-ACT Coalition Agreement and National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023

promise: Require primary and intermediate schools to teach an hour of reading, an hour of writing and an hour of maths a day, starting in 2024.
keyNumber: 1 hour each of reading, writing and maths a day from 2024; 98% of schools teaching the new English and maths learning areas by Term 1 2025
statusReason: The requirement was imposed on the promised timetable, and independent review found near-universal uptake of the associated teaching changes.
whatHappened: The requirement was announced on 1 December 2023 as part of the 100-day plan and applied to primary schools from 2024. The rewritten English and maths curricula and a structured literacy requirement reinforced it. In its 2025 review the Education Review Office found 98% of schools had begun teaching the new English (Years 0-6) and maths (Years 0-8) learning areas from Term 1 2025. It also found 88% of teachers had changed how they teach English and 85% how they teach maths.
sourceDoc: Coalition 100-day plan, National-ACT Coalition Agreement and National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023

promise: Appoint an expert group to redesign the English and maths curricula for primary school students. Refocus the curriculum on academic achievement, including a structured approach to teaching reading.
keyNumber: New English and maths curricula compulsory from Term 1 2026; other learning areas phased in 2027-2028
statusReason: The curriculum rewrite was completed and made compulsory for English and maths within the term. The remaining subjects were released and scheduled.
whatHappened: Rewritten English and maths curricula for Years 0-8 were introduced from Term 1 2025, alongside structured literacy, Ministry-funded workbooks and lesson plans, and teacher professional development. Final Years 0-10 English and maths documents were released on 20 October 2025 and became compulsory in Term 1 2026. The remaining learning areas were released from late October 2025 and phased in during 2027 and 2028. Updated science and social sciences curricula were released in August 2026. ERO found 92% of Years 0-3 teachers consistently using phonics instruction and 82% of teachers having accessed structured literacy professional development. It also reported that small and rural schools were less likely to have implementation plans, and that Māori-medium settings struggled to access suitable resources.
sourceDoc: Coalition 100-day plan and National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023

promise: Introduce standardised assessments in schools and require regular reporting to parents.
keyNumber: Twice-yearly standardised assessment for Years 3-8 and a mandatory phonics check from 2026
statusReason: Mandatory standardised assessment and reporting were in place from 2026, as the agreement required. The wider qualifications replacement is scheduled beyond this term.
whatHappened: From 2026 a phonics check became mandatory, and twice-yearly standardised assessments in reading, writing and maths were required for Years 3-8. These use the new SMART assessment system alongside PATs and e-asTTle. Separately, the Government confirmed the replacement of NCEA. NCEA Level 1 is removed from 2028, in favour of curriculum-focused Year 11 learning and a foundational literacy and numeracy award. New subject-based Year 12 and Year 13 qualifications start in 2029 and 2030 respectively.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023
