promise: Reintroduce partnership schools and introduce a policy to allow state schools to become partnership schools. Budget 2024 funded $153 million over four years for 15 new charter schools and 35 state school conversions.
keyNumber: 15 new schools and 35 conversions funded -> 16 charter schools and 1,471 students by March 2026; only 6 state schools interested in conversion in the April 2025 round
statusReason: The model was reinstated in law and more charter schools are now open than under the previous partnership scheme. But the funded target of 35 state school conversions was nowhere near met.
whatHappened: The Education and Training Amendment Act 2024 passed on 25 August 2024 and came into force in October 2024, with applications opened from July 2024. The first charter schools opened in 2025. As at 1 March 2026 there were 16 charter schools with 1,471 students, and the first seven had grown from 215 to over 658 students. Four more schools were due to open later in 2026, and legislation was passed in June 2026 to let sponsors run multiple schools. Conversions proved much harder than expected: only six state schools expressed interest in the April 2025 conversion round, and David Seymour publicly acknowledged conversions were tougher than anticipated. Charter per-student funding in 2024 was about $8,278 (primary) and $10,741 (secondary), slightly below the state equivalents.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023 and coalition 100-day plan

promise: Improve the cost-effectiveness of the school lunch programme.
keyNumber: About $8 per meal -> $3 per meal target; $134m savings claimed for 2025, but only about 50% of meals met nutrition standards May-Dec 2025
statusReason: Large cost savings were achieved and the programme kept feeding more than 200,000 students a day. But the Auditor-General could not verify the savings claims, and found serious nutrition, waste and delivery failures.
whatHappened: On 8 May 2024 Associate Minister David Seymour announced a redesigned Healthy School Lunches Programme, projected to save about $107 million a year. Budget 2024 allocated $478 million and extended coverage to up to 10,000 two to five year olds. A new alternative provision model started at the beginning of the 2025 school year, run by the School Lunch Collective (Compass, Libelle and Gilmours) at a target of $3 a meal against roughly $8 previously. Delivery problems followed: late and missed deliveries, meals arriving after lunchtime, and complaints including halal meals containing ham. Libelle went into liquidation. The Auditor-General reported in 2026 that the Ministry claimed $134 million of savings in 2025 and expected $120 million in 2026, but did not have reliable ways to measure and monitor performance. Only just over 50% of meals assessed between May and December 2025 complied with nutrition standards, waste ran at 8.82kg per 100 lunches against a target of 7kg, and surplus rates hit 17% against a 10% maximum. Funding of $212 million was committed to continue the programme.
contestedNote: The Government's reading is that the commitment was to cost-effectiveness, and that more than $100 million a year was saved while student numbers were maintained and early learning coverage was added. The Auditor-General's reading is that the savings figures cannot be relied on because monitoring was inadequate, and that quality, nutrition compliance and delivery reliability fell well short. Both accounts accept the cost per meal fell from about $8 to $3.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023

promise: Stop first year Fees Free and replace it with a final year Fees Free, with no change before 2025.
keyNumber: First year Fees Free -> final year Fees Free from Jan 2025 -> scheme abolished from end of 2026
statusReason: The promised switch to final-year Fees Free was delivered on time in 2025. The coalition then abolished the scheme entirely in 2026, so the promised entitlement no longer exists at the end of the term.
whatHappened: The switch was legislated and took effect from 1 January 2025. Students starting study from 2025 became eligible for a fee subsidy of up to about $12,000 in their final year rather than their first, saving roughly $130 million a year. Then on 8 May 2026 Finance Minister Nicola Willis and Winston Peters confirmed the whole scheme would end in Budget 2026. That removes about $350 million a year of spending and saves more than $1 billion over the forecast period. Fees Free finishes at the end of 2026, and those completing a qualification in 2026 can still claim up to 31 December 2027. Students who began study in 2024 and 2025 expecting a final-year entitlement lose it.
contestedNote: One reading is that the promise was delivered exactly as written: the switch happened in 2025 with no change before then, and the later abolition is a separate policy decision backed by evidence the scheme did not widen access. The other reading is that the commitment was to a final-year Fees Free entitlement. Students who arranged their study around it had it withdrawn before they could use it, so the promise was not kept in substance.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023 (also in the National-ACT agreement and the 100-day plan)

promise: Begin disestablishing Te Pūkenga and return polytechnics to regional governance.
keyNumber: 16 merged polytechnics -> 10 re-established regionally from 1 Jan 2026, 4 still in a transitional federation
statusReason: The merger has been unwound and ten polytechnics are independent again. But four institutions remained under the transitional entity at the start of 2026, so the change was not complete.
whatHappened: Disestablishment began in the 100-day plan. Restructuring during 2025 involved more than 150 job cuts and a campus closure. The Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill was passed in October 2025, and ten regional polytechnics were re-established as standalone institutions from 1 January 2026. Four (NorthTec, WITT, Whitireia/WelTec and Tai Poutini Polytechnic) remained inside Te Pūkenga while working towards viability, with Te Pūkenga continuing as a transitional entity for up to a year.
sourceDoc: Coalition 100-day plan and National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023

promise: 80% of students to be present for more than 90% of the term. Enforce compulsory education by collecting and publishing attendance data centrally.
keyNumber: 80% attending regularly promised -> 59.0% (Term 1 2023) to 68.8% (Term 1 2026)
statusReason: Term unfinished. The reporting and enforcement machinery was delivered and attendance has risen almost 10 points from the baseline, but the 80% target has not been reached.
whatHappened: Daily school attendance data began to be collected and published from Term 1 2025. Attendance Management Plans became mandatory for schools from Term 1 2026, and a reformed Attendance Service model launched the same term, supporting close to double the number of students. Regular attendance rose from a Term 1 2023 baseline of 59.0% to 65.9% in Term 1 2025 and 68.8% in Term 1 2026, still 11.2 percentage points below the target. The Government reported Term 2 2026 in-person attendance as the highest since 2016.
sourceDoc: Government Targets (Target 6), set March 2024; truancy commitments in the National-ACT and National-NZ First coalition agreements

promise: 80% of Year 8 students to be at or above the expected curriculum level for their age in reading, writing and maths by December 2030.
keyNumber: 80% of Year 8 students at or above curriculum level by December 2030
statusReason: Term unfinished and the target date is 2030. The delivery machinery has been built, but the outcome cannot yet be judged.
whatHappened: The target was formally adopted as one of the nine government targets. The supporting programme is in place: the rewritten English and maths curricula compulsory from Term 1 2026, structured literacy, an hour a day of each of reading, writing and maths in primary schools, a mandatory phonics check, and twice-yearly standardised assessment for Years 3-8 from 2026. Because nationally consistent standardised assessment only began in 2026, comparable Year 8 achievement data across the term is limited. The target date is 2030, beyond this parliamentary term.
sourceDoc: Coalition 100-day plan and Government Targets (Target 7), set March 2024

promise: Restore balance to the Aotearoa New Zealand's Histories curriculum. Refocus the curriculum on academic achievement rather than ideology, including removing and replacing the gender, sexuality and relationship-based education guidelines.
keyNumber: Rewritten social sciences curriculum released Aug 2026, in force from 2027-2028
statusReason: Term unfinished. The rewritten social sciences and science curricula were released in August 2026 but do not take effect until 2027 and 2028.
whatHappened: The histories content sits within the social sciences learning area, which was rewritten as part of the wider Years 0-10 curriculum programme. Updated science and social sciences curricula were released on 12 August 2026. The new learning areas are to be phased in during 2027 and 2028 rather than taking effect during this term. The relationships and sexuality education content sits within the health and physical education learning area. That area is part of the same phased rewrite and had not come into force by August 2026.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023 (also in the National-ACT agreement)

promise: Amend the Education and Training Act 2020 so that tertiary education providers receiving taxpayer funding must commit to a free speech policy.
keyNumber: Free speech policy required of taxpayer-funded tertiary providers -> legislated Nov 2025, university statements adopted by April 2026
statusReason: The Act was passed and policies are in place. But the duty applies to universities rather than to all tertiary providers receiving taxpayer funding, as the agreement was worded.
whatHappened: The Education and Training Amendment Act 2025 passed in November 2025. It requires university councils to protect and promote academic freedom and freedom of expression, to adopt a statement on freedom of expression within six months of commencement, and to maintain a complaints procedure. From their 2026 annual reports, universities must report on how the council has complied and on the number and nature of complaints received. Universities adopted their freedom of expression statements by April 2026. As enacted, the duties apply to universities rather than to every taxpayer-funded tertiary provider. ACT leader David Seymour drove the work, and in November 2025 directed officials to consult free speech advocacy groups on the drafting.
sourceDoc: National. ACT Coalition Agreement, 24 November 2023

promise: Achieve 100 per cent renewable electricity generation by 2030 in a normal hydrological year, bringing forward the previous 2035 goal by five years.
keyNumber: 100 per cent renewable electricity by 2030 -> 88.1 per cent in 2023, 85.5 per cent in 2024
statusReason: The renewable share rose materially during the two terms. But no settled pathway to 100 per cent existed at the handover, and the enabling storage project was never decided.
whatHappened: The renewable share of generation was about 84 per cent when the target was announced in September 2020. It reached 88.1 per cent in 2023, the year of the handover. It then fell to 85.5 per cent in 2024, as low hydro inflows and falling gas supply pushed coal generation up 118 per cent year on year to 5.1 per cent of total generation. The main enabling project, the NZ Battery pumped hydro scheme at Lake Onslow, was stopped in late 2023 before any build decision. The incoming Government did not adopt the 2030 target.
contestedNote: One reading: the target date of 2030 fell outside the term, and the renewable share did rise, so the promise could not fairly be marked failed at the handover. Another: no funded pathway to the last 10-15 percentage points was ever settled, the dry-year solution was abandoned, and the 2024 fall back to 85.5 per cent shows the system was still dependent on gas and coal.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 campaign energy policy, announced 17 September 2020

promise: Spend $70 million investigating a pumped hydro scheme at Lake Onslow (the NZ Battery project) to solve the dry-year problem, and decide whether to build it.
keyNumber: $70m investigation plus a build decision -> studies delivered, no build decision, investigations stopped late 2023
statusReason: The investigation the promise funded did take place. But the decision it was supposed to lead to was never made before the term ended.
whatHappened: The NZ Battery project ran from 2020. It produced feasibility, hydrology, landscape and cultural studies on Lake Onslow, and later broadened to alternative sites and non-hydro options, including grid batteries, green peaker generation and carbon capture. No build decision was ever made. MBIE records that the Government stopped the Lake Onslow investigations in late 2023, and the incoming Government confirmed in December 2023 that it was dumping the project. MBIE continued dry-year security work inside its wider electricity system programme.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 campaign energy policy. NZ Battery / Lake Onslow investigation

promise: Introduce a Winter Energy Payment of up to $700 a year for couples and people with dependants, and $450 for single people. Pay it automatically to superannuitants and main benefit recipients over the colder months, starting 1 July 2018.
keyNumber: $450 single / $700 couples from 1 July 2018 -> delivered on time to over 1 million people
statusReason: Introduced on the promised date at the promised rates to the promised group.
whatHappened: The Families Package legislation passed in December 2017 and the Winter Energy Payment began on 1 July 2018, at the promised rates of $450 for single people and $700 for couples and people with dependants. It reached over a million people in its first year. It ran from 1 July to 30 September in 2018, and from 1 May to 1 October in later years. It was temporarily doubled in 2020 during COVID-19, and remained in place at the October 2023 handover.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 Families Package. Winter Energy Payment

promise: Request the Climate Commission to plan the transition to 100 per cent renewable electricity by 2035, including geothermal, in a normal hydrological year.
keyNumber: Plan for 100 per cent renewable electricity by 2035 -> no binding pathway adopted; 88.1 per cent renewable in 2023
statusReason: The Commission was created and did advise on electricity. But no 100 per cent transition plan with a defined pathway was adopted.
whatHappened: The Climate Change Commission was established under the Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Act 2019, and electricity decarbonisation formed part of its advice on emissions budgets. In September 2020 Labour replaced the 2035 goal with a 100 per cent by 2030 aspiration, and no binding 2035 transition pathway was legislated. Renewable generation was 88.1 per cent in 2023, fell to 85.5 per cent in 2024, and hit a record quarterly high of 96.4 per cent in the December 2025 quarter.
contestedNote: On one reading the procedural commitment, to ask the Commission to plan the transition, was met: the Commission was established and advised on electricity decarbonisation. On another, the specific 2035 target was quietly replaced by a different aspiration and then dropped entirely, so the transition plan the Greens negotiated for never happened.
sourceDoc: Labour-Greens confidence & supply agreement 2017

promise: Scrap the Lake Onslow pumped hydro (NZ Battery) project.
keyNumber: Scrap Lake Onslow -> investigations stopped December 2023
statusReason: The project was stopped within weeks of taking office, as promised.
whatHappened: The Government confirmed in December 2023 that it was stopping the NZ Battery project and the Lake Onslow investigations. It described the scheme as a $16 billion project and the spending on it as wasteful. MBIE folded remaining dry-year security work into its wider electricity system programme. Energy academics criticised the decision as short-sighted, and by 2026 there was renewed public discussion of reviving an Onslow-type scheme, but no project was restarted.
sourceDoc: National 2023 campaign commitment to scrap the Lake Onslow / NZ Battery project

promise: Reverse the 2018 ban on new offshore oil and gas exploration outside onshore Taranaki, with legislation passed by the end of 2024.
keyNumber: Legislation by end of 2024 -> Act passed 31 July 2025; 1 offshore exploration permit granted by Aug 2026
statusReason: The ban was reversed as promised but roughly seven months late, and only one exploration permit had resulted a year on.
whatHappened: The Crown Minerals Amendment Bill was introduced on 25 September 2024, but did not pass its third reading until 31 July 2025. It received royal assent on 5 August 2025, about seven months later than the commitment. The Act removed the exploration ban beyond onshore Taranaki, and shifted the Crown Minerals Act's purpose from managing prospecting and extraction to promoting it. The first offshore exploration permit since the reversal was granted to EnZed Energy on 29 July 2026, covering 546 square kilometres off Taranaki. There was a sole applicant, and the initial work programme was limited to reinterpreting existing seismic data. Gas reserves fell 23 per cent to 731 petajoules by January 2026, the lowest in two decades.
sourceDoc: Coalition agreement commitment to reverse the offshore oil and gas exploration ban; legislation promised by the end of 2024

promise: Review the performance of the electricity market and improve its regulation so competition works and power is affordable and reliable.
keyNumber: Electricity market review -> report Oct 2025, structural separation rejected, hedge access rules from 1 July 2026, penalties from $2m to $10m in 2027
statusReason: The review was completed and binding conduct rules took effect. But the enforcement regime that gives them teeth does not arrive until 2027.
whatHappened: The Frontier Economics review and the Government's response were released on 1 October 2025. The Government did not adopt structural separation of the four gentailers. The review considered but did not recommend it, and officials judged behavioural rules faster to implement and less disruptive to investment. On 26 May 2026 the Energy Minister announced level playing field rules. From 1 July 2026 Contact, Genesis, Mercury and Meridian must offer independent retailers the same hedge contract terms as their own retail arms, unless a difference is objectively justifiable. Those four companies hold about 85 per cent of generation and about 85 per cent of household customers. They must also file annual compliance plans and show every six months that retail prices reflect costs. Maximum penalties are to rise from $2 million to the greater of $10 million, three times commercial gain, or 10 per cent of turnover, once legislation passes in 2027. Household power bills had risen roughly a third over four years.
contestedNote: The Government and the Electricity Authority argue that behavioural level playing field rules address the vertical integration problem faster and with less investment risk than a break-up. Independent retailers, some business groups and opposition parties argue only structural separation of generation from retail would fix it, and note the higher penalties do not take effect until 2027.
sourceDoc: Government energy security package announced 26 August 2024, improve electricity market regulation and review market performance

promise: Remove the regulatory barriers to building a liquefied natural gas import facility so New Zealand can import gas when domestic supply is short.
keyNumber: LNG import facility -> at contracting stage Aug 2026, target operation 2027 to early 2028
statusReason: Regulatory barriers were addressed and a facility is at contracting stage, but nothing is built and the term is not finished.
whatHappened: On 9 February 2026 the Government announced it would contract to build an LNG import facility in Taranaki, having shortlisted leading proposals. Contract signing was targeted for mid-2026, with the facility potentially operating in 2027 or early 2028. The design brings in large shipments only when needed, to limit exposure to international gas price volatility. The Government estimated it would save households about $50 a year by damping price spikes, and be worth about $1.2 billion a year to the economy by 2035 if domestic gas keeps declining. No facility was operating as at August 2026.
sourceDoc: Government energy security package announced 26 August 2024, remove regulatory barriers to LNG imports

promise: Establish a $200 million co-investment fund and take Crown cornerstone stakes in new gas field developments, to reduce sovereign risk and lift domestic gas supply.
keyNumber: $200m gas co-investment fund -> fund created May 2025 and widened Nov 2025; gas reserves still fell 23 per cent to 731 PJ by Jan 2026
statusReason: The fund exists and was broadened, but no completed investment or reversal of the gas production decline is yet evident.
whatHappened: Budget 2025 created the $200 million commercial co-investment fund for new gas field development. On 6 November 2025 its scope was widened to cover more drilling in existing fields and production facility upgrades, exploration and appraisal drilling, greenfield exploration beyond Taranaki, and gas storage. Ministers cited a worsening supply outlook. Kanoa was to call for expressions of interest that month, and no investment had been concluded at that point. Gas reserves fell 23 per cent to 731 petajoules by January 2026, and 2026 production was forecast to fall 15 per cent year on year to about 85 petajoules.
sourceDoc: Budget 2025 gas co-investment fund and Crown cornerstone stake policy

promise: Make it faster and cheaper to consent renewable electricity generation and network infrastructure. Do this through a one-stop-shop fast-track approvals regime and new national direction under the Resource Management Act.
keyNumber: Faster consenting for renewables -> 6 renewable projects approved under fast-track by July 2026, including a 380MW wind farm
statusReason: The regime was legislated, the national direction was made, and six renewable projects had been consented through it by mid-2026.
whatHappened: The Fast-track Approvals Act 2024 created a referral and expert-panel pathway. On 2 April 2026 the 380MW, 55-turbine Southland Wind Farm was approved after a five-month panel process. It would be New Zealand's largest and had previously been declined resource consent. By 3 July 2026 six renewable energy projects had been approved through fast-track, including the 190MW Mahinerangi wind farm expansion, alongside hydro schemes at Kaimai, Pukaki, Tekapo and Waitaha. On 15 January 2026 the Government introduced a new National Policy Statement for Infrastructure, and amended the national policy statements for Renewable Electricity Generation and Electricity Networks.
sourceDoc: Coalition Government fast-track consenting programme and RMA national direction for infrastructure and renewable electricity

promise: Take urgent action to secure electricity supply and manage dry-year risk after the 2024 gas shortage and wholesale price spike. This includes easing restrictions on lines companies owning generation and securing gentailer access to hydro contingent storage.
keyNumber: Secure supply after the 2024 crisis -> wholesale prices peaked above $800/MWh in Aug 2024; Crown put up to $200m into Genesis in Feb 2026
statusReason: Specific measures were implemented and the immediate crisis eased. But structural dry-year and gas-decline risk remains unresolved, with the LNG facility and new gas investment still pending.
whatHappened: Wholesale prices rose from roughly $300/MWh to over $800/MWh between July and early August 2024. Hydro storage was at a six-year low. Gas production was down 12.5 per cent in 2023 and a further 27.8 per cent in the first quarter of 2024, and wind output was often below 300MW against more than 1,000MW of capacity. Coal generation rose 118 per cent in 2024 to 5.1 per cent of the total, and several North Island mills closed or curtailed production. The Government eased lines company generation restrictions and addressed hydro contingent storage access. In February 2026 it bought up to $200 million of new Genesis Energy shares to fund flexible generation, while keeping the Crown's 51 per cent stake. Renewable generation reached a record 96.4 per cent in the December 2025 quarter under favourable hydrology.
sourceDoc: Government energy security package announced 26 August 2024

promise: Investigate the feasibility of reopening the Marsden Point oil refinery as part of a fuel security study.
keyNumber: Investigate reopening Marsden Point -> study completed 2024-25; refinery not reopened
statusReason: The commitment as written was to investigate, and the investigation was commissioned and completed.
whatHappened: The study was commissioned in 2024. MBIE engaged Envisory and Castalia in 2024-25 to examine the costs and benefits of re-establishing the refinery, with peer review by Beca. That work fed into the 2025 Fuel Security Study and Fuel Security Plan. The refinery closed in 2022 and operates as an import terminal. It was not reopened and no decision to reopen it was taken. NZ First had campaigned on restoring refining capacity.
contestedNote: Read as written, the coalition commitment was only to investigate, and that happened, so it is delivered. Read against NZ First's public campaign that Marsden Point should refine fuel again, nothing changed: the site remains an import terminal and no reopening decision was made.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First coalition agreement 2023, investigate reopening the Marsden Point oil refinery

promise: Establish a fuel security plan to safeguard New Zealand's transport, logistics and emergency services from any international or domestic disruption to fuel supply.
keyNumber: Fuel security plan -> released November 2025, about two years after the coalition agreement
statusReason: The plan was published and then put to use, though about two years after the commitment was signed.
whatHappened: MBIE ran a 2025 Fuel Security Study and consulted on a draft plan in July and August 2025. The Fuel Security Plan was released in November 2025 as the Government's medium- to long-term resilience strategy. It was tested in 2026. In March the Government set up a ministerial group to oversee fuel security, joined an international oil response and widened fuel supply options. In April it announced an additional 90 million litres of diesel.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First coalition agreement 2023, fuel security plan

promise: End energy poverty and ensure everyone has a warm, dry home, including through a large-scale programme of home insulation and heating retrofits for low-income owner-occupiers.
keyNumber: 26,500 retrofits a year -> 122,589 retrofits delivered 2018 to August 2023 (81,920 insulation, 40,669 heating)
statusReason: The retrofit programme ran at or above its annual target for the whole term and was expanded. The broader goal of ending energy poverty was not achieved.
whatHappened: The Warmer Kiwi Homes programme began in 2018. It offered grants covering the bulk of the cost of ceiling and underfloor insulation and an efficient heater, for low-income homeowners in deprived areas. By August 2023 it had delivered 122,589 retrofits since 2018: 81,920 insulation claims and 40,669 heating claims, against a target of 26,500 retrofits a year. Budget 2023 extended the programme with $402.6 million over four years to June 2027, added hot water heat pumps and about 5 million LED bulbs, and widened eligibility to deprivation index level 7 areas. Cost cover was 90 per cent for the most deprived areas and Community Services Card holders. Energy hardship itself was not eliminated, and a separate Energy Hardship Expert Panel was still working at the end of the term.
sourceDoc: Labour-Green Confidence and Supply Agreement 2017, policy goal 13, end energy poverty and ensure everyone has warm, dry homes

promise: Introduce higher water quality standards for New Zealand's rivers, lakes and aquifers.
keyNumber: Higher water quality standards -> NPS-FM 2020 and NES-Freshwater in force 3 Sept 2020
statusReason: A new national freshwater framework covering the whole system was gazetted within the term. But several proposals were weakened, and on-the-ground implementation by councils was still years away.
whatHappened: The Action for Healthy Waterways / Essential Freshwater package was launched on 5 September 2019. Four instruments were gazetted and came into force on 3 September 2020: the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management 2020, National Environmental Standards for Freshwater, stock exclusion regulations, and amended water measurement and reporting regulations. The NPS-FM 2020 introduced Te Mana o te Wai and a hierarchy of obligations, putting the health of water bodies first, human health second and economic use third. Some proposals were scaled back in the final package: stream reclamation assessments were made less stringent, controls on higher-risk farming were narrowed mainly to feedlots and dairy intensification, and specified vegetable growing areas in Pukekohe and Horowhenua received exemptions. Regional councils were required to notify freshwater plans by 31 December 2024, a deadline none met before the change of government.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, item 47, higher water quality standards

promise: Significantly increase the Department of Conservation's funding.
keyNumber: Significantly increase DOC funding -> approx $181.6m (2018), $10.7m (2019) and $501.8m (2020) in new funding
statusReason: Conservation funding rose substantially in every Budget of the term, which is what the commitment asked for.
whatHappened: DOC received funding increases in successive Budgets: about $181.62 million in Budget 2018, a further $10.7 million in Budget 2019, and $501.8 million in Budget 2020. The last of these came largely through Jobs for Nature nature-based employment funding in the COVID-19 response. Much of the 2020 uplift was time-limited rather than baseline funding, and Jobs for Nature contracts began winding down from 2023. Under the following government, DOC's baseline was reduced by about $8 million a year of ongoing savings in Budget 2025, including closure of the Nature Heritage Fund and the Crown Land Acquisition Fund.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, item 42, significantly increase Department of Conservation funding

promise: Fund work to counter the spread of myrtle rust and to address kauri dieback disease.
keyNumber: Kauri dieback and myrtle rust response -> $13.75m over three years announced 20 Nov 2018
statusReason: Dedicated funding and a national management programme for both diseases were established within the term.
whatHappened: On 20 November 2018 the Government announced $13.75 million over three years for research into myrtle rust and kauri dieback. A National Pest Management Plan for kauri dieback was then developed, and Tiakina Kauri was set up within Biosecurity New Zealand as a dedicated kauri protection agency. Protecting kauri was carried into the 2020 Labour-Greens cooperation agreement as a shared biodiversity commitment.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, items 44b and 44c, counter myrtle rust and address kauri dieback

promise: Introduce a royalty on exports of bottled water.
keyNumber: Royalty on bottled water exports -> none introduced
statusReason: No royalty was introduced at any point in the term, despite the explicit coalition commitment.
whatHappened: A technical advisory group was set up and officials worked on options, but Cabinet had made no decision by March 2019 and no royalty was introduced. The commitment did not survive into the 2020-2023 term, when NZ First was out of Parliament, and no water export royalty has been legislated. The related commitment not to introduce water resource rentals during the 2017-2020 term was kept.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, item 46, royalty on exports of bottled water

promise: Introduce no water resource rentals during the 2017-2020 parliamentary term.
keyNumber: No water resource rentals this term -> none introduced, confirmed 17 April 2019
statusReason: No water resource rentals were introduced during the term, as committed.
whatHappened: On 17 April 2019 the Government confirmed it would not introduce water resource rentals during the term. Water allocation and charging were left to be dealt with separately. The Essential Freshwater package that followed in 2020 regulated water quality and use without imposing rentals or charges on takes.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, item 45, no water resource rentals this term

promise: Increase support for pilot programmes trialling alternatives to 1080 for predator control.
keyNumber: Pilot alternatives to 1080 -> $19.5m from the Provincial Growth Fund, Feb 2019
statusReason: Dedicated funding for alternative predator-control tools was allocated within the term as promised, though 1080 use continued.
whatHappened: On 19 February 2019 the Government allocated $19.5 million from the Provincial Growth Fund to Predator Free 2050 Limited, for innovative predator control tools and landscape-scale eradication projects. Trap networks, self-resetting traps, lures and detection technology were funded alongside continued 1080 use, which was not reduced. The National-led government later disestablished Predator Free 2050 Limited in May 2025, absorbing its functions into DOC and booking about $3.6 million a year of savings.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, item 44a, pilot alternatives to 1080

promise: Establish a tyre stewardship fund to deal with end-of-life tyres.
keyNumber: Tyre stewardship scheme -> tyres declared a priority product 29 July 2020
statusReason: The regulatory step promised (a mandatory tyre stewardship scheme) was taken within the term.
whatHappened: On 29 July 2020 the Government declared tyres a priority product under the Waste Minimisation Act 2008, which requires a regulated product stewardship scheme. Tyres were one of six priority products declared at the same time. The accredited scheme, Tyrewise, began operating with fees on imported tyres from 2024, several years after the declaration.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, item 43, establish a tyre stewardship fund

promise: Resolve the outstanding issues preventing passage of the Kermadec Ocean Sanctuary Bill. The bill would create a 620,000 square kilometre fully protected sanctuary covering about 15 percent of New Zealand's exclusive economic zone.
keyNumber: 620,000 sq km ocean sanctuary -> not enacted; bill abandoned 28 March 2024
statusReason: The outstanding issues were never resolved and the bill did not pass during the term.
whatHappened: The previous National government introduced the bill after John Key's 2015 announcement. It had passed its second reading and then stalled over fishing quota rights and Treaty settlement obligations. It made no progress through the 2017-2020 term. Iwi leaders rejected a revised Labour proposal in June 2023, and a last-ditch ministerial push in August 2023 failed before the election. On 28 March 2024 the incoming coalition formally scrapped all work on the legislation, with Fisheries Minister Shane Jones describing it as a 620,000 square kilometre economic no-go zone. The existing 12-nautical-mile Kermadec marine reserve remains.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, item 48, resolve the outstanding issues with the Kermadec Ocean Sanctuary Bill

promise: Work to achieve the outcomes of Te Mana o te Taiao, the Aotearoa New Zealand Biodiversity Strategy 2020. Protect kauri, build on pest management programmes, and act to minimise waste and problem plastics.
keyNumber: Container return scheme with 20c deposit -> proposed March 2022, dropped 2023 without legislation
statusReason: Strategy documents, pest programmes and kerbside recycling reform were delivered. But the flagship waste measure, the container return scheme, was abandoned, and the biodiversity strategy carried no binding targets.
whatHappened: Te Mana o te Taiao was published in 2020, with an implementation plan in 2022, but it is a non-statutory strategy without binding targets. Predator Free 2050 and Jobs for Nature funding continued, and a kauri dieback National Pest Management Plan was made. On waste, the Government legislated a phased expansion and increase of the waste disposal levy, and standardised kerbside recycling. But the container return scheme announced in March 2022, a 20 cent deposit expected to cut beverage container litter by more than half, was dropped in 2023 before legislation, despite 98 percent support in public consultation. A staged ban on some single-use plastics proceeded, but later stages were revisited. Predator Free 2050 Limited was disestablished in May 2025, and DOC's baseline was cut by about $8 million a year in Budget 2025.
contestedNote: The Greens and Labour point to Jobs for Nature, kerbside standardisation and the biodiversity strategy as substantive delivery. Critics note the strategy was non-binding, the container return scheme was designed and then shelved, and no measurable reversal of biodiversity decline occurred within the term.
sourceDoc: Labour-Greens Cooperation Agreement 2020, protecting our environment and biodiversity through Te Mana o te Taiao, protecting kauri, building on pest management programmes, and taking action to minimise waste and problem plastics

promise: Replace the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management 2020 with provisions that better reflect the interests of all water users and rebalance Te Mana o te Wai. Exempt or relieve councils from NPS-FM 2020 obligations as soon as practicable.
keyNumber: Replace NPS-FM 2020 -> not yet replaced; council deadline moved from 31 Dec 2024 to 31 Dec 2027
statusReason: The hierarchy has been disapplied from consenting and council deadlines deferred. But the promised replacement national policy statement had not been gazetted as at the most recent published version of the NPS-FM 2020.
whatHappened: On 14 December 2023 Cabinet agreed to replace the NPS-FM. It said the work would take 18-24 months, and pushed the council notification deadline out from 31 December 2024 to 31 December 2027. The Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2024, in force from 25 October 2024, barred consent authorities from applying the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy of obligations when deciding consents. It also removed freshwater farm plan requirements in five regions and eased section 107 discharge permit tests. Consultation on the replacement national direction ran to 27 July 2025, with three options for Te Mana o te Wai, including removing it entirely. As at the December 2025 reprint, the NPS-FM 2020 remained in force with Te Mana o te Wai and the hierarchy still in the document, amended only to add operational need for quarrying and mining.
contestedNote: The Government argues the substantive rebalancing has already been achieved through the 2024 RMA amendments, and that full replacement is sequenced with the wider RMA rewrite. On the literal commitment, the NPS-FM 2020 is still the operative national direction and the term is not finished.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First and National-ACT Coalition Agreements 2023, replace the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management 2020

promise: Stop implementing new Significant Natural Areas, and seek advice on how existing SNAs operate, as part of Resource Management Act reform.
keyNumber: Cease new SNAs -> suspended for 3 years from 14 March 2024
statusReason: New SNA implementation was halted within four months of taking office, exactly as the agreement specified.
whatHappened: On 14 March 2024 Associate Environment Minister Andrew Hoggard announced a three-year suspension of the requirement for councils to comply with the SNA provisions of the National Policy Statement for Indigenous Biodiversity. The suspension lasts while the RMA is replaced. In practice this told councils not to proceed with new SNA mapping. Existing council obligations to protect areas of significant indigenous vegetation under section 6(c) of the RMA were unaffected, and SNAs already in operative district plans remain.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023, cease implementation of new Significant Natural Areas

promise: Repeal the Natural and Built Environment Act 2023 and Spatial Planning Act 2023 by Christmas 2023. Replace the Resource Management Act 1991 with new resource management laws premised on the enjoyment of property rights as a guiding principle.
keyNumber: Repeal NBA/SPA by Christmas and replace the RMA -> repeal done Dec 2023; RMA 1991 still operative at Aug 2026
statusReason: The repeal was completed on time. But the full replacement of the RMA has not yet taken effect and the term is unfinished.
whatHappened: Labour's two replacement statutes were repealed in December 2023 under urgency, in the Government's first weeks. A phased programme followed. Phase two brought amendments including the Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2024, in force 25 October 2024, and the Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Act 2024. Phase three, replacing the RMA itself with new planning and natural environment legislation, was announced and progressed through 2025-2026. The RMA 1991 remains the operative statute as at August 2026.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023, repeal the Natural and Built Environment Act and Spatial Planning Act by Christmas and replace the RMA with laws premised on property rights

promise: Update the Crown Minerals Act 1991 to clarify its role as promoting the use of Crown minerals. Explore a critical minerals list with a preferential development pathway.
keyNumber: Crown Minerals Act purpose changed to promotion -> royal assent 5 Aug 2025; 94.5% of 5,524 submitters opposed
statusReason: The statutory purpose was changed to promotion by Act of Parliament within the term.
whatHappened: The Crown Minerals Amendment Bill was introduced on 24 September 2024 and passed on 31 July 2025, receiving royal assent on 5 August 2025. It changed the Act's purpose from managing to promoting the use of Crown minerals, removed the offshore petroleum exploration ban, and created a Tier 3 permit category for small-scale gold mining. It also replaced trailing decommissioning liability with ministerial discretion over financial security. Of 5,524 select committee submissions, 94.5 percent opposed the bill. A separate critical minerals list was developed as part of the Government's minerals strategy.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023, update the Crown Minerals Act 1991 to clarify its role as promoting the use of Crown minerals

promise: Establish a one-stop-shop fast-track consenting regime to improve the speed and process of resource approvals for major infrastructure and development projects.
keyNumber: One-stop-shop fast-track regime -> Act in force 23 Dec 2024; 149 projects listed including 11 mining
statusReason: A permanent one-stop-shop fast-track regime was legislated within the first 13 months and is operating with 149 listed projects.
whatHappened: The Fast-track Approvals Bill was introduced on 7 March 2024 and passed its third reading on 17 December 2024, receiving royal assent on 23 December 2024. The Act creates a permanent expedited pathway, allowing projects to be exempted from requirements under the Resource Management Act 1991, Conservation Act 1987, Wildlife Act 1953 and Reserves Act 1977, including activities on conservation land. Treaty settlement land, protected customary rights areas and iwi-settlement aquaculture areas are excluded. After sustained opposition from Labour, the Greens, Te Pāti Māori, Forest and Bird, the Environmental Defence Society and Greenpeace, and nationwide protests, the ministerial power to approve projects directly was removed at select committee. Approval was left with independent expert panels, while the Minister retains referral and referral-stage decline powers. 149 projects were listed, including 44 housing, 43 infrastructure, 22 renewable energy, 11 mining and 7 aquaculture or farming projects.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023, fast-track consenting for major infrastructure and development projects

promise: Start an urgent review of how the National Policy Statement for Indigenous Biodiversity 2023 is being implemented.
keyNumber: Urgent review of the NPS-IB -> SNA compliance suspended for 3 years from March 2024; NPS-IB otherwise unchanged
statusReason: The review was started urgently and produced the SNA suspension. But the NPS-IB itself has not been amended or replaced, and the work is now bundled into the RMA rewrite.
whatHappened: A review was begun promptly. Its most visible outcome was the 14 March 2024 suspension, for three years, of the requirement for councils to comply with the NPS-IB's Significant Natural Areas provisions. The rest of the NPS-IB remained in place. Its future was folded into the wider replacement of the resource management system rather than resolved separately, so a new or amended national policy statement for indigenous biodiversity had not been issued as at August 2026.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023, commence an urgent review into the implementation of the National Policy Statement on Indigenous Biodiversity

promise: Deliver longer durations for marine farming permits and remove regulations that impede the productivity of the seafood sector.
keyNumber: Longer marine farming permits -> all existing coastal permits extended by 20 years (not beyond 2050)
statusReason: Legislation automatically extending marine farm permits by 20 years passed within the first year.
whatHappened: The Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Act 2024 was enacted on 27 August 2024. It automatically extends all existing aquaculture coastal permits by 20 years, without requiring reconsenting, capped so that no permit runs beyond 2050. Aquaculture projects were also made eligible for the fast-track regime, with 7 aquaculture or farming projects among the 149 listed.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023, deliver longer durations for marine farming permits

promise: Minimise waste to landfill, with significant reductions achieved by 2020.
keyNumber: Significant reduction in waste to landfill by 2020 -> plastic bag ban from 1 July 2019; levy $10 to $60 per tonne phased from 2021, expanded to C&D landfills from July 2022
statusReason: Two substantial waste measures were delivered. But the levy reform arrived after the agreement's 2020 deadline, and landfill volumes did not fall by then.
whatHappened: Green Associate Environment Minister Eugenie Sage announced a mandatory phase-out of single-use plastic shopping bags in August 2018, and the ban took effect on 1 July 2019. New Zealand was one of the first countries to ban them outright. On the levy, Sage announced in 2021 that the waste disposal levy would rise from $10 a tonne, unchanged since 2009, to $60 a tonne progressively over four years. It would also be extended from municipal landfills, about 10 per cent of landfills, to construction and demolition landfills from 1 July 2022. Alongside this, $124 million from the COVID-19 Response and Recovery Fund went to recycling infrastructure. Both the levy increase and the levy expansion took effect after the 2020 deadline in the agreement, and total waste to landfill was not reduced by 2020.
sourceDoc: Labour-Green Confidence and Supply Agreement 2017, policy goal 9, minimise waste to landfill, with significant reductions by 2020

promise: Safeguard New Zealand's marine ecosystems, including by establishing ocean sanctuaries.
keyNumber: 620,000 sq km Kermadec Ocean Sanctuary -> not enacted in six years; bill scrapped 28 March 2024
statusReason: No ocean sanctuary was established in six years, and the one bill on the table never advanced.
whatHappened: The flagship measure available was the Kermadec Ocean Sanctuary Bill. It would have created a 620,000 square kilometre fully protected sanctuary covering about 15 per cent of New Zealand's exclusive economic zone. The bill had passed its second reading before the 2017 election, then stalled over fishing quota rights held under a 1992 Treaty settlement. It made no progress through either Labour-led term. In January 2020 the Greens' own conservation spokespeople publicly recorded that the government had failed to deliver the sanctuary. Iwi leaders rejected a revised proposal in June 2023, and a final ministerial push in August 2023 failed before the election. No new ocean sanctuary was established during the period, and the incoming government formally scrapped the bill on 28 March 2024.
sourceDoc: Labour-Green Confidence and Supply Agreement 2017, policy goal 8, safeguard marine ecosystems and establish ocean sanctuaries

promise: Safeguard indigenous biodiversity by reducing the extinction risk of 3,000 threatened species.
keyNumber: Reduce extinction risk for 3,000 species -> $81.2m over four years for predator control in Budget 2018; no reporting against the 3,000 figure
statusReason: Substantial and specific funding was delivered, but the numeric species goal in the agreement was never measured or reported against.
whatHappened: Green Conservation Minister Eugenie Sage secured more than $81.2 million over four years for predator control in Budget 2018, which the Department of Conservation described as one of its biggest ever funding increases. She also secured more than $16 million over four years for departmental capability. Predator Free 2050 programmes were expanded, including regional projects in Wellington, Taranaki and Banks Peninsula, and a kauri dieback National Pest Management Plan took effect on 2 August 2022 with $32 million behind it. However, the 3,000-species extinction risk goal was never converted into a measurable programme or reported against, and Te Mana o te Taiao, the 2020 biodiversity strategy, carried no binding targets. Predator Free 2050 Limited was disestablished in May 2025.
sourceDoc: Labour-Green Confidence and Supply Agreement 2017, policy goal 6, safeguard indigenous biodiversity by reducing the extinction risk of 3,000 species

promise: Re-examine the Defence procurement programme within the context of the 2016 Defence Capability Plan budget.
keyNumber: 2016 plan re-examined -> $20b Defence Capability Plan 2019, 4 P-8As and 5 C-130Js ordered
statusReason: The procurement programme was reviewed and rebuilt into a published capability plan, and the two largest replacement purchases were committed inside the term.
whatHappened: Defence Minister Ron Mark ran a full policy and capability review in the 2017-2020 term. It produced the Strategic Defence Policy Statement 2018 and the Defence Capability Plan 2019, a roughly $20 billion programme of investment to 2030. Two major replacements were locked in. Four Boeing P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft were announced in July 2018 and formally ordered in March 2019 for about US$1.46 billion. Five Lockheed Martin C-130J-30 Hercules were selected in June 2019, with the sale confirmed in June 2020 for about US$1.4 billion. The P-8As were delivered between December 2022 and July 2023. The C-130J-30s arrived from 8 August 2024, with all five in service by 19 December 2024.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, item 27, re-examine the Defence procurement programme within the context of the 2016 Defence Capability Plan budget

promise: Work towards a free trade agreement with the Russia-Belarus-Kazakhstan Customs Union.
keyNumber: FTA with Russia-Belarus-Kazakhstan promised -> 0 negotiating rounds, no agreement
statusReason: Talks were never restarted, and no agreement or negotiating round resulted from the commitment.
whatHappened: Negotiations with the Customs Union had been suspended since 2014 over Russia's annexation of Crimea, and were never resumed during the 2017-2020 term. No round of talks was held and no agreement was concluded. The commitment did not carry into the 2020-2023 term after NZ First left Parliament. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, New Zealand instead legislated sanctions against Russia. No such agreement appears among New Zealand's free trade agreements.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, item 60, work towards a Free Trade Agreement with the Russia-Belarus-Kazakhstan Customs Union

promise: Negotiate and bring into force a comprehensive free trade agreement with the United Kingdom.
keyNumber: UK FTA -> in force 31 May 2023, tariffs removed on 99.5 percent of NZ exports
statusReason: The agreement was negotiated, signed, ratified and in force before the end of the term.
whatHappened: Negotiations opened with a first virtual round on 13-24 July 2020. Terms were concluded on 20 October 2021, the agreement was signed on 28 February 2022, and New Zealand ratified it in March 2022. It entered into force on 31 May 2023, eliminating tariffs on 99.5 percent of New Zealand exports to the UK, including meat, butter and cheese. The estimated economic benefit was in the order of $970 million. In the first twelve months of operation the UK was New Zealand's fastest growing export market.
sourceDoc: Labour-led Government trade agenda, conclude a comprehensive free trade agreement with the United Kingdom after Brexit

promise: Conclude a comprehensive free trade agreement with the European Union.
keyNumber: EU FTA -> signed July 2023, in force 1 May 2024
statusReason: The agreement was negotiated and signed within the term. But entry into force and the resulting benefits fell after the handover, and agricultural access was narrower than sought.
whatHappened: Negotiations ran through the term and concluded in mid-2022. The agreement was signed in July 2023, shortly before the general election. It had not been ratified by the European Parliament or entered into force at the October 2023 handover. It took effect on 1 May 2024, under the successor government, giving New Zealand exporters duty-free or preferential access across most product lines. Dairy and beef access was limited to quotas that New Zealand negotiators had sought to expand.
sourceDoc: Labour-led Government trade agenda, conclude a high-quality free trade agreement with the European Union

promise: Sign the Trans-Pacific Partnership only on terms that keep New Zealand's ability to ban overseas buyers from buying existing homes, and that limit investor-state dispute settlement.
keyNumber: CPTPP -> signed 8 Mar 2018, in force for NZ 30 Dec 2018, ISDS provisions suspended
statusReason: The housing ban was kept and put in place before entry into force, and ISDS was suspended and further limited by side letters. But ISDS was suspended rather than removed, and the rest of the agreement carried over largely unchanged.
whatHappened: The renamed CPTPP was signed in Santiago on 8 March 2018. A set of the original TPP's investor-state dispute settlement provisions was suspended, and New Zealand negotiated side letters with several parties that further limited ISDS. New Zealand ratified on 25 October 2018 and the agreement entered into force for New Zealand on 30 December 2018. The Overseas Investment Amendment Act 2018 took effect on 22 October 2018, before entry into force. It classified existing residential land as sensitive and barred most non-resident overseas buyers, with Australian and Singaporean buyers exempt under earlier agreements. The United Kingdom later acceded, signing on 16 July 2023 at the CPTPP Commission meeting in Auckland. Its accession entered into force on 15 December 2024.
contestedNote: The Government argued it had materially changed the deal by suspending ISDS, securing side letters, and legislating the foreign buyer ban in time. Critics, including the Green Party and trade campaigners, argued the suspensions could be revived and that side letters covered only some partners. On their reading, the agreement was in substance the deal Labour had opposed in opposition.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 manifesto and campaign commitments on the Trans-Pacific Partnership, preserve the right to ban foreign purchases of existing homes and curb investor-state dispute settlement

promise: Complete and sign an upgrade of the 2008 New Zealand-China free trade agreement to improve access for New Zealand exporters.
keyNumber: China FTA upgrade -> signed 26 Jan 2021; all dairy tariffs gone 1 Jan 2024
statusReason: The upgrade was negotiated and signed within the term, and delivered the tariff outcomes sought.
whatHappened: An initial upgrade was concluded in November 2019, easing Chinese restrictions on New Zealand wood and paper products. New Zealand and China signed the full upgrade protocol on 26 January 2021. It removed or reduced tariffs on dairy, timber and seafood lines, and modernised rules of origin and services commitments. China removed its remaining dairy safeguard tariffs on 1 January 2024, worth an estimated $330 million a year. Two-way trade reached NZ$37.9 billion in 2023, making China New Zealand's largest trading partner. The same period also saw public friction over Huawei's exclusion from 5G, Hong Kong, Xinjiang and cyber attribution statements.
sourceDoc: Labour-led Government trade agenda, complete the upgrade of the 2008 New Zealand-China free trade agreement

promise: Progressively increase real defence spending to reach 2 percent of GDP by 2030.
keyNumber: 2 percent of GDP by 2030 promised -> about 1 percent at the start of the term, $12b four-year plan announced April 2025
statusReason: Large funding increases and a formal path above 2 percent are in place. But spending had not reached 2 percent as at August 2026, and the official timetable runs past 2030.
whatHappened: On 7 April 2025 Defence Minister Judith Collins released the Defence Capability Plan 2025. It committed NZ$12 billion over four years and set a path to lift defence spending above 2 percent of GDP, from a base of roughly 1 percent. Budget 2025 funded NZ$2.7 billion of capability uplift, including NZ$2 billion for new maritime helicopters. Budget 2026, delivered on 28 May 2026, added NZ$2.3 billion of capital and NZ$1.2 billion of operating funding for defence and intelligence. That included NZ$158 million for military drones and naval fleet maintenance. Purchases confirmed under the plan include five MH-60R Seahawk helicopters and two Airbus A321XLR transports. These were announced on 21 August 2025 under a six-year lease-to-buy arrangement worth about NZ$700 million, with delivery in 2028. The published trajectory reaches 2 percent over about eight years rather than by 2030.
sourceDoc: New Zealand First 2023 Policy Manifesto, progressively increase real Defence spending to reach 2% of GDP by 2030

promise: Establish a permanent, ring-fenced Defence Capital Fund within the Budget to fund defence capability and estate procurement.
keyNumber: Permanent ring-fenced Defence Capital Fund promised -> not established; funding via four-year plan and annual Budgets
statusReason: Defence capital was funded generously, but through normal appropriations. The specific permanent ring-fenced fund promised was not established.
whatHappened: Defence capital has instead been funded through the ordinary Budget process and the four-year Defence Capability Plan 2025. Budget 2025 and Budget 2026 each carried large defence capital allocations. That was NZ$2.7 billion of capability funding in 2025, and NZ$2.3 billion of capital funding for defence and intelligence in 2026. These came as separate budget appropriations rather than a standing ring-fenced fund. No permanent Defence Capital Fund appears in the Budget documents for either year.
contestedNote: NZ First can argue the substance was achieved. A multi-year, publicly committed capital programme now exists in the Defence Capability Plan 2025, with $12 billion of funding over four years. The counter-reading is that the promise was specifically institutional: a permanent fund ring-fenced from Budget-by-Budget decisions. No such vehicle has been created, leaving defence capital exposed to future fiscal rounds.
sourceDoc: New Zealand First 2023 Policy Manifesto, establish a permanent, ring-fenced Defence Capital Fund as part of the Budget

promise: Instruct NZDF uniformed staff to deliver a tri-service Defence Command Paper setting out the long-term size, structure and equipment needs of the Defence Force.
keyNumber: Tri-service command paper promised -> Defence Capability Plan 2025 released 7 April 2025, $12b over four years
statusReason: A long-term capability document covering all three services was delivered early in the term, though not in the specific form the manifesto described.
whatHappened: The Government produced the Defence Capability Plan 2025, released on 7 April 2025. It sets out a four-year, NZ$12 billion investment programme and longer-term capability intentions across the three services, including maritime helicopters, air transport, strike capability, uncrewed systems and estate. It was published as a ministerial capability plan rather than as a separately branded tri-service command paper written by uniformed staff. The period also exposed the pressures the paper was meant to address. HMNZS Manawanui grounded and sank off Samoa on 5 October 2024, the first Royal New Zealand Navy vessel lost in peacetime. An inquiry found human error. Budget 2025 wrote off NZ$77 million, including NZ$32 million for salvage and clean-up. Three officers were confirmed for court martial on 2 March 2026. The ship was not replaced, and HMNZS Otago absorbed its duties. Retention measures included two rounds of NZ$10,000 payments for critical trades, NZ$490 million of housing investment at Waiouru, and relaxed entry standards to lift recruitment.
contestedNote: One reading is that the Defence Capability Plan 2025 is the promised document in substance: a tri-service statement of size, structure and equipment with funding attached. The other is that the promise was about process as much as content. It required uniformed leadership, rather than ministers and officials, to set out what New Zealand needs, and no document of that description was published.
sourceDoc: New Zealand First 2023 Policy Manifesto, instruct NZDF uniformed staff to deliver a tri-service Defence Command Paper setting long-term size, structure and equipment needs

promise: Continue work towards a full free trade agreement with the United States.
keyNumber: US FTA sought -> no negotiations; 10 percent US tariff Apr 2025 rising to 15 percent Aug 2025
statusReason: No FTA negotiations with the United States were begun. New US tariffs on New Zealand goods dominated the period instead.
whatHappened: No negotiations were launched. On trade, the relationship moved the other way. In April 2025 the United States imposed a 10 percent tariff on New Zealand exports as part of its Liberation Day tariff package. On 1 August 2025 an executive order raised the rate to 15 percent. Trade Minister Todd McClay said New Zealand would engage with Washington to seek changes. On 14 November 2025 the United States lifted tariffs on more than 200 food products, including beef, offal and kiwifruit. Those products are worth about NZ$2.21 billion a year to New Zealand exporters. No free trade agreement or negotiating mandate existed as at August 2026.
sourceDoc: New Zealand First 2023 Policy Manifesto, continue work towards a full free trade agreement with the United States

promise: Launch a Closer Commonwealth Economic Relations agreement with the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, Singapore, Malaysia and Brunei, with India and other Commonwealth states invited as associates.
keyNumber: 6-country Commonwealth agreement promised -> not launched
statusReason: The proposed Commonwealth grouping was never launched. Trade liberalisation with those countries went through existing agreements instead.
whatHappened: No Commonwealth economic agreement was launched or negotiated. Trade integration with those partners went through existing structures instead. The United Kingdom acceded to the CPTPP, with its accession in force from 15 December 2024. New Zealand hosted the CPTPP Commission in Auckland on 20-21 November 2025. New agreements concluded in the term were bilateral or regional rather than Commonwealth-wide. They were the Gulf Cooperation Council FTA in October 2024, the UAE comprehensive economic partnership signed on 13 January 2025, and the India FTA signed in April 2026. No CCER framework appears among New Zealand's agreements or negotiations as at August 2026.
sourceDoc: New Zealand First 2023 Policy Manifesto, launch Closer Commonwealth Economic Relations with the UK, Australia, Canada, Singapore, Malaysia and Brunei

promise: Deepen the Pacific Reset into engagement with the wider Indo-Pacific, in recognition of the region's importance to New Zealand's security and wellbeing.
statusReason: Pacific and Indo-Pacific engagement clearly deepened in diplomacy, defence agreements and aid. But New Zealand's influence in the Pacific was visibly contested, and aid funding remained modest.
whatHappened: Foreign Minister Winston Peters ran an intensive programme of Pacific travel between May and August 2024, and continued into 2026. He signed an aid renewal statement with Kiribati in Tarawa on 19 January 2026. Funding announcements included NZ$6.2 million in climate and disaster support for the Marshall Islands in August 2024, and resumed NZ$1 million annual UNRWA funding in June 2024. Budget 2026 allocated NZ$110 million for international development assistance with an emphasis on the Pacific, plus NZ$145 million to protect diplomatic and trade missions. Indo-Pacific security engagement widened. New Zealand signed a visiting forces agreement with the Philippines on 30 April 2025. It also continued exploratory talks on AUKUS Pillar Two, after the partners said in September 2024 they were consulting New Zealand on maritime autonomous systems. New Zealand did not join. The reset also met resistance. New Zealand publicly objected to the Cook Islands' strategic partnership with China, signed on 14 February 2025 without consultation. It also objected to Chinese naval exercises in the Tasman Sea in February 2025.
sourceDoc: New Zealand First 2023 Policy Manifesto, deepen the Pacific Reset to the greater Indo-Pacific region

promise: Prioritise free and fair trade agreements, including a free trade agreement with India.
keyNumber: India FTA -> negotiations opened April 2025, signed April 2026, tariffs removed on 95 percent of NZ exports
statusReason: An India FTA was launched and signed within the term, alongside two other new agreements, matching the commitment.
whatHappened: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and Trade Minister Todd McClay led a delegation to India from 15 to 19 March 2025. The two governments agreed to open negotiations in April 2025. On 22 December 2025 they announced they would sign in 2026. They signed the New Zealand-India Free Trade Agreement in New Delhi in late April 2026 (27 April India time, 28 April New Zealand time). It eliminates tariffs on 95 percent of New Zealand exports, including kiwifruit, apples, meat, wool, coal and forestry, and gives duty-free access for Indian exports. It also includes an investment commitment of NZ$20 billion over two decades. Most dairy products are excluded from tariff elimination. Other agreements concluded in the term were the Gulf Cooperation Council FTA in October 2024 and the UAE comprehensive economic partnership signed on 13 January 2025. The UAE agreement cuts tariffs on 98.5 percent of New Zealand exports to the UAE.
contestedNote: The Government presents the agreement as delivering the commitment in full. Dairy exporters and some trade analysts note that dairy, New Zealand's largest export category, is largely carved out of tariff elimination. On that reading the deal delivers the promised agreement but not the market access the sector had sought. The agreement was also signed rather than in force as at August 2026.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023, as an export dependent nation, prioritise free and fair trade agreements, including with India

promise: Keep New Zealand's nuclear-free policy while exploring participation in the non-nuclear second pillar of AUKUS, covering advanced technology co-operation.
keyNumber: AUKUS Pillar Two -> exploratory consultations only, no participation decision by Aug 2026
statusReason: Exploration and consultation continued through the term exactly as described. But no participation decision had been made as at August 2026, and the promise was to explore rather than to join.
whatHappened: Luxon affirmed the nuclear-free policy and said New Zealand was open to joining the non-nuclear pillar during his December 2023 visit to Sydney. Australia's Defence Minister Richard Marles confirmed in February 2024 that Australian officials would brief New Zealand counterparts on Pillar Two. In September 2024 the AUKUS partners said they were consulting New Zealand, Canada and South Korea about collaboration on advanced capabilities, naming maritime autonomous systems as an initial area. As at August 2026 New Zealand had not joined Pillar Two, and no decision to do so had been announced. Domestic support narrowed over the period. Labour had opened the exploration in 2023 under Defence Minister Andrew Little. It reversed position in February 2024, and its associate foreign affairs spokesperson described AUKUS as an offensive warfighting alliance.
contestedNote: Supporters of the Government say the commitment was only ever to explore Pillar Two. They say consultations with the AUKUS partners show it has been honoured without compromising the nuclear-free policy. Critics argue that nearly three years of exploration with no decision either way amounts to drift. Opponents of AUKUS say any participation would erode New Zealand's independent foreign policy. On their reading, the absence of a decision is the outcome they sought rather than delivery of a promise.
sourceDoc: National's stated position on AUKUS Pillar Two entering government, set out by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon during his December 2023 visit to Sydney

promise: Increase defence spending as part of ACT's alternative budget, after deferring the planned increase in its revised fiscal plan of 21 September 2023.
statusReason: Defence funding has risen sharply under the government ACT is part of. But the build-up runs beyond the current term, and the party's original commitment carried no firm target date.
whatHappened: The coalition government ACT joined committed NZ$12 billion over four years in the Defence Capability Plan 2025, released on 7 April 2025. The plan states a path to lift defence spending above 2 percent of GDP. Budget 2025 provided NZ$2.7 billion of capability funding, including NZ$2 billion for maritime helicopters. Budget 2026 added NZ$2.3 billion of capital and NZ$1.2 billion of operating funding for defence and intelligence. The increases came in the second half of the term rather than at its start, consistent with the deferral ACT itself signalled before the election.
sourceDoc: ACT 2023 election fiscal plan, proposed defence spending boosts, revised on 21 September 2023 to delay tax cuts and the defence increase after the pre-election fiscal update

promise: Run a 'National Interest Test' before New Zealand accepts any agreement from the UN or its agencies that limits national decision-making. By 1 December 2023, reserve against the proposed amendments to the World Health Organization's International Health Regulations.
keyNumber: Reservation due by 1 Dec 2023 -> lodged; 2024 IHR amendments formally rejected 16 March 2026
statusReason: The national interest test was created and applied to the WHO instruments named in the agreement. Both the reservation and the later rejection were lodged.
whatHappened: New Zealand lodged a reservation against the proposed WHO International Health Regulations amendments in late 2023, while a national interest assessment was carried out. The World Health Assembly adopted a further package of IHR amendments on 1 June 2024. New Zealand did not accept them, and formally told the WHO Director-General of its rejection on 16 March 2026, invoking Article 61. That made it one of a small number of countries to reject the package outright. On 16 May 2025 Foreign Minister Winston Peters and Health Minister Simeon Brown announced a full national interest test on the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement. It would be run before New Zealand made any commitment. Peters said 'decisions about how New Zealand responds to any health emergency are made in Wellington, not Geneva'. Newsroom reported in 2026 that officials had advised in favour of the IHR amendments before ministers rejected them.
sourceDoc: National. NZ First Coalition Agreement, 24 November 2023 (Strengthening Democracy and Freedoms)

promise: Act on the Health and Disability System Review to replace the district health board structure with a single national health service.
keyNumber: 20 DHBs -> 1 national agency (Health NZ) from 1 July 2022
statusReason: The structural change promised was legislated and put in place in full within the term, though the decision to abolish DHBs was announced mid-term in April 2021.
whatHappened: The review reported on 16 June 2020. In April 2021 the Government announced it would abolish all 20 DHBs and create Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora. The Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act passed its third reading on 7 June 2022. The 20 DHBs were disestablished on 1 July 2022, when Health NZ, the Public Health Agency and iwi-Māori partnership boards began operating. The new agency then ran large deficits: $722m in 2023/24 and $947m in 2024/25. In July 2024 the Health Minister replaced its board with Commissioner Lester Levy, citing overspending of about $130m a month. A board was reinstated on 23 July 2025.
contestedNote: Supporters point out the promised structure was delivered on time and in law. Critics, including the incoming government, argue the reform delivered a centralised organisation that lost financial control. Health NZ reported deficits of $722m (2023/24) and $947m (2024/25) and was placed under a commissioner in July 2024. Whether that is a failure of the promise, or of its execution after the handover, is disputed.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 commitment to act on the Health and Disability System Review (Simpson Review), commissioned by the Labour government in May 2018

promise: Establish an independent Māori Health Authority with commissioning powers to address Māori health inequities.
keyNumber: Te Aka Whai Ora established 1 July 2022; $188m allocated in Budget 2022
statusReason: The authority was established by legislation and operating before the end of the term, as promised.
whatHappened: The Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 created Te Aka Whai Ora | Māori Health Authority. It began operating on 1 July 2022 as an independent statutory entity, able to commission kaupapa Māori services and co-commission with Health NZ. Budget 2022 allocated $188 million for its commissioning and iwi partnership work. It operated for two years before the incoming government disestablished it on 30 June 2024.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 term commitment, following the Health and Disability System Review, to establish an independent Māori health authority

promise: Rebuild Dunedin Hospital, starting construction before 2020 and completing it before 2027.
keyNumber: Construction start before 2020 and completion before 2027 promised -> main build not started by 2020, completion pushed to 2029
statusReason: There was real progress: the site was secured, the business case approved, and enabling works and the outpatient building were underway. But neither the promised construction start date nor the completion date was met.
whatHappened: In May 2018 Health Minister David Clark announced a new hospital on the former Cadbury factory site, estimated at about $1.4 billion with completion by 2026. Site acquisition, demolition and enabling works ran through the term, and the outpatient building was separated out. But the main inpatient build had not started by the 2020 deadline, and the completion date slipped to 2029. By May 2024 the estimated cost had risen above $2 billion.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 election campaign commitment on the new Dunedin Hospital

promise: Legislate a smokefree generation, ban tobacco sales to anyone born on or after 1 January 2009, cut nicotine levels in smoked tobacco, and sharply reduce the number of tobacco retailers.
keyNumber: 3 measures legislated Dec 2022 -> repealed 6 March 2024
statusReason: The law promised was passed within the term. Its later repeal was the act of a different government and is recorded separately.
whatHappened: The Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022 passed its third reading 76-43 on 13 December 2022 and received royal assent on 16 December 2022. It contained all three measures, with provisions taking effect from 1 January 2023 and 1 October 2023. The incoming National-led government repealed it. A repeal bill was introduced on 27 February 2024, passed on 28 February 2024 and took effect on 6 March 2024. That was before the denicotinisation and generation-ban provisions had taken effect.
sourceDoc: Labour's Smokefree Aotearoa 2025 Action Plan (December 2021) and resulting legislation

promise: Invest $1.9 billion in mental health and build a new frontline mental health and addiction service reaching 325,000 people a year (6.5% of the population) by 2023/24.
keyNumber: 325,000 people a year by 2023/24 promised -> 207,000 reached in 2023/24
statusReason: Nearly all the money was spent and a large new service was built. But the headline access target was missed by more than a third at the end of the term.
whatHappened: Budget 2019 allocated about $1.96 billion across 29 initiatives in 12 portfolios, with health receiving 57% ($1.12b over four years). By 30 June 2023, 92% of the money had been spent or committed, leaving $163.8m unspent. The Access and Choice primary mental health programme, funded $664m over five years, reached just over 207,000 people in 2023/24. That is 3.9% of the population and 64% of the 325,000 target. Services were available to 68% of the enrolled population as at 30 June 2024. The Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission projected the target would be met in 2025/26.
sourceDoc: Labour's mental health commitment delivered through the Budget 2019 Wellbeing Budget $1.9 billion mental health package

promise: Ensure everyone has access to timely and high quality mental health services, including free counselling for those under 25 years.
keyNumber: Free counselling for all under-25s promised -> regional pilot (Wellington region) plus general expansion of primary mental health services
