statusReason: Free counselling for under-25s was delivered only as a regional pilot. The universal entitlement described in the agreement did not eventuate by the end of the term.
whatHappened: A free youth mental health pilot, Piki, began in Porirua in February 2019. In May 2019 it was expanded across the Wellington, Hutt Valley and Kapiti region for 18 to 25 year olds. It was never rolled out nationally as a universal entitlement. Instead the Government built the wider Access and Choice programme, which by 2023/24 was reaching 207,000 people of all ages against a 325,000 target. The Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission reported in 2024 that young people in particular were missing out on services.
sourceDoc: Labour-Green Confidence and Supply Agreement 2017

promise: Cooperate on improving child and youth wellbeing, including child and youth mental health support.
statusReason: Services expanded. But the agreement set no specific measurable commitment, and independent monitoring found young people's access remained a gap at the end of the term.
whatHappened: Child and youth mental health support kept expanding through the Access and Choice programme and school-based services funded from the 2019 package. But the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission reported in 2024 that young people were still missing out on access to mental health services. Access and Choice coverage overall reached 207,000 people in 2023/24 against the 325,000 target.
sourceDoc: Labour-Green Cooperation Agreement 2020

promise: Progressively increase the age for free breast screening to 74.
keyNumber: Free breast screening to age 74 promised -> age range unchanged at 45-69 at Oct 2023 handover
statusReason: The screening age range was unchanged across both Labour-led terms, despite the commitment being in the signed coalition agreement.
whatHappened: The age range for free breast screening stayed at 45 to 69 throughout the 2017-2023 period. No extension was funded or started before the October 2023 handover. The extension only began under the next government, with a Nelson and Marlborough pilot from 1 October 2024 and a national phased rollout from 1 October 2025.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017

promise: Re-establish the Mental Health Commission.
statusReason: A standing independent mental health commission was re-created by statute and is operating.
whatHappened: The Government held the He Ara Oranga inquiry into mental health and addiction in 2018, then legislated to create a permanent independent commission. Te Hiringa Mahara | Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission was established as a permanent independent Crown entity. It has since published regular monitoring of the mental health system, including reports on the $1.9 billion Budget 2019 package and the Access and Choice programme.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017

promise: Fund 13 new cancer treatments, at $280 million over four years ($70m a year), starting 1 July 2024, paid for by reinstating the $5 prescription co-payment.
keyNumber: 13 named treatments and $280m over 4 years promised -> $604m over 4 years announced June 2024, up to 7 of the 13 funded plus substitutes
statusReason: More money and more medicines were funded in the end than promised. But it came a year late, not on the promised start date, and only about half the specific named treatments were funded.
whatHappened: Budget 2024, delivered 30 May 2024, contained no money for the 13 treatments. Finance Minister Nicola Willis said it had not been possible. After sustained criticism, on 24 June 2024 the Government announced a $604 million pre-commitment to Pharmac over four years. It covered up to 26 cancer treatments and up to 28 other medicines (around 54 in total), expected to benefit about 175,000 people in the first year. Health Minister Shane Reti said that of the 13 treatments listed in 2023, up to seven would be included. The rest would be replaced by alternatives judged as good or better. Pembrolizumab became available from 1 October 2024 and nivolumab from 1 November 2024, with the rest phased in over the following year.
contestedNote: The Government's reading is that the promise was over-delivered: more medicines, more money, and every cancer type in the manifesto covered by an equivalent or better treatment. Critics read it the other way. The specific promise was those 13 treatments from 1 July 2024. Budget 2024 funded none of them, and only up to seven of the 13 named drugs were funded at all.
sourceDoc: National 2023 campaign announcement, 21 August 2023

promise: Increase Pharmac funding by $724 million over four years.
keyNumber: $724m over 4 years promised -> $604m for new medicines alone (June 2024) on top of Budget 2024 baseline increases
statusReason: Pharmac's funding rose by more than the promised amount across the term, counting the Budget 2024 baseline uplift and the June 2024 $604m new-medicines pre-commitment.
whatHappened: Pharmac's baseline was lifted at Budget 2024. In June 2024 the Government made a further $604 million four-year pre-commitment specifically for new medicines. Pharmac reported the combined pharmaceutical budget on a steadily rising trajectory, with a large increase in 2024. The June 2024 tranche alone funded or widened access to up to 54 medicines. The National-NZ First coalition agreement separately committed to increasing Pharmac funding every year.
sourceDoc: National 2023 health policy

promise: Disestablish the Māori Health Authority.
keyNumber: Te Aka Whai Ora disestablished 30 June 2024, after 2 years of operation
statusReason: The authority was disestablished by legislation within four months of the government taking office, as the agreement required.
whatHappened: The Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill was introduced on 27 February 2024. It passed all stages by 28 February 2024 under urgency, without select committee consideration. Te Aka Whai Ora ceased to exist on 30 June 2024, and its functions and staff moved into the Ministry of Health and Health NZ. Iwi-Māori partnership boards were retained. In November 2024 the Waitangi Tribunal released its Hautupua report. It found the Crown had breached Treaty principles by not consulting Māori, and recommended the Crown reconsider a standalone Māori health authority.
contestedNote: The Government's position is that a separate commissioning agency duplicated Health NZ. It says responsibility for Māori health outcomes now sits with the whole system, and that iwi-Māori partnership boards were kept. The Waitangi Tribunal found the Crown did not act in good faith, did not consult Māori, and acted on political rather than evidential grounds. It also found the authority was integral to equitable delivery. Both readings agree on the facts of what was repealed and when. They differ on the significance.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023 (the same commitment appears in the National-NZ First agreement and the coalition 100-day plan)

promise: Repeal the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022 to remove the requirements for denicotinisation and the reduction in retail outlets.
keyNumber: 3 smokefree measures repealed, in force 6 March 2024
statusReason: The repeal was passed within the 100-day plan window, and in the terms set out in the coalition agreements.
whatHappened: The Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Amendment Bill was introduced on 27 February 2024, passed under urgency on 28 February 2024 and took effect on 6 March 2024. It removed the three measures of the 2022 Act before they had come into force. Those were the denicotinisation requirement, the reduction in the number of tobacco retailers, and the prohibition on sales to anyone born on or after 1 January 2009. The coalition also legislated separately on vaping, including a ban on disposable vapes and higher penalties for sales to under-18s.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023 (also in the National-NZ First agreement and the coalition 100-day plan)

promise: Set five major health targets for the health system, including for wait times and cancer treatment, and publish performance against them.
keyNumber: 5 health targets promised -> 5 set March 2024 and reported quarterly since
statusReason: The targets were set and are reported publicly each quarter, which is what the commitment required. Whether the targets themselves are met is tracked separately.
whatHappened: Five health targets were set in March 2024. They are shorter emergency department stays, shorter waits for elective treatment, shorter waits for first specialist assessment, faster cancer treatment, and childhood immunisation. Results have been published quarterly since. Two of the five (ED stays and elective waits) also sit in the nine whole-of-government targets. In the January to March 2026 quarter, 74.4% of ED patients were seen within six hours and 64.9% were treated within four months for elective care. In the same quarter, 61.2% were seen within four months for a first specialist assessment, 86.2% started cancer treatment within 31 days, and 83.5% of two year olds were fully immunised.
sourceDoc: Coalition 100-day plan and National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023

promise: 95% of patients to be admitted, discharged or transferred from an emergency department within six hours.
keyNumber: 95% within 6 hours promised -> 68.0% (Sep 2023 baseline) to 74.4% (Mar 2026 quarter)
statusReason: Term unfinished. There is measurable improvement on the baseline, but the target remains a long way off as at March 2026.
whatHappened: The baseline was 68.0% in September 2023. Performance reached 72.1% in December 2024, 74.2% in December 2025 and 74.4% in the January-March 2026 quarter. That is an improvement of about 6 percentage points over the baseline, but still more than 20 points short of the target. The Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet rates the target 'feasible', while noting that whole-of-system improvements are needed to reduce what it calls unacceptable emergency department waits.
sourceDoc: Government Targets (Target 1), set March 2024

promise: 95% of people to wait less than four months for elective treatment.
keyNumber: 95% within 4 months promised -> 62.0% (Sep 2023 baseline) to 64.9% (Mar 2026 quarter)
statusReason: Term unfinished. Volumes and the share treated within four months have risen from the baseline, but the target is far from being met.
whatHappened: The baseline was 62.0% in September 2023. Performance fell to 59.2% in December 2024, then rose to 65.9% in September 2025, 64.5% in December 2025 and 64.9% in the January-March 2026 quarter. Treatment volumes rose from 46,841 to 51,513 elective treatments in the December quarter year on year. Health NZ outsourced work to private hospitals to lift throughput. The target remains about 30 percentage points away.
sourceDoc: Government Targets (Target 2), set March 2024

promise: Build the new Dunedin Hospital, including $30 million to restore beds, operating theatres and a PET scanner that had been cut from the design.
keyNumber: 351 beds in the new build vs 396 in the old hospital; cost about $1.88b, opening 2031
statusReason: The hospital is being built and construction is well advanced. But the scope was reduced rather than restored, and the promised restoration of beds and theatres did not occur.
whatHappened: By May 2024 costs had risen above $2 billion and the project was paused. On 26 September 2024 ministers said it could not proceed within budget and proposed scaling it back sharply. About 35,000 people marched in protest in Dunedin on 28 September 2024. On 31 January 2025 Health Minister Simeon Brown confirmed a new inpatient building at about $1.88 billion. It will have 351 beds and 24 theatres, compared with 396 beds in the old hospital. Construction restarted in July 2025, with completion scheduled for 2031. Tower cranes went up in June 2026 and steelwork began in August 2026. The Otago Daily Times reported in May 2026 that the project budget had been lifted to about $2.1 billion.
contestedNote: The Government's reading is that it inherited an unaffordable design heading for a $3 billion blowout, made it deliverable and got construction underway. Local campaigners read it as the coalition cutting a hospital it had promised to enhance, delivering fewer beds than the building it replaces. Both agree on the final numbers: 351 beds, about $1.88b, opening 2031.
sourceDoc: National 2023 election campaign commitment on the new Dunedin Hospital

promise: Sign a memorandum of understanding with Waikato University and progress a third medical school, subject to a full cost-benefit analysis presented to Cabinet.
keyNumber: $82.85m Crown funding; 120 extra doctor training places a year from 2028
statusReason: The commitment was to progress the school subject to a cost-benefit analysis. That analysis was done, and the school was approved and funded within the term.
whatHappened: A cost-benefit analysis was presented to Cabinet, as the National-ACT agreement required. On 21 July 2025 the Government approved the new Waikato medical school. It has $82.85 million of Crown funding, alongside more than $150 million from the University of Waikato plus philanthropic support. It will be a graduate-entry programme, adding 120 doctor training places a year from 2028, with an emphasis on primary care and rural health. Ground was broken during 2026. The Government separately added 100 more medical training places at Auckland and Otago.
sourceDoc: Coalition 100-day plan and National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023

promise: Extend free breast cancer screening to those aged up to 74.
keyNumber: Screening to age 74 promised -> phased rollout started 1 Oct 2025, full coverage due end of 2029
statusReason: The extension has begun and is funded, but full coverage to age 74 is not due until the end of 2029. This is the same commitment NZ First made in 2017 and did not deliver in the previous era.
whatHappened: Legislation and funding were put in place, and a pilot ran in Nelson and Marlborough from 1 October 2024. The national extension began on 1 October 2025. It is being phased in one year of age at a time each October, through to the end of 2029, when the full 70-74 range will be covered. Health NZ estimates up to 54,000 additional women screened a year once fully implemented, with around 60 invasive cancers a year detected earlier.
sourceDoc: NZ First 2023 health policy; also in the National-ACT coalition agreement and the coalition 100-day plan

promise: Fund birthing units and maternity care properly, including providing for a three day stay for new mothers.
keyNumber: 3-day postnatal stay promised -> $34.4m over 4 years in Budget 2026, bill still before Parliament in Aug 2026
statusReason: Funding is committed and the legislation adopted, but the entitlement was not yet law at the end of the period assessed.
whatHappened: The Government adopted a member's bill from National MP Catherine Wedd in September 2025, creating an entitlement to a three-day postnatal stay. Budget 2026 allocated $34.4 million over four years to expand maternity capacity, infrastructure and workforce so longer stays can be delivered. As at August 2026 the Three Day Postnatal Stay Amendment Bill was still going through Parliament, so the legal entitlement was funded but not yet in force. The New Zealand College of Midwives argued the funding should be usable flexibly rather than tied to inpatient stays.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023

promise: Encourage more people to study nursing and midwifery, and to stay here, with a bonding scheme.
keyNumber: Bonding scheme promised -> up to 400 graduate nurses a year given $15,000-$20,000 incentives; about 1,800 graduate nurse roles offered in 2026
statusReason: Financial incentives for graduate nurses were introduced and graduate placements grew. But this was a targeted recruitment payment rather than the general study-and-stay bonding scheme described in the 100-day plan.
whatHappened: On 3 March 2025 the Government announced about $30 million over five years in recruitment incentives. These would place up to 400 graduate registered nurses a year into primary and community care, at $20,000 per nurse in rural areas and $15,000 in cities. The package also included 100 clinical placements for overseas-trained doctors and a $285 million performance-based uplift for general practice from 1 July 2025. By July 2026 Health NZ was offering around 1,800 graduate nurse roles a year, up from 1,716 offers the previous year. Over the preceding 12 months, 1,845 graduate registered nurses were employed across the wider health sector.
sourceDoc: Coalition 100-day plan 2023

promise: End all Covid-19 vaccine mandates still in operation.
keyNumber: All remaining mandates to end -> government mandates already revoked in 2022; no action on employer mandates by Aug 2026
statusReason: The promised end state, no government Covid-19 vaccine mandates in operation, holds. But it was already true when the promise was made, and no action was taken on the employer-imposed requirements that remained.
whatHappened: All government-imposed Covid-19 vaccination requirements, including those for health, disability and corrections workers, had already been revoked in late 2022 under the previous government. That was more than a year before the coalition agreement was signed on 24 November 2023. What remained were vaccination requirements imposed by individual employers under their own health and safety assessments. In May 2024 Health Minister Shane Reti said the Government was still working out what the commitment covered, asking 'what was exactly meant by that? Was it also meant to cover the workplace mandates as well?' NZ First said it was 'still working through the details'. No order, regulation or Act removing or prohibiting employer-imposed vaccination requirements had been made by August 2026.
contestedNote: Read narrowly, the commitment was satisfied on day one: no government mandates were in operation, so nothing needed to be ended. Read as supporters of the policy understood it, it covered workplace vaccination requirements still being applied by employers, and on that reading nothing was delivered. The Government itself said publicly that it was unsure which reading applied.
sourceDoc: National. NZ First Coalition Agreement, 24 November 2023 (Strengthening Democracy and Freedoms)

promise: Require Medsafe to approve new pharmaceuticals within 30 days of them being approved by at least two overseas regulatory agencies.
keyNumber: 30-day approval after 2 overseas regulators -> legislated 12 November 2025
statusReason: The 30-day rule and the two-overseas-regulator test were legislated in the terms set out in the agreement.
whatHappened: The Medicines Amendment Bill passed its third reading on 12 November 2025. It allows medicines already approved by two or more recognised overseas regulators to receive ministerial approval in New Zealand within 30 days. The recognised regulators are those of Australia, the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, the European Union, Singapore and Switzerland. Health Minister Simeon Brown and Associate Health Minister David Seymour said the change would shave months off the approval process at no cost. The change came almost two years into the term.
sourceDoc: National. NZ First Coalition Agreement, 24 November 2023 (Health)

promise: Repeal the Therapeutic Products Act 2023.
keyNumber: Repeal promised -> Therapeutic Products Act 2023 repealed 13 December 2024
statusReason: The Act was repealed as promised. The promise was to repeal, not to replace.
whatHappened: Repeal of the Act appeared in the Government's 100-day plan announced in December 2023. The Therapeutic Products Act Repeal Bill was introduced in 2024 and passed on 13 December 2024, becoming the Therapeutic Products Act Repeal Act 2024 (2024 No 55). Associate Health Minister Casey Costello said the Medicines Act 1981 and the Dietary Supplements Regulations 1985 would keep applying while replacement regulation was developed. Cabinet had agreed in September 2024 to develop separate legislation for medicines and medical devices, and standalone legislation for natural health products. That replacement legislation had not been enacted as at August 2026.
sourceDoc: National. NZ First Coalition Agreement, 24 November 2023 (Health)

promise: Build 100,000 affordable homes over 10 years through KiwiBuild, including 1,000 in the first year.
keyNumber: 100,000 homes over 10 years -> approx 2,229 completed by Dec 2023
statusReason: The promising party formally abandoned the headline target in 2019, and delivery reached roughly 2 per cent of the promised number by the end of the term.
whatHappened: KiwiBuild launched in 2018, with $2 billion of capital allocated in December 2017. By 23 January 2019 only 33 homes had been built, and Housing Minister Phil Twyford conceded the 1,000-home first-year target would be missed. On 4 September 2019 incoming Housing Minister Megan Woods announced a 'reset'. It scrapped the 100,000-home target entirely, replacing it with progressive home ownership and lower deposit requirements. About 2,229 KiwiBuild homes had been completed by December 2023.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 manifesto / KiwiBuild campaign policy

promise: Ban non-resident overseas buyers from buying existing residential homes in New Zealand.
keyNumber: Ban promised -> in force 22 Oct 2018 (Australia and Singapore exempt)
statusReason: Legislated and in force within the first year of the term, substantially as promised, with the trade-treaty exemptions that were flagged at the time.
whatHappened: The Overseas Investment Amendment Bill was introduced on 14 December 2017, passed its third reading on 15 August 2018 and received Royal assent on 22 August 2018. It took effect on 22 October 2018. It reclassified existing residential land as 'sensitive land', so most people who are not New Zealand citizens or permanent-resident-visa holders can no longer buy an existing house. Australian and Singaporean citizens are exempt under trade arrangements, and overseas persons may still buy to develop new housing.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 campaign commitment to ban non-resident foreign buyers of existing homes

promise: Require every rental home to be warm and dry, by setting enforceable minimum standards for heating, insulation, ventilation, moisture and draught stopping.
keyNumber: All rentals compliant by 1 July 2024 -> final private-rental deadline moved to 1 July 2025
statusReason: The legislation and standards were delivered early in the term. But the deadline for full private-rental compliance was extended, and fell after the promising government left office.
whatHappened: The Healthy Homes Guarantee Act passed its third reading 63-57 on 29 November 2017 and received Royal assent on 4 December 2017. The detailed Healthy Homes Standards regulations came into force on 1 July 2019. Compliance was phased: boarding houses from 1 July 2021, Kāinga Ora and registered community housing providers from 1 July 2024, and all private rentals by 1 July 2025. That last date was pushed back during the term from the original 1 July 2024 final deadline. Ceiling-insulation exemptions were reinstated for some homes from 25 September 2025.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 manifesto / Healthy Homes Guarantee Bill

promise: Deliver 18,000 additional public and transitional housing places by 2024.
keyNumber: 18,000 public and transitional places by 2024 -> 12,017 net additional public homes plus 4,000+ transitional places by June 2023
statusReason: The build programme was the largest since the 1970s, and the combined public plus transitional total was close to the 18,000 places promised. But it did not arrest growth in the waiting list.
whatHappened: By June 2023 the Government reported a net increase of 12,017 public homes since October 2017, 9,917 of them new builds. That took total public homes to 78,251, plus more than 4,000 additional transitional housing places, with over 4,500 public housing places under construction. Budget 2023 funded a further 3,000 public homes by June 2025. Demand outstripped supply: the social housing register stood at 25,483 applicants in late 2023, well above 2017 levels.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 election platform, public housing build programme

promise: Reform the Residential Tenancies Act to improve security of tenure for renters, including removing no-cause terminations and limiting rent increases.
keyNumber: No-cause terminations removed and rent rises limited to once a year -> both enacted in 2020
statusReason: The promised statutory changes were enacted and in force for the rest of the term. A different government reversed them later.
whatHappened: The Residential Tenancies Amendment Act 2020 removed the landlord's ability to end a periodic tenancy without giving a reason. It also eliminated rental bidding and limited rent increases to once every 12 months. The changes took effect during the 2020-2023 term and remained in force at the October 2023 handover. The incoming government reversed them from 30 January 2025.
sourceDoc: Labour renters policy (2017 and 2020 terms), restated in Labour's 2023 housing platform

promise: Build 5,000 new public and community homes a year, lift Kāinga Ora's borrowing cap from $7.1 billion to $12 billion, and clear the social housing waiting list within five years.
keyNumber: 5,000 homes a year and waiting list cleared by 2025 -> approx 2,000 a year, register at 25,483 in late 2023
statusReason: None of the three parts was achieved: the annual build rate, the borrowing cap change, or the waiting-list target. The Greens did not hold the housing portfolio in Cabinet.
whatHappened: The Labour-led government the Greens supported did not adopt the policy. Public housing delivery ran at roughly 2,000 net additional homes a year rather than 5,000. The net increase was 12,017 public homes over the six years to June 2023. The social housing register was not cleared. It stood at 25,483 applicants in late 2023, higher than when the policy was announced.
sourceDoc: Green Party 2020 'Homes for All' housing policy, released 9 August 2020

promise: Develop a rent-to-own scheme or similar progressive home ownership models as part of the KiwiBuild programme, with a set allocation of KiwiBuild homes.
statusReason: Progressive home ownership products were created, but not as a defined allocation within KiwiBuild, and at modest scale.
whatHappened: No dedicated rent-to-own allocation was carved out of KiwiBuild as originally described. The September 2019 KiwiBuild reset instead introduced alternative ownership products, including rent-to-own style models and a reduced 5 per cent deposit requirement. A separate Progressive Home Ownership Fund, with the First Home Partner shared-equity scheme, was established from 2020. Volumes under these schemes were small next to the KiwiBuild programme.
sourceDoc: Labour-Green Party Confidence and Supply Agreement, October 2017

promise: Strengthen the Overseas Investment Act and create a comprehensive register of foreign-owned land and housing.
keyNumber: Two commitments -> ban delivered Oct 2018, comprehensive foreign ownership register not established
statusReason: The main limb, strengthening the Overseas Investment Act, was delivered in full early in the term. The separate comprehensive register was not created as described.
whatHappened: The Overseas Investment Amendment Act 2018 received Royal assent on 22 August 2018 and took effect on 22 October 2018. It made existing residential land 'sensitive' and in practice barred most non-resident foreign buyers, with penalties of up to $20,000 for non-compliance. A single comprehensive public register of foreign-owned land and housing was not established as a standalone instrument. Monitoring continued through existing Overseas Investment Office consent records and Statistics New Zealand property transfer data.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement, 24 October 2017

promise: Restore full interest deductibility for residential rental property owners, reversing Labour's 2021 interest limitation rules.
keyNumber: Full deductibility restored -> 80% from 1 Apr 2024, 100% from 1 Apr 2025
statusReason: Full deductibility was restored on the announced timetable within the term.
whatHappened: Finance Minister Nicola Willis confirmed the commitment in December 2023. On 10 March 2024 the Government announced the phasing: 80 per cent of interest expenses deductible from 1 April 2024, and 100 per cent from 1 April 2025. The change was legislated and took effect on those dates.
sourceDoc: National 2023 election housing and tax policy

promise: Reduce the bright-line test on residential property from 10 years back to two years.
keyNumber: 10 years -> 2 years from 1 July 2024
statusReason: Delivered in full and on the date announced.
whatHappened: The Government announced in December 2023 that the bright-line test would return to two years from 1 July 2024. The change was legislated and took effect on that date. Properties sold from 1 July 2024 are only caught if held for less than two years.
sourceDoc: National 2023 election housing and tax policy

promise: Bring back 90-day no-cause terminations for periodic tenancies, and remove the automatic rollover of fixed-term tenancies.
keyNumber: 90-day no-cause notice restored -> in force 30 Jan 2025
statusReason: Both limbs were legislated and in force within about 14 months of taking office.
whatHappened: The Residential Tenancies Amendment Act 2024 was passed, and the main changes took effect on 30 January 2025. Landlords can again end a periodic tenancy with 90 days' notice and no stated ground. Notice for specified grounds fell to 42 days, and tenant notice to 21 days. Either party can end a fixed-term tenancy at expiry with between 90 and 21 days' notice and no reason required. This applies to fixed terms expiring on or after 1 May 2025.
sourceDoc: National 2023 election housing policy

promise: Allow foreign buyers to buy homes worth more than $2 million, taxed at 15 per cent, raising around $700 million a year to help fund tax cuts.
keyNumber: $2m threshold with 15% tax and approx $700m a year -> dropped; $5m threshold for investor-visa holders from early 2026, no 15% tax
statusReason: The manifesto policy was abandoned in coalition negotiation before the Government took office. The later $5 million investor-visa change is a materially narrower policy.
whatHappened: The policy was dropped in the November 2023 coalition negotiations after NZ First refused to accept it, and the tax package was refinanced from other sources. A narrower change was made later. Parliament passed amendments under urgency in December 2025. They allow holders of the Active Investor Plus 'golden visa', who invest at least $5 million, to buy or build a home, effective early 2026. Officials estimated only about 5,000 to 6,000 properties nationally sit above the $5 million threshold, under 0.5 per cent of housing stock.
sourceDoc: National 2023 tax plan, announced 30 August 2023

promise: Retain the First Home Grant for first-home buyers (in contrast to ACT, which campaigned to abolish it).
keyNumber: First Home Grant retained -> abolished 22 May 2024; $245m of savings, $140m redirected to approx 1,500 social homes
statusReason: The scheme National said it would keep was scrapped by National in its first Budget, six months into the term.
whatHappened: On 22 May 2024, as part of Budget 2024, the Government announced the immediate abolition of the First Home Grant. Kāinga Ora stopped accepting new applications from that date, though existing applications were processed. Housing Minister Chris Bishop said the grant was an expensive and inefficient way to support first home buyers. Its value had fallen from nearly 10 per cent of a standard deposit in 2010 to just over 4 per cent in 2024. The change saved $245 million over the four-year forecast period. Of that, $140 million was redirected to about 1,500 new social housing places delivered by community housing providers. The First Home Loan was retained.
sourceDoc: National 2023 election housing policy (support for retaining the First Home Grant)

promise: Allow councils to opt out of the mandatory Medium Density Residential Standards, while requiring them to zone for housing growth.
keyNumber: MDRS optional for all councils -> opt-out enacted for Auckland and Christchurch (Aug 2025); wider changes still in progress
statusReason: Auckland and Christchurch were enabled to opt out, and the policy framework is set. But the general opt-out and the 30-year zoning obligations were not yet law for most councils at August 2026, and the term is unfinished.
whatHappened: Going for Housing Growth stage one was announced on 4 July 2024. The MDRS would become optional, subject to a council ratification vote. Tier 1 and 2 councils would have to live-zone at least 30 years of feasible housing capacity, up from three years. Minimum floor area and balcony rules would be abolished, and Auckland's Rural-Urban Boundary removed. The Resource Management (Consenting and Other System Changes) Amendment Act came into force in August 2025. It provides a process for Auckland and Christchurch to opt out of the MDRS. The wider Pillar 1 package for other councils was still being consulted on and legislated as at August 2026. A submissions summary is due later in 2026.
sourceDoc: National 2023 housing policy and National-ACT coalition agreement (flexibility of the Medium Density Residential Standards)

promise: Reduce the number of households living in emergency housing motels by 75 per cent by 2030.
keyNumber: 75% reduction by 2030 -> 3,141 households (Dec 2023) to 591 (Dec 2024) and 471 (May 2026)
statusReason: The stated numeric target was met, and exceeded, five years ahead of the deadline.
whatHappened: Households in emergency housing motels fell from a peak of 4,983 in November 2021, and 3,141 in December 2023, to 591 in December 2024. That is an 81 per cent reduction against the December 2023 baseline. The Government announced on 24 January 2025 that the target had been met five years early. Numbers fell further, to 471 households by May 2026. The reduction followed the Priority One policy for families with children, tighter eligibility gateways and expanded social housing supply. In August 2026 the Ministry of Social Development removed the emergency-housing reduction measures from regional performance letters. It said numbers were expected to stay broadly stable.
contestedNote: The Government says the fall reflects people moving into stable housing, supported by more social homes and Housing First places. It points to $24.5 million for homelessness services and 300 new Housing First placements. Critics, including the Auckland City Mission, opposition parties and frontline charities, say the target gave Ministry of Social Development staff an incentive to decline applications. The City Missioner described staff as 'perversely incentivised to say no'. Critics also say rough sleeping rose over the same period. MSD dropped the related staff performance measures in August 2026. Both readings accept the headline motel numbers. They differ on where the people went.
sourceDoc: Coalition Government Targets, announced 2024

promise: Conduct an independent review of Kāinga Ora's financial situation, procurement and asset management, and act on its findings.
keyNumber: Independent review promised -> delivered May 2024; peak debt forecast cut from approx $29b to $19.5b by 2029/30
statusReason: The review was commissioned, completed, published and acted on within the term, with a published turnaround plan and reported results against it.
whatHappened: The review was commissioned in December 2023 and released on 20 May 2024. It was led by Sir Bill English with Ceinwen McNeill and Simon Allen. It found the agency was underperforming and not financially viable without significant savings. It also found debt had risen from $2.3 billion in 2017/18 to $16.5 billion in 2023/24. Cabinet reconstituted the board, appointing Simon Moutter as chair from 4 June 2024. It also issued a new Letter of Expectations and required a turnaround plan, which was released 4 February 2025. In 2024/25 Kāinga Ora delivered $211 million of operating savings against a $41 million target, and 2,564 net new homes against a 2,230 target. Peak debt forecasts were cut from about $29 billion to $19.5 billion by 2029/30. Around 321 jobs were cut in September 2024.
sourceDoc: Coalition Government commitment to an independent review of Kāinga Ora, announced December 2023

promise: Allow a granny flat of up to 70 square metres to be built without a building consent or a resource consent.
keyNumber: 70 sqm granny flats consent-free -> in force January 2026
statusReason: Both the building and resource consent exemptions were legislated and in force, at the promised 70 square metre size.
whatHappened: The Building and Construction (Small Standalone Dwellings) Bill passed on 23 October 2025. It created a building consent exemption for simple standalone dwellings of up to 70 square metres that comply with the Building Code and are built by authorised building professionals. The council must be notified before and after the work. A National Environmental Standard for Detached Minor Residential Units removed the resource consent requirement, and the combined regime was in place from January 2026. On 28 April 2026 the Government announced further changes, to allow off-site construction before a Project Information Memorandum is issued and to cover CodeMark-certified structural insulated panels. These are to be made by Order in Council in the third quarter of 2026. MBIE reported more than 52,000 downloads of the guidance within months.
sourceDoc: Coalition Government policy programme, granny flats consent exemption (announced 2024)

promise: Abolish the First Home Grant and the progressive home ownership scheme.
keyNumber: First Home Grant abolished -> closed to new applicants 22 May 2024
statusReason: The First Home Grant, the central element of the policy, was abolished in the Government's first Budget.
whatHappened: Budget 2024, announced on 22 May 2024, scrapped the First Home Grant with immediate effect, and Kāinga Ora accepted no new applications from that date. The change saved $245 million over four years, with $140 million redirected to around 1,500 community housing provider social homes. The First Home Loan was retained. Progressive home ownership funding was later folded into the Government's contestable Flexible Fund arrangements.
sourceDoc: ACT 2023 election housing policy

promise: Allow landlords to charge a pet bond, so that more rentals will accept pets.
keyNumber: Pet bond allowed -> up to 2 weeks' rent from 1 Dec 2025
statusReason: Legislated as promised, in force from 1 December 2025.
whatHappened: The Residential Tenancies Amendment Act 2024 introduced pet provisions that took effect on 1 December 2025. Landlords may require a pet bond of up to two weeks' rent. Tenants must get written consent to keep a pet, and a landlord may refuse only on reasonable grounds.
sourceDoc: ACT 2023 election housing policy (adopted in the National-ACT coalition agreement)

promise: Eliminate the bright-line test on residential property entirely.
keyNumber: Bright-line abolished -> reduced to 2 years, still in force at Aug 2026
statusReason: The test was shortened rather than eliminated, so ACT's specific promise did not happen.
whatHappened: The coalition adopted National's policy instead. The bright-line test was reduced from 10 years to two years with effect from 1 July 2024, but was not abolished. Sales within two years of purchase remain taxable. No proposal to remove the test altogether was advanced during the term.
sourceDoc: ACT 2023 election housing and tax policy

promise: Oppose and unwind the National Policy Statement on Urban Development and the Medium Density Residential Standards.
keyNumber: Remove NPS-UD and MDRS -> MDRS made optional for Auckland and Christchurch; NPS-UD retained
statusReason: The MDRS limb was largely advanced. But the NPS-UD was kept rather than removed, and intensification obligations on councils were extended.
whatHappened: The MDRS were made optional in policy from July 2024. The Resource Management (Consenting and Other System Changes) Amendment Act, in force August 2025, gave Auckland and Christchurch a route to opt out. Further changes for other councils were still in the legislative pipeline at August 2026. The coalition kept the NPS-UD, retaining and in places strengthening intensification requirements, and added obligations to zone 30 years of housing capacity. A replacement planning system to succeed the Resource Management Act was announced in December 2025.
sourceDoc: NZ First 2023 election housing policy

promise: Take action on homelessness through the Aotearoa New Zealand Homelessness Action Plan, a cross-agency plan backed by over $300 million. It committed to 1,000 additional transitional housing places and 18 immediate actions.
keyNumber: 1,000 additional transitional housing places by end 2020 -> 1,005 delivered as at February 2021
statusReason: The named plan and its numeric transitional housing target were delivered on time. But homelessness, as measured by emergency housing and register numbers, rose across the term.
whatHappened: The plan was launched on 13 February 2020 with over $300 million in extra funding. It committed to 1,000 additional transitional housing places by the end of 2020, on top of more than 1,300 already created. Marama Davidson took the Homelessness portfolio in November 2020. The second progress report, released 15 May 2021, recorded 1,005 transitional housing places delivered as at February 2021. It also recorded about $4 million through the Local Innovation Fund for seven initiatives, 37 projects funded through He Taupua, and 342 households engaged in a rapid rehousing pilot with 140 housed. All 18 immediate actions got under way. Against that, households in emergency housing motels and the number on the public housing register both rose sharply over the term. The 2023 Census recorded continued severe housing deprivation.
contestedNote: Supporters point out the plan's own targets were met or exceeded, and that it was the first cross-agency homelessness plan. Critics note the plan's stated purpose was to reduce homelessness. They point out that emergency housing motel numbers and the public housing register both grew sharply while it was in force.
sourceDoc: Labour-Greens Cooperation Agreement 2020, action on homelessness, with Marama Davidson as Associate Minister of Housing (Homelessness)

promise: Reduce net migration by 20,000 to 30,000 a year, mainly by tightening student visas and low-skilled work visas.
keyNumber: cut of 20,000-30,000 a year promised -> net migration gain of 126,000 in the December 2023 year, a record
statusReason: By the October 2023 handover, net migration was at a record high rather than 20,000-30,000 lower. The policy package was never scaled to deliver the promised cut.
whatHappened: Jacinda Ardern confirmed in October 2017 that the coalition negotiation had not changed Labour's policy. The detailed package announced in mid-2018 tightened post-study work visas. Officials estimated it would affect only 9,000 to 12,000 of about 18,266 post-study visa holders. By then the government was calling the 20,000-30,000 figure an estimate rather than a commitment. Net migration then fell sharply for reasons unrelated to policy when the border closed in March 2020, and turned negative during 2021-22. After the border reopened it rebounded to a record. There was a net gain of 126,000 in the December 2023 year, and 245,600 migrant arrivals in the year to October 2023, up 165 percent on the year before. Along the way the government granted residence to 212,649 people through the one-off 2021 Resident Visa.
contestedNote: Labour argues COVID-19 distorts the comparison. The border was shut for two years, then a catch-up surge followed reopening, so no year in the term was a normal test of the policy. Critics note the target was quietly downgraded to an 'estimate' in 2018, before COVID. They also note the government chose to grant residence to more than 212,000 people and to reopen work visa settings after 2021.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 immigration policy

promise: Cut net migration to around 10,000 a year.
keyNumber: 10,000 net migration a year sought -> no migration number in the signed coalition agreement
statusReason: The 10,000 target was dropped in the coalition negotiation and does not appear in the signed agreement.
whatHappened: NZ First campaigned on a net migration figure roughly a fifth of Labour's. Labour's policy prevailed in the coalition negotiation. Jacinda Ardern said on 21 October 2017 that 'Labour's policy remains absolutely unchanged as a result of these negotiations'. The signed coalition agreement contained no net migration number at all. It committed only to ensure work visas reflect genuine skills shortages, cut down on low-quality international education courses, and act on migrant exploitation.
sourceDoc: NZ First 2017 immigration policy

promise: Ensure work visas issued reflect genuine skills shortages and cut down on low quality international education courses.
statusReason: The visa settings were changed broadly as described. The effect on overall student numbers was smaller and less even than intended.
whatHappened: Changes announced in 2018 came into force in late November 2018. They removed employer-assisted post-study work visas and gave graduates at bachelor's level and above a three-year open post-study work visa. Students studying below degree level had to complete two years of study to qualify for a one-year visa. Partner and dependent rights were restricted to students in long-term skill shortage areas at postgraduate level. First-time student visas were down 7 percent in the year to May 2019, though applications from some markets rose. An independent review of the coalition agreement recorded the commitment as fully implemented.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First coalition agreement, October 2017

promise: Take serious action on migrant exploitation, particularly of international students.
keyNumber: action on migrant exploitation promised -> Migrant Exploitation Protection Visa from 1 Jul 2021, but 145 employer accreditations revoked and a critical review of the AEWV in Feb 2024
statusReason: Real protections were built. But the same government's flagship work visa scheme created large-scale exploitation risk, and a formal review found the agency should have done more to prevent it.
whatHappened: MBIE ran a Temporary Migrant Worker Exploitation Review from 2018, backed by $50 million over four years. From 1 July 2021 a Migrant Exploitation Protection Visa let exploited migrants leave an employer and stay lawfully for up to six months. It came with a dedicated 0800 reporting line and extra funding for Immigration NZ and Employment NZ investigators. Against that, the Accredited Employer Work Visa (AEWV) scheme introduced in July 2022 became the largest source of exploitation complaints. An independent assurance review released on 27 February 2024 found serious weaknesses in employer accreditation and job checks. There were nearly 33,000 accredited employers, over 108,000 approved AEWV applications, 145 accreditations revoked and 53 suspended. MBIE accepted all findings and all 10 recommendations. The Human Rights Commission published a critical human rights review of the scheme in 2024.
contestedNote: The government points to the Migrant Exploitation Protection Visa, the $50m package and increased enforcement as delivery of the commitment. Critics say the AEWV, launched under the same government, enabled exploitation on a scale that outweighed those protections. MBIE itself accepted it 'should have done more' on risk.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First coalition agreement, October 2017

promise: Raise the annual refugee quota to 1,500 within three years, with funding for resettlement services.
keyNumber: quota of 1,500 promised -> quota lifted from 1,000 to 1,500 from 1 July 2020; 797 arrivals in the year to June 2020
statusReason: The quota was lifted to 1,500 on the promised timetable. Border closures then meant actual arrivals fell far short of the quota for several years.
whatHappened: Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern announced the increase from 1,000 to 1,500 on 19 September 2018, to take effect from July 2020. The package included $6.2 million operating funding over four years and $7.7 million capital for two new accommodation blocks at the Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre. It also included $32.5 million over three years for public housing for about 150 additional refugee families, and six new settlement locations. The quota did rise to 1,500 places from 1 July 2020. Actual arrivals then collapsed. There were 797 in the year to 30 June 2020 against a 1,000 quota, and no quota arrivals in July 2020 because of COVID-19 border restrictions.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 immigration policy

promise: Increase New Zealand's annual refugee quota to around 6,000 places.
keyNumber: quota of about 6,000 sought -> quota reached 1,500 from July 2020
statusReason: The quota reached 1,500, a quarter of the level the Greens sought, and no further increase followed.
whatHappened: The Greens campaigned for a quota about six times the level in place in 2017. The government lifted the quota to 1,000 from July 2018 and to 1,500 from July 2020. It stayed at 1,500 through the end of the term. No further increase toward the Greens' figure was made in the 2017-2020 confidence and supply period or the 2020-2023 cooperation agreement period.
sourceDoc: Green Party 2017 refugee policy

promise: Provide a one-off simplified residence pathway for about 165,000 migrants already in New Zealand on eligible work visas, and decide most applications within a year.
keyNumber: about 165,000 migrants promised a pathway -> 103,961 applications approved covering 212,649 residents
statusReason: The pathway was opened on the announced timetable and granted residence to more people than the announcement estimated.
whatHappened: Applications opened in two phases from 1 December 2021 and closed on 31 July 2022. Immigration New Zealand received 106,349 applications covering 217,586 people and approved 103,961 of them. That made 212,649 new New Zealand residents, well above the 165,000 estimated when the policy was announced. Processing ran past the one-year expectation for some applicants.
sourceDoc: Labour government policy announcement, 30 September 2021 (one-off 2021 Resident Visa)

promise: Introduce a multiple-entry Parent Visa Boost valid for five years and renewable for a further five. Children or grandchildren sponsor it, health insurance is compulsory, and there is no access to NZ Super or other entitlements.
keyNumber: 5-year renewable parent visitor visa promised -> opened 29 Sep 2025; 708 applications and 230 approvals by 2 Feb 2026
statusReason: The visa was created with the duration, renewal, sponsorship and insurance conditions promised, and is open.
whatHappened: Immigration Minister Erica Stanford confirmed in 2024 that work on the renewable parent visa was under way as a manifesto commitment. The Parent Boost Visitor Visa opened for applications on 29 September 2025. It allows stays of up to five years, with the option of a second five-year visa, sponsorship by a child or grandchild, and a health insurance requirement. By 2 February 2026 Immigration New Zealand had received 708 applications. It had approved 230 and declined 6, with 44 withdrawn and 108 approved in principle pending insurance.
sourceDoc: National 2023 immigration policy announcement, 23 September 2023

promise: Maintain the parent category visa cap at 1,000 places, with sponsors required to adequately support family members.
keyNumber: cap of 1,000 sought -> 2,500 parent resident approvals in principle issued in 2025/26
statusReason: The 1,000 cap was not carried into either coalition agreement and the parent categories operated well above it.
whatHappened: The National-NZ First coalition agreement contains no parent category cap. The National-ACT coalition agreement instead committed to a five-year renewable parent visa. The Parent Resident Visa continued to allow approvals of up to 2,500 a year. In 2025/26 exactly 2,500 approvals in principle were issued (2,103 from the ballot pool and 483 from the queued pool). The separate Parent Boost Visitor Visa opened on 29 September 2025 with no numerical cap of the kind NZ First proposed.
sourceDoc: NZ First 2023 election policies. Immigration

promise: Replace the Accredited Employer Work Visa with a Critical Skill and Labour Shortage Visa that prioritises New Zealand workers.
keyNumber: AEWV replacement sought -> AEWV retained and amended
statusReason: The replacement visa was dropped in the coalition negotiation. In its place came a commitment to improve the existing scheme, which is what happened.
whatHappened: The National-NZ First coalition agreement committed only to 'improve the Accredited Employer Work Visa to focus the immigration system on attracting the workers and skills New Zealand needs' and to ensure Immigration New Zealand undertakes proper risk management and verification. No Critical Skill and Labour Shortage Visa was created. The AEWV remained the main employer-assisted work visa and was reformed in stages instead. The changes included tighter skills and English requirements from 2024, removal of the median wage threshold in favour of market-rate pay, and a shift toward a higher-trust model for compliant employers.
sourceDoc: NZ First 2023 election policies. Immigration

promise: Improve the Accredited Employer Work Visa so the immigration system attracts the workers and skills New Zealand needs. Ensure Immigration New Zealand undertakes proper risk management and verification, and ensure those responsible for abusing migrant workers face consequences.
keyNumber: AEWV reform promised -> 145 accreditations revoked, review recommendations accepted Feb 2024; net migration 130,900 (Feb 2024 year) to 17,600 (Jun 2026 year)
statusReason: The scheme was reviewed, tightened and then rebuilt broadly as the agreement described. The 'Essential Worker' workforce planning mechanism in the same agreement remains an investigation rather than a system.
whatHappened: An independent assurance review of the AEWV released on 27 February 2024 found weaknesses in accreditation and job checks. MBIE accepted all 10 recommendations, and by then 145 employer accreditations had been revoked and 53 suspended. The government tightened the scheme through 2024, adding English language and skills threshold requirements and restricting migrant employment durations. In 2025 it removed the median wage threshold, instead requiring that migrants be paid the market rate for the role, and moved toward a higher-trust model for established compliant employers. Erica Stanford said the scheme had nearly ground to a halt, with waits of more than six months, before the changes. Net migration fell from a peak of 130,900 in the year to February 2024 to a gain of 17,600 in the June 2026 year.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First coalition agreement, 24 November 2023

promise: Remove the median wage requirement from skilled migrant and employer-assisted work visas. Allow family members of visa holders to work, and increase the Recognised Seasonal Employer worker cap.
keyNumber: median wage requirement removed -> replaced with market-rate pay requirement for AEWV roles
statusReason: The median wage change and the skilled migrant rework were delivered. The wider package was implemented in stages, with some thresholds only taking effect in 2026.
whatHappened: The median wage threshold was removed from the Accredited Employer Work Visa and replaced with a requirement that employers pay the market rate for the role. Skilled Migrant Category settings were reworked from August 2024, with new work experience, English language and continuous stay rules. New wage thresholds were set at 1.1 times the median wage from mid-2026. Erica Stanford also confirmed policy decisions on partner work rights alongside the parent visa and investor visa work.
sourceDoc: National-ACT coalition agreement, 24 November 2023

promise: Replace the investor visa category with settings that actually attract international investment to New Zealand.
keyNumber: 116 applications over 2.5 years under old settings -> 837 applications and NZ$2.3b transferred since April 2025
statusReason: The category was rebuilt, and application and investment volumes rose by an order of magnitude against the previous settings.
whatHappened: Revised Active Investor Plus settings took effect on 1 April 2025. They split the visa into a Growth category (NZ$5 million over three years into higher-risk investments) and a Balanced category (NZ$10 million over five years). They also removed the English language requirement and reduced time-in-New Zealand requirements for more active investors. Within under three months, 189 applications had been received, against 116 over the previous two and a half years under the old settings. By 2026 Immigration New Zealand reported 837 applications and 395 approvals since April 2025, covering 2,732 people, with NZ$2.3 billion in capital transferred to New Zealand and a further NZ$2.41 billion in the pipeline. The largest applicant groups were from the United States (277), China (156) and Hong Kong (110).
sourceDoc: National 2023 policy to attract top talent and investment; confirmed as an investor visa replacement by Immigration Minister Erica Stanford in 2024

promise: Revive the international education sector after the COVID-19 collapse.
keyNumber: 83,400 enrolments in 2024 -> 85,535 in Jan-Aug 2025; targets of 105,000 by 2027 and NZ$7.2b exports by 2034
statusReason: Enrolments and export earnings are rising and the visa settings are in place. The enrolment and export targets run to 2027 and 2034, beyond this term.
whatHappened: The government set targets to lift international enrolments from 83,400 in 2024 to 105,000 by 2027 and 119,000 by 2034. It also set a target to double the economic impact of education exports from NZ$3.6 billion in 2024 to NZ$7.2 billion by 2034. Between January and August 2025 New Zealand hosted 85,535 international students, 14 percent more than the same period in 2024, and education-related travel exports reached NZ$4.5 billion in the year to September 2025. Post-study settings were widened from 16 November 2026. A new six-month Short Term Graduate Work Visa covers NZQCF Level 5-7 graduates, and Post Study Work Visa eligibility was extended to Level 7 graduate diploma holders who already hold a bachelor's degree.
sourceDoc: National 2023 international education policy announcement, 21 September 2023

promise: Reduce New Zealand's prison population by 30 percent over 15 years.
keyNumber: 30 pct cut over 15 years promised -> muster 10,645 (Mar 2018) to 8,893 (Sep 2023), about 16 pct
statusReason: The muster fell about 16 percent, well short of 30 percent on the headline measure. The target was also dropped before the 15-year horizon.
whatHappened: Justice Minister Andrew Little announced the 30 percent target in 2018, when the muster stood at 10,645 (31 March 2018: 7,329 sentenced, 3,316 remand). The muster fell to 8,893 by 30 September 2023 (5,006 sentenced, 3,817 remand), a fall of about 16 percent in absolute terms. Over the same period the imprisonment rate per 100,000 people fell from about 213 to about 149. During the 2023 campaign Labour dropped the target. Corrections Minister Kelvin Davis said it had 'largely been achieved' and the focus had moved to rehabilitation and recidivism. The incoming government formally abolished the target in December 2023.
contestedNote: Labour argued the target was met early because it was framed against the imprisonment rate per head of population. That rate fell from about 213 to about 149 per 100,000, close to 30 percent. Critics point out the headline prison muster fell by roughly 16 percent. They also note that much of the fall was in sentenced prisoners while the remand population grew, and that the target was abandoned rather than achieved over its stated 15-year period.
sourceDoc: Labour government criminal justice target announced by Justice Minister Andrew Little, 2018 (Hapaitia te Oranga Tangata programme)

promise: Strive towards adding 1800 new Police officers over three years, with a serious focus on combatting organised crime and drugs.
keyNumber: 1,800 new police over 3 years -> 1,800th new constable sworn in 21 Nov 2019 (gross); net 1,800 above attrition not confirmed in that window
statusReason: The gross recruitment count promised in the agreement was met inside three years. The net increase in officers after attrition took much longer and was disputed throughout.
whatHappened: Police recruitment was funded through Budget 2018 and Budget 2019. The 1800th new constable since the government took office was sworn in on 21 November 2019, about two years into the three-year window, and the government declared the coalition commitment met. A second, separate measure, 1800 additional officers net of attrition, was not reached in the same timeframe. Police Minister Stuart Nash said that net figure was expected around 2021-22, and the shortfall was still being reported in 2022. A McGuinness Institute review of the coalition agreement recorded the commitment as fully implemented.
contestedNote: The agreement did not say whether the 1800 was gross recruits or a net increase. The government counted new constables sworn in and declared success in November 2019. The opposition and later commentators argued the meaningful measure was net officer growth after attrition, which lagged.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First coalition agreement, October 2017

promise: Establish a Criminal Cases Review Commission to investigate possible miscarriages of justice.
statusReason: The Commission was legislated for and stood up within the coalition's term.
whatHappened: The Criminal Cases Review Commission Act was passed in 2019 and the Commission (Te Kahui Tatari Ture) was established as an independent Crown entity. An independent review of the 2017 coalition agreement recorded the commitment as fully implemented.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First coalition agreement, October 2017

promise: Repeal the three strikes sentencing regime.
keyNumber: repeal promised 2017 -> blocked June 2018, enacted 15 Aug 2022
statusReason: The repeal happened as promised, but only in the second term. The coalition partner blocked it for the whole of the first term.
whatHappened: Andrew Little planned to take a repeal to Cabinet in June 2018. On 11 June 2018 the item was pulled after New Zealand First refused to support it, saying it did not want the repeal separated from a broader criminal justice reform package. The repeal only proceeded in the second term, once Labour governed alone. The Three Strikes Legislation Repeal Bill had its first reading on 17 November 2021 and received Royal assent on 15 August 2022. Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori supported it, and National and ACT opposed it. The next government reinstated the regime in 2024.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 justice policy; repeal announced by Justice Minister Andrew Little in 2018

promise: Undertake a comprehensive reform of the criminal justice system, guided by an independent advisory group and a public criminal justice summit.
statusReason: The review process promised was set up and reported. Its central recommendations were not turned into legislation within the term.
whatHappened: The Hapaitia te Oranga Tangata programme was launched in 2018. An independent advisory group, Te Uepu Hapai i te Ora, was appointed, and a criminal justice summit was held in August 2018. Te Uepu reported in 2019, recommending far-reaching change to sentencing, bail and parole. No comprehensive sentencing, bail or parole overhaul was legislated before the October 2023 handover. The main statutory change achieved was the three strikes repeal in 2022. Labour dropped its prison population target during the 2023 campaign.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 justice policy, delivered as Hapaitia te Oranga Tangata: Safe and Effective Justice (August 2018)

promise: Ban military-style semi-automatic firearms and assault rifles, buy them back from owners, and establish a national firearms registry.
keyNumber: ban and buyback promised -> about 51,000 firearms bought back for about NZ$100m; registry live 24 June 2023
statusReason: The ban, the buyback and the registry were all legislated and implemented within the term, on the timetable set out.
whatHappened: Parliament banned the most lethal semi-automatic firearms within weeks of the March 2019 attacks, passing the first tranche 119 votes to 1. A six-month buyback closed in December 2019. It collected about 51,000 firearms from about 33,000 people, plus about 5,000 under a no-questions-asked amnesty, at a cost of about NZ$100 million. The Arms Legislation Act 2020 (Royal assent 24 June 2020) created the firearms registry, shortened licences from ten to five years and added new offences. Labour, the Greens and NZ First supported it, and National and ACT opposed it. The registry went live on 24 June 2023. By 28 September 2023 it held 10,044 licence holders and 47,162 firearms, with full registration required by 31 August 2028.
contestedNote: The government presented the buyback as a large-scale removal of the most dangerous firearms from circulation. The Council of Licensed Firearms Owners estimated about 170,000 such firearms existed beforehand and argued roughly two-thirds were never handed in. There is no agreed independent estimate of the pre-ban stock, so how complete the buyback was remains disputed.
sourceDoc: Government commitment announced by Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern, March 2019, after the Christchurch attacks; carried through in the Arms Legislation Act 2020

promise: Create a specific ram-raid offence. Allow 12 and 13 year olds to be dealt with in the Youth Court for ram raiding, and target adults who recruit children into ram raids.
keyNumber: new ram-raid offence promised -> bill lapsed after first reading (29 Aug 2023), discontinued Feb 2025
statusReason: The bill was introduced and passed only its first reading. The promised offence never became law.
whatHappened: Ram raids rose sharply from 2017, peaking at 714 recorded incidents in 2022. The government responded with a retail crime package in November 2022, including a fog cannon subsidy of $4,000 per shop and a $6 million Retail Crime Prevention Fund. It also introduced the Ram Raid Offending and Related Measures Amendment Bill, which passed its first reading on 29 August 2023. The bill did not pass before the election. The incoming government formally discontinued it on 5 February 2025 in favour of its own youth offending legislation.
sourceDoc: Labour government policy announcement, 2023 (Ram Raid Offending and Related Measures Amendment Bill)

promise: Reform sentencing, bail and parole laws to enable the gradual replacement of most prisons with community-based rehabilitation.
statusReason: The Greens' central sentencing, bail and parole reform was not enacted. The policy direction was reversed after 2023.
whatHappened: No sentencing, bail or parole overhaul of this kind was legislated during the 2020-2023 term. The main justice statute change was the repeal of three strikes in August 2022. The prison muster fell to 8,893 by September 2023, but the government dropped its own prison reduction target during the 2023 campaign. The muster then rose again under the next government, to 11,255 by March 2026.
sourceDoc: Green Party 2020 justice policy

promise: Commit to training no fewer than 500 new frontline police within the first two years.
keyNumber: 500 new frontline police within 2 years -> deadline of 27 Nov 2025 missed; projected date pushed to Sep 2026
statusReason: The commitment carried an explicit two-year deadline, which passed on 27 November 2025 without being met. The target had still not been confirmed as reached by August 2026.
whatHappened: Within weeks of the agreement being signed, Police Minister Mark Mitchell described the goal as 500 additional officers over the three-year term, before NZ First pushed the two-year framing back. Applications surged, with more than 5,500 in 2024, and wings expanded from 80 to 100 recruits from April 2025. But the two-year deadline of 27 November 2025 passed with the target unmet. The projected date was pushed back to early 2026, then May 2026, August 2026 and then September 2026, with Treasury warning even that would require significant catch-up. In April 2026 the Police Commissioner sought answers after recruiting again fell below expected levels. Recruit training was extended from 16 to 20 weeks.
contestedNote: The government argues the officers are being delivered, just later than planned. It points to recruit training being lengthened from 16 to 20 weeks to protect standards, and to Australian police forces actively recruiting New Zealand officers. Critics say a promise with a stated two-year deadline that was missed, and then repeatedly re-dated, is a broken promise regardless of the eventual total.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First coalition agreement, 24 November 2023

promise: Ban gang patches in public places, stop gang members gathering in public, and give police greater search powers over gang members.
keyNumber: gang patch ban promised -> Gangs Act in force 21 Nov 2024; 337 charges and 76 patches seized by 24 Feb 2025
statusReason: The legislation promised was passed and brought into force within the first year of the term and is being enforced.
whatHappened: The Gangs Act 2024 passed its third reading on 19 September 2024 (68-55), received Royal assent on 23 September 2024 and came into force on 21 November 2024. It bans gang insignia in public places, allows police to issue seven-day dispersal notices and lets District Courts impose three-year non-consorting orders. The companion Sentencing Amendment Act 2024 made gang membership an aggravating factor. Enforcement began within minutes, with the first seizure in Hastings three minutes after the law took effect. By 24 February 2025 police had seized 76 gang patches and 67 firearms and laid 337 insignia charges. Two further gangs were added to the identified-gangs list from 3 February 2025, taking the total to 37. The Greens and Te Pāti Māori opposed the legislation, and the Law Society raised freedom of expression and association concerns.
sourceDoc: National-ACT and National-NZ First coalition agreements and the 100-day plan, November 2023

promise: Restore the Three Strikes law, with amendments including a limited benefit for guilty pleas.
keyNumber: three strikes restored -> Act in force 17 June 2025, covering 42 offences with 12 and 24 month sentence thresholds
statusReason: The law was restored with the amendments the agreement itself specified, and is in force.
whatHappened: The Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Bill had its first reading on 25 June 2024, third reading on 13 December 2024 and Royal assent on 17 December 2024, coming into force on 17 June 2025. It covers 42 serious violent and sexual offences (adding strangulation and suffocation). But it applies only where the sentence exceeds 12 months for a first strike and 24 months for later strikes, widens the 'manifestly unjust' exception, and gives a limited guilty plea discount. Qualifying strikes from the old regime that meet the new thresholds were reactivated. The Sensible Sentencing Trust criticised the new regime as weaker than the 2010 law. The Law Society and Human Rights Commission warned of disproportionate effects on Māori and Pasifika.
sourceDoc: National-ACT coalition agreement, 24 November 2023

promise: Amend sentencing law to limit the discounts judges can apply, and to remove concurrent sentences for offending committed while on bail, parole or in custody.
keyNumber: cap on sentencing discounts promised -> 40 pct cap on personal mitigating factors, in force 29 June 2025
statusReason: The discount cap and the cumulative sentencing changes promised were legislated and are in force.
whatHappened: The Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act 2025 came into force on 29 June 2025. It caps total sentence discounts for personal mitigating factors at 40 percent, unless that would be manifestly unjust. It puts guilty plea discounts on a sliding scale capped at 25 percent, falling to 5 percent if the plea comes during trial. It also prevents repeat discounts for youth and remorse, and encourages cumulative rather than concurrent sentencing for offending on bail, in custody or on parole.
sourceDoc: National-ACT and National-NZ First coalition agreements, November 2023

promise: Amend the Sentencing Act so the needs of victims and communities are prioritised, and stop taxpayer funding for section 27 cultural reports.
statusReason: Both the cultural reports change and the victim-focused sentencing amendments were made within the term.
whatHappened: The incoming government removed funding for section 27 cultural reports in December 2023. The Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act 2025, in force 29 June 2025, requires courts to take victims' interests into account at sentencing. It adds aggravating factors for offending against victims who were in state or faith-based care, and extends child-victim protections from under-14s to under-18s for violence and neglect offences. It also creates aggravating factors for serious retail crime against sole workers and home-based businesses.
sourceDoc: National-ACT and National-NZ First coalition agreements, November 2023

promise: Abolish the previous government's prisoner reduction target, and increase funding for Corrections to ensure there is enough prison capacity.
keyNumber: prison capacity funding promised -> about NZ$1.9b in Budget 2024; 596 beds opened June 2025; muster 8,893 (Sep 2023) to 11,255 (Mar 2026)
statusReason: The target was abolished, and major capacity funding and one large new facility were delivered. But most of the promised extra beds are not due until 2029, and the muster has grown faster than capacity.
whatHappened: The prison population reduction target was abolished in December 2023. Budget 2024 allocated close to $2 billion over four years to prisons, staff and rehabilitation. That included an 810-bed extension at Waikeria (600 beds previously funded plus a new 210-bed wing), 685 new frontline Corrections staff and $78 million for rehabilitation for remand prisoners. A 596-bed development at Waikeria (500 high-security beds plus 96 mental health and addiction beds) opened on 5 June 2025, with 300 extra frontline staff recruited. The further 810 beds are scheduled for completion in 2029, after this term. The muster reached 11,255 at 31 March 2026 (6,606 sentenced, 4,537 remand), up from 8,893 in September 2023.
sourceDoc: National-ACT coalition agreement and the 100-day plan, November 2023

promise: Repeal and replace Part 6 of the Arms Act relating to shooting clubs and ranges, and rewrite the Arms Act 1983.
keyNumber: Arms Act rewrite promised -> Arms Bill Royal assent 5 Aug 2026, most provisions in force 23 Sep 2026
statusReason: Both the Part 6 replacement and the full Arms Act rewrite were passed inside the term.
whatHappened: The Arms (Shooting Clubs, Shooting Ranges, and Other Matters) Amendment Act passed on 26 March 2025 and came into force on 29 June 2025, completing the Part 6 commitment. Public consultation on a full rewrite ran in January-February 2025 and drew about 8,500 submissions. Cabinet decisions were announced on 11 November 2025. The Arms Bill was introduced on 8 December 2025, had its first reading on 9 December 2025, and received Royal assent on 5 August 2026, with most provisions taking effect on 23 September 2026. The new law creates an independent firearms regulator with a chief executive appointed by the Governor-General and reporting to the Minister. It also makes gang membership a disqualifier for a licence, adds new offences and infringement powers, and increases penalties.
sourceDoc: National-ACT coalition agreement, 24 November 2023

promise: Move responsibility for the Arms Act to the Ministry of Justice and review the effectiveness of the Firearms Registry by June 2024.
keyNumber: registry review due June 2024 -> published May 2025; registry retained
statusReason: The transfer and the review both happened, but the review was published about eleven months after the deadline in the agreement.
whatHappened: Responsibility for firearms policy moved to the Ministry of Justice, with Associate Justice Minister Nicole McKee (ACT) leading the work. The Firearms Registry Review was not published by the June 2024 deadline. It was released in May 2025. In May 2025 ACT invoked the coalition agreements' 'agree to disagree' provision over firearms decisions. The registry was retained. McKee said in November 2025 that she disagreed with the registry but could not get enough coalition support to scrap it. The Arms Bill passed in August 2026 keeps it while creating a standalone regulator separate from Police. McKee also invoked the agree-to-disagree clause over her proposal to allow access to military-style semi-automatics under strict conditions for club and competitive use, which coalition partners rejected.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First coalition agreement, 24 November 2023

promise: Establish military-style academies for serious repeat youth offenders, backed by legislation creating Young Serious Offender declarations.
keyNumber: military-style academies promised -> 10-person pilot Jul 2024 to Aug 2025; 7 of 10 reoffended; second programme from 9 Mar 2026
statusReason: A pilot ran and a second programme was scheduled. But the enabling legislation had not completed passage, and the promised permanent academy regime was not yet operating at scale.
whatHappened: A 12-month pilot ran from late July 2024 to August 2025 with 10 young men aged 14-17, all Māori. One was withdrawn and eight completed. Seven of the ten reoffended, most within two months of moving to the community phase. One participant died in a car accident and another escaped custody. An independent 82-page evaluation published in November 2025 found meaningful and positive change for participants, including reduced severity of offending. It also concluded the implementation was rushed, therapeutic and clinical support was inadequate, whānau engagement came too late, cultural elements did not go far enough, and the cohort was too small to give meaningful data. The Oranga Tamariki (Responding to Serious Youth Offending) Amendment Bill was introduced in November 2024 and was still progressing through Parliament. A second academy programme was set to begin on 9 March 2026, with academy orders of 3 to 12 months for 15-17 year olds declared Young Serious Offenders.
contestedNote: The government points to the evaluation's finding of positive change and reduced severity of offending among participants, and to the wider fall in serious repeat youth offending. Critics point to seven of ten participants reoffending. They also cite the evaluation's own caution that the cohort was far too small to support any conclusion about effectiveness.
sourceDoc: National 2023 youth justice policy, delivered as Oranga Tamariki Military-Style Academies
