promise: 20,000 fewer people are victims of an assault, robbery or sexual assault.
keyNumber: 20,000 fewer violent crime victims promised -> about 46,000 fewer (185,000 in Oct 2023 to 138,795 in Feb 2026)
statusReason: The reduction reported is more than double the promised 20,000, and has held across successive quarterly reports.
whatHappened: The target is measured against a baseline of 185,000 adult victims in the year to October 2023, using the New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey. The December 2025 factsheet reported 135,797 victims in the year to October 2025, about 49,000 fewer than baseline. The March 2026 factsheet reported 138,795 victims to February 2026, about 46,000 fewer than baseline. Both were rated 'on track'.
contestedNote: The measure is a sample survey estimate with confidence intervals, not a count of reported crimes. The size of the fall therefore carries statistical uncertainty, and the government's own factsheets publish margins of error. The term is also not finished, so the final position will not be known until after November 2026.
sourceDoc: National 2023 campaign commitment, adopted as Government Target 4

promise: A 15 percent reduction in the total number of children and young people with serious and persistent offending behaviour.
keyNumber: 15 pct cut in serious repeat youth offenders promised -> 25 pct cut (1,100 in Jun 2023 to 829 in Mar 2026)
statusReason: The reported reduction of 25 percent exceeds the promised 15 percent, ahead of the target date.
whatHappened: The June 2023 baseline was 1,100. The March 2026 factsheet reported 829 children and young people with serious and persistent offending behaviour, a 25 percent reduction, rated 'on track'. Ram raids fell from a peak of 714 recorded incidents in 2022 to 207 in 2024. Offenders aged 14-17 involved in ram raids fell from 440 in 2023 to 157 in 2024. Progress is uneven across police districts. At December 2025 eight of twelve districts had fallen by at least 20 percent, while Eastern district was above baseline. The government attributes the fall to military-style academies, intensive case management and fast-track responses. The decline in ram raids began in 2023, before the change of government.
contestedNote: The government credits its youth justice measures. Others note that ram raids and youth offending were already falling from their 2022 peak before the change of government, after the previous government's Fast Track and retail crime programmes. That makes it hard to attribute the fall to any single set of policies.
sourceDoc: National 2023 campaign commitment, adopted as Government Target 3

promise: Lead a whole-of-government response to family violence and sexual violence, including coordinating budget proposals across agencies, under a new dedicated ministerial portfolio.
keyNumber: First national FVSV strategy -> Te Aorerekura launched December 2021 with $114.5m over four years in Budget 2022
statusReason: The portfolio was created, the national strategy was published within the term and dedicated multi-year funding was secured for it.
whatHappened: Marama Davidson became New Zealand's first Minister for the Prevention of Family and Sexual Violence in November 2020. Te Aorerekura, the first national strategy to eliminate family violence and sexual violence, was launched in December 2021. It had a 25-year horizon, six strategic shifts and a two-year action plan, and was developed jointly with tangata whenua and the specialist sector. On 10 May 2022 Davidson announced $114.5 million over four years in Budget 2022 to implement it. That included $37.6 million for community initiatives, $38.1 million for integrated community-led responses and $26.7 million for workforce capability. The strategy remained in place at the October 2023 handover.
sourceDoc: Labour-Greens Cooperation Agreement 2020. Marama Davidson appointed Minister for the Prevention of Family and Sexual Violence, leading the whole-of-government response and coordinating related budget proposals

promise: Protect freedom of speech by ruling out the introduction of hate speech legislation, and stop the Law Commission's work on hate speech legislation.
keyNumber: Hate speech legislation ruled out -> no incitement bill introduced by August 2026
statusReason: Both limbs were carried out. No hate speech legislation was introduced, and the Law Commission's hate speech work was stopped.
whatHappened: Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith confirmed in early 2024 that the Government would not proceed with the previous government's proposed incitement (hate speech) law changes. He directed the Law Commission to stop its review of hate speech law, including work that would have extended protection to religious belief. Goldsmith said 'we opposed and will not continue Labour's proposed hate speech laws, because they would have undermined free speech', and confirmed that separate work on hate crime would continue. The Federation of Islamic Associations of New Zealand publicly questioned the decision in April 2024. No hate speech or incitement bill was introduced during the term to August 2026. Work instead proceeded on treating hostility as an aggravating factor at sentencing and on a separate Law Commission reference.
sourceDoc: National. NZ First Coalition Agreement, 24 November 2023 (Strengthening Democracy and Freedoms)

promise: Extend legal protections for groups that experience hate speech, including for reasons of religion, gender, disability or sexual orientation.
keyNumber: Protections promised on 4 additional grounds -> none legislated by October 2023
statusReason: The commitment was first narrowed to one ground and then explicitly removed from the legislative programme by the promising party in February 2023.
whatHappened: The proposal originated in recommendation 40 of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the Christchurch attacks. Six proposals to strengthen incitement law were released for public consultation in mid-2021 and drew a large and divided response. In November 2022 the Government narrowed the plan to cover religious belief only, dropping gender, disability and sexual orientation. On 8 February 2023 Chris Hipkins removed the remaining proposal from the legislative programme and referred the whole area to the Law Commission. He said that would let the Commission 'consider a difficult and highly contested area of law in totality'. No change to incitement law was enacted before the October 2023 handover, and the incoming government stopped the Law Commission's work in 2024.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 manifesto

promise: Commit to re-entry of the Pike River mine.
keyNumber: Re-entry promised -> 2.26km of drift recovered by 17 Feb 2021; main workings not entered; about $48m spent
statusReason: Re-entry happened and the full drift was recovered and examined. But the main mine workings where the men died were never entered, and no bodies were recovered.
whatHappened: The Pike River Recovery Agency was established on 31 January 2018 with a dedicated minister. Manned re-entry of the mine drift began on 21 May 2019 when the concrete seal was breached. In March 2020 Cabinet approved a further $10.8 million plus a $4.2 million contingency to complete the work. The minister confirmed at the time that recovery would not go beyond the end of the drift into the main mine workings. The team reached a roof fall 2.26 kilometres up the drift on 17 February 2021, the end point of the recovery. Forensic examination and deep borehole drilling followed. By March 2022 remains of eight of the 29 men had been located by borehole but could not be retrieved. The agency closed on 1 July 2022 and the site was handed to the Department of Conservation. Total expenditure was about $48 million.
sourceDoc: Labour. NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017 (priority 54: commit to re-entry to Pike River)

promise: Respond to the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the terrorist attack on the Christchurch masjidain with a view to eradicating violent extremism.
keyNumber: 44 recommendations accepted -> 36 implemented or integrated, 8 not progressed (confirmed 2 August 2024)
statusReason: A full response was mounted and most recommendations were implemented. Eight were still outstanding at the end of the term and were later dropped.
whatHappened: The Royal Commission's report, containing 44 recommendations, was released on 8 December 2020, and the Government accepted all 44 in principle on the same day. It established Kapuia, a ministerial advisory group including affected communities, and set up the Ministry for Ethnic Communities in 2021. The Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet tracked progress publicly. The tracker was current to August 2023 at the change of government, with most recommendations complete or under way. On 2 August 2024 the successor government concluded the coordinated response. It reported 36 of the 44 recommendations implemented or integrated into agency work, and confirmed the remaining eight would not be progressed. Those eight included a separate national intelligence agency, a counter-terrorism advisory group, a public reporting system for concerning behaviour, mandatory firearms injury reporting and amendments to hate speech law.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 manifesto

promise: Set higher water quality standards for rural as well as urban waterways, using measurements that take account of seasonal differences.
keyNumber: Higher rural water standards -> NPS-FM 2020, NES-Freshwater and stock exclusion rules in force 3 Sept 2020; farm plans started in 5 regions by 2023
statusReason: The rules were made and came into force. The on-farm instruments were still being phased in region by region when the term ended.
whatHappened: The Essential Freshwater package was gazetted and came into force on 3 September 2020. It included the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management 2020, the National Environmental Standards for Freshwater, stock exclusion regulations and amended water measurement and reporting rules. On-farm, this brought stock exclusion from waterways on a staged timetable, consent or permitted-activity rules for intensive winter grazing, and freshwater farm plans under a new Part 9A of the Resource Management Act. Farmers were given 18 months to get a certified plan once regulations started in their region. Rollout was slower than the design. Plans had started in only five regions (Waikato, Southland, West Coast, Otago and Manawatu-Whanganui) by the change of government, and independent tracking of the coalition agreement records the water quality commitment as only partially implemented.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, priority 47, higher water quality standards for urban and rural

promise: Increase the resourcing of Biosecurity New Zealand within the Ministry for Primary Industries.
statusReason: Recorded as fully implemented in independent tracking of the coalition agreement.
whatHappened: Biosecurity New Zealand's resourcing was increased across the term, and independent tracking of the 2017 coalition agreement records this priority as fully implemented. The system was tested heavily during the period by the Mycoplasma bovis eradication programme and border restrictions. The following government continued to fund biosecurity responses, including foot and mouth disease preparedness exercises and the H5 bird flu response in 2026.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, priority 4, increase MPI Biosecurity New Zealand resourcing

promise: Hold a Select Committee inquiry into biosecurity.
statusReason: Recorded as not implemented. The inquiry never took place.
whatHappened: No Select Committee inquiry into biosecurity was held. Independent tracking of the 2017 coalition agreement records this priority as not implemented. The associated commitment to increase Biosecurity New Zealand's resourcing was implemented.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, priority 4a. Select Committee inquiry into biosecurity

promise: Re-establish a New Zealand Forestry Service, located in regional New Zealand.
keyNumber: Re-establish a Forestry Service -> Te Uru Rākau established, based in Rotorua
statusReason: The agency was created and located in a regional centre as promised.
whatHappened: Te Uru Rākau (Forestry New Zealand) was established as a business unit within the Ministry for Primary Industries, with its head office in Rotorua. Independent tracking of the coalition agreement records the priority as fully implemented. It administered the associated One Billion Trees programme, which had 149,399,000 trees planted by May 2020.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, priority 3, re-establish the New Zealand Forestry Service

promise: Recognise and promote the potential of aquaculture as a driver of regional economic growth.
keyNumber: Aquaculture strategy -> published, targeting a $3 billion industry by 2035
statusReason: The strategy the commitment called for was published within the term. The $3 billion figure is a 2035 goal, not a term commitment.
whatHappened: The Government released an aquaculture strategy setting a goal of a $3 billion aquaculture industry by 2035, and independent tracking of the coalition agreement records the priority as fully implemented. The sector continued to be supported by later governments, including fast-tracked open ocean salmon farming approval in August 2026 and longer marine farming permit durations.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, priority 6, recognise the potential for aquaculture

promise: Examine agricultural debt mediation, along with receivership fees and charges.
keyNumber: Examine farm debt mediation -> Farm Debt Mediation Act passed, Royal assent December 2019
statusReason: The commitment was to examine the issue and it produced legislation within the term.
whatHappened: The Farm Debt Mediation Bill was passed and received Royal assent in December 2019. It created a compulsory mediation scheme before a secured creditor can take enforcement action against a farm business. Independent tracking of the coalition agreement records the priority as fully implemented.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, priority 7, examination of agricultural debt mediation

promise: Honour the Crown's existing irrigation investment commitments.
statusReason: Existing commitments were honoured, which is what the agreement required.
whatHappened: Existing Crown Irrigation Investments commitments were honoured, while no new government funding for large irrigation schemes was provided. Independent tracking of the coalition agreement records the priority as fully implemented. This sat directly against the Labour-Green confidence and supply agreement, which committed to 'winding down Government support for irrigation'.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, priority 5, honour existing Crown Irrigation investment commitments

promise: Provide assistance to the agricultural sector to reduce biological emissions and improve water quality, and to shift to more diverse and sustainable land use including more forestry.
keyNumber: Farm-level emissions pricing designed under He Waka Eke Noa -> no pricing system in force by Oct 2023; scheme disbanded in 2024
statusReason: Research, planting and partnership assistance were delivered, but the pricing and land-use transition the commitment pointed to never took effect.
whatHappened: Agriculture was kept out of the reformed Emissions Trading Scheme in October 2019 in favour of the He Waka Eke Noa primary sector partnership. A legislated backstop would have brought processors into the ETS from 2025 if no alternative was agreed. He Waka Eke Noa reported in 2022 and the Government proposed a farm-level split-gas levy in October 2022. But no farm emissions pricing system was in force when Labour left office in October 2023. Support did flow through research and mitigation programmes and through the One Billion Trees planting programme. The incoming coalition then disbanded He Waka Eke Noa in 2024 and removed agriculture from the ETS entirely. In the January 2026 amendment to the second emissions reduction plan, it confirmed it would not introduce on-farm emissions pricing by 2030.
sourceDoc: Labour-Green Confidence and Supply Agreement 2017

promise: Improve water quality and prioritise achieving healthy rivers, lakes and aquifers, with stronger regulatory instruments, funding for freshwater enhancement and a wind-down of Government support for irrigation.
keyNumber: Wind down support for irrigation -> existing Crown Irrigation commitments honoured in full
statusReason: Stronger freshwater regulation and enhancement funding arrived. The irrigation wind-down was constrained by a competing commitment in the other coalition agreement.
whatHappened: The regulatory side was delivered through the Essential Freshwater package, in force from 3 September 2020. It introduced Te Mana o te Wai and a hierarchy putting the health of water bodies first, together with stock exclusion rules and freshwater farm plans. Government support for irrigation was not wound down in the way the agreement implied. The parallel Labour-NZ First coalition agreement committed to honouring existing Crown Irrigation investment commitments, and that commitment was recorded as fully implemented. Freshwater enhancement funding was provided through Jobs for Nature and catchment programmes.
contestedNote: The Greens can point to the 2020 freshwater rules as the strongest regulatory instruments ever applied to farming. Critics of the claim note that the commitment to wind down irrigation support was cut across by the NZ First commitment to honour existing Crown irrigation investments, which was implemented in full.
sourceDoc: Labour-Green Confidence and Supply Agreement 2017

promise: Reverse the recent ban on live animal exports while ensuring the highest standards of animal welfare.
keyNumber: Reverse the live export ban -> legislation timetable slipped from early 2025; exports had not resumed by Aug 2026
statusReason: Consultation and policy work proceeded. But the ban had not been lifted and the trade had not resumed nearly three years into the term.
whatHappened: On 27 June 2024 the Government said it would consult before September 2024, take Cabinet decisions by the end of 2024 and introduce legislation amending the Animal Welfare Act 1999 in early 2025. By 20 November 2024 the timetable had shifted. Officials would engage with industry and animal welfare groups over November and December 2024, a discussion document would be released for public comment in 2025, and legislative proposals would go to a select committee during 2025. Ministers said exports would only restart once strengthened welfare standards were in effect, and that exports for slaughter, stopped in 2007, would not resume. The trade was valued at $374 million in 2022. No announcement that livestock exports by sea had resumed had been made as at August 2026.
contestedNote: The Government's position is that the reversal is on track and deliberately sequenced behind new welfare standards, which would make this in-progress. Read against the promise itself, the ban is still in force close to three years after the commitment was signed. That reads as well short of delivery.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023 (the same commitment appears in the National-ACT agreement)

promise: Stop exotic planting on Land Use Capability class 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 land from entering the Emissions Trading Scheme for carbon sequestration. The aim is to protect productive farmland from carbon farming.
keyNumber: No exotic ETS forestry on LUC 1-5 -> legislated 2025, with LUC 6 capped at 15,000 hectares a year
statusReason: The LUC 1-5 restriction the manifesto specified was legislated, with an added annual cap on LUC 6 and a 25 per cent on-farm allowance.
whatHappened: The policy was announced on 4 December 2024. The Climate Change Response (Emissions Trading Scheme. Forestry Conversions) Amendment Bill was introduced on 10 June 2025 and passed its first reading on 25 June 2025, with effect intended from October 2025. Exotic forestry on actively farmed LUC 1-5 land is restricted from entering the ETS. LUC 6 land is capped at 15,000 hectares of new ETS registrations a year, allocated by ballot from mid-2026 with a reserved share for small block holders. Landowners may still put up to 25 per cent of LUC 1-6 land into ETS forestry. There are transitional exemptions for investments made between 1 January 2021 and 4 December 2024, and specific protections for Māori-owned land.
sourceDoc: New Zealand First 2023 Policy Manifesto: 'Right tree, right place'

promise: Direct government agencies, where practical and appropriate, to prefer woollen fibres rather than artificial fibres in government buildings.
keyNumber: Prefer wool in government buildings -> Kāinga Ora carpet tender reopened to wool Jan 2025; detailed direction still being worked through
statusReason: The one clear procurement outcome was a single agency reopening a tender. Sector investment has been large, but a whole-of-government wool preference direction has not been published.
whatHappened: In January 2025 Kāinga Ora reopened its carpet tender to include wool suppliers, after ministers objected to woollen carpets being ruled out. The Housing Minister said at the time the Government was still 'working through the finer details' of the wool preference commitment. Separate support for the sector followed, rather than a published procurement rule. It included a government woolshed roadshow in April 2024, the reopening of a wool scouring facility in April 2024, and an export deal for wool particle technology in December 2025. On 11 June 2026 the Government announced an $8 million contribution to a $20 million Wool Source manufacturing plant in Christchurch, with capacity of one million kilograms a year.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023

promise: Cease the implementation of new Significant Natural Areas and seek advice on the operation of existing Significant Natural Areas.
keyNumber: Cease new SNAs -> three-year suspension announced 14 March 2024, legislated 24 October 2024
statusReason: Both limbs of the commitment (stopping new SNAs and reviewing existing ones) were actioned and legislated within the first year.
whatHappened: On 14 March 2024 the Government announced a three-year suspension of councils' obligation to identify new Significant Natural Areas under the National Policy Statement for Indigenous Biodiversity. It told councils they no longer needed to comply with the SNA provisions. The scope of a review of existing SNAs was announced on 28 August 2024. The suspension passed its third reading on 24 October 2024 as part of the first Resource Management Act amendment bill.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023

promise: Improve farm plans so they are more cost-effective and pragmatic for farmers, tailored to the risks on the property and catchment rather than applied broadly.
keyNumber: Cheaper, more pragmatic farm plans -> minimum farm size lifted from 20ha to 50ha, about 8,000 farms exempted
statusReason: The system was legislatively rewritten along the lines promised, with a narrower scope and industry certification.
whatHappened: On 10 April 2024 the Government announced the freshwater farm plan system would be reworked because it was 'too costly and complex, and too broadly applied'. The rollout was paused from September 2024, and Southland farmers were given more time in November 2024. The Resource Management (Consenting and Other System Changes) Amendment Act, announced as law on 20 August 2025, allowed approved industry organisations such as Horticulture New Zealand's NZGAP and Fonterra's Tiaki to certify and audit plans. It also refocused plans on actual farm risks and lifted the minimum farm size requiring a plan from 20 hectares to 50 hectares for sheep, beef, arable, orcharding and viticulture. About 8,000 smaller, lower-risk farms no longer need a plan. An improved farm plan system for Southland was announced on 18 May 2026.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023, improve Farm Environment Plans so they are more cost-effective and pragmatic for farmers

promise: Support Farm Environment Plans administered by regional councils and targeted at a catchment level, and adopt standardised farm level reporting.
keyNumber: Catchment-level farm plans -> $36m over four years for catchment group support announced June 2024
statusReason: Catchment-level support and standardised measurement were delivered, but certification was shifted partly away from regional councils rather than administered by them.
whatHappened: Budget 2024 provided $36 million over four years for regionally based MPI staff supporting catchment groups. It was announced on 5 June 2024, with $7 million going directly to 11 catchment groups and collectives. Further catchment group funding was announced in May 2025, and longer-term certainty for rural catchment groups was announced on 11 June 2026. On standardised reporting, the Government announced a standardised on-farm emissions measurement tool on 13 December 2024. Farm plans themselves moved away from purely council administration. The 2025 Resource Management amendment allows approved industry bodies, not only regional councils, to certify and audit freshwater farm plans.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023

promise: Double the value of New Zealand's exports within a decade, with food and fibre exports carrying much of the growth.
keyNumber: Double exports in a decade -> food and fibre exports forecast at $64.3b for the year to June 2026, projected $70.1b by 2030
statusReason: Export values are rising and hitting records. But the forecast growth path to 2030 is far short of doubling, and the ten-year period runs past the current term.
whatHappened: The Ministry for Primary Industries' June 2026 outlook forecast food and fibre export revenue of $64.3 billion for the year to 30 June 2026, up 6 per cent. That was made up of dairy at $28.6 billion (up 5 per cent) and meat and wool at $14.1 billion (up 14 per cent). Horticulture was $9.5 billion (up 7 per cent), and processed foods and other products $3.5 billion (up 5 per cent). The same forecast projects $70.1 billion by June 2030. The December 2025 forecast had been $62 billion. Trade agreements concluded in the period include the NZ-EU FTA entering into force on 1 May 2024, a Gulf Cooperation Council deal in October 2024 and a free trade agreement with India announced on 22 December 2025.
sourceDoc: National 2023 commitment to double the value of New Zealand's exports within a decade, as restated by the Government at Fieldays 2026

promise: Cut red tape and regulatory blocks on irrigation, water storage, managed aquifer recharge and flood protection schemes.
keyNumber: Cut rural red tape -> 12 national direction instruments amended and 4 new ones proposed from May 2025; RMA replacement bills still in Parliament in Aug 2026
statusReason: A large deregulation programme is well advanced but the central resource management replacement was still before Parliament as at August 2026.
whatHappened: Consultation opened on 29 May 2025 on a sweeping national direction package. It covered amendments to 12 instruments and 4 new ones across infrastructure, primary sector and freshwater, with a target of 16 new or updated national direction instruments in place by the end of 2025. The primary sector package proposed removing restrictions on non-intensive grazing of beef cattle and deer in wetlands, and removing LUC 3 land from the National Policy Statement on Highly Productive Land. It also proposed streamlining aquaculture consent changes, easing forestry rules and creating special agricultural areas around horticulture hubs such as Pukekohe and Horowhenua. Updated national direction for natural hazards and highly productive land was announced on 15 January 2026. The Natural Environment Bill and Planning Bill replacing the Resource Management Act were reported back from select committee in July 2026, with the Agriculture Minister calling it a significant step for the primary sector.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023

promise: Double the cap on Recognised Seasonal Employer workers to give horticulture and viticulture a bigger seasonal workforce.
keyNumber: Double the RSE cap -> about 17,000 RSE workers a year as at July 2026, scheme changes staged 2027-2029
statusReason: The scheme was reviewed and reworked but the published intake remains at about 17,000 a year, nowhere near double.
whatHappened: An RSE modernisation package was announced on 28 July 2026. It includes a graduated accreditation system recognising employers with a strong track record, and more flexibility for workers to move between employers with added safeguards. It also sets clearer rules on recoverable transport, insurance and accommodation costs, and adds internet access to accommodation standards. The changes are staged from early 2027 through to 2029. The Government's own statement records about 17,000 RSE workers a year across 207 accredited employers, alongside horticulture export growth from $2.5 billion in 2007 to nearly $9 billion. No doubling of the scheme's cap has been announced.
contestedNote: Read strictly, no doubling of the cap has been announced and annual intake remains around 17,000. Read generously, RSE settings have been reworked to expand employer capacity, and the changes do not take effect until 2027-2029, so the outcome is not yet measurable.
sourceDoc: National 2023 horticulture policy, as summarised in RNZ's guide to party policy

promise: Review the suitability of the systems dealing with by-catch within the Quota Management System, while retaining the QMS itself.
keyNumber: Review bycatch systems -> consultation drew over 22,000 submissions; retention ban on 19 reef fish species kept, 19 March 2026
statusReason: The bycatch review the manifesto promised was carried out with public consultation and produced ministerial decisions. Parts of the package remain undecided.
whatHappened: The Government consulted on a wider package of commercial fishing rule changes, including a proposal to let commercial fishers retain and sell 19 non-quota reef fish species taken as bycatch. The consultation drew more than 22,000 submissions. On 19 March 2026 the Oceans and Fisheries Minister decided to keep the existing ban, in place since 1993, saying he had weighed the costs and benefits along with feedback from recreational fishers and the public. Further decisions from the same consultation were still to be announced, including proposed changes to the deemed value regime consulted on in January 2026.
sourceDoc: New Zealand First 2023 Policy Manifesto, fisheries

promise: Amend the National Environmental Standards for Plantation Forestry to place a duty on harvesters to contain and remove post-harvest slash.
statusReason: The change is being carried inside a wider resource management rewrite still before Parliament rather than delivered as a standalone amendment.
whatHappened: Forestry rules were folded into the wider national direction programme consulted on from 29 May 2025, which included reducing inefficiencies in forestry regulation. They were also folded into the Resource Management Act replacement bills reported back from select committee in July 2026. Slash management in the worst-affected region remained an active problem. On 17 August 2026 the Government appointed a facilitator to restore confidence in Tairawhiti forestry. A specific standalone duty on harvesters to contain and remove slash had not been separately announced as in force by August 2026.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023

promise: Merge Radio New Zealand and Television New Zealand into one new public media entity, Aotearoa New Zealand Public Media. It would run as an autonomous Crown entity from 1 March 2023.
keyNumber: Merged entity from 1 March 2023 -> cancelled 8 Feb 2023 at a sunk cost of about $19.6m
statusReason: The promising party cancelled the merger outright in February 2023, after the bill had already passed its first reading.
whatHappened: Broadcasting Minister Willie Jackson introduced the Aotearoa New Zealand Public Media Bill on 23 June 2022. It passed its first reading on 26 July 2022. The start date slipped from 1 March 2023 to July 2023. On 8 February 2023 Prime Minister Chris Hipkins announced the merger would stop entirely, as part of a policy reprioritisation towards cost-of-living measures. RNZ received an extra $10 million instead. By April 2023 the cancelled project had cost about $19.6 million. That was roughly $12 million on contractors and consultants, $2.6 million on offices and overheads, and $3 million in compensation to TVNZ, RNZ and NZ On Air.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 term commitment to a new public media entity, following the 2019 advisory group process and Cabinet consideration in January 2020

promise: Ban foreign donations to political parties and candidates above a nominal threshold.
keyNumber: Foreign donation cap cut to $50
statusReason: The ban was legislated and in force well before the end of the term.
whatHappened: A law was passed banning foreign donations above NZ$50 to political parties and candidates. It replaced the previous $1,500 threshold. The change was in force for the 2020 general election and stayed in place for the rest of the term.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017-2020 term commitment to tighten electoral donation rules against foreign influence

promise: Restore the right to vote for prisoners serving sentences of less than three years, reversing the 2010 blanket ban.
keyNumber: Voting restored for sentences under 3 years; ban retained for 3 years and over
statusReason: The promised partial restoration was legislated within the term. Lifting the wider ban was never promised.
whatHappened: A law passed in 2020 restored the vote to prisoners serving sentences of under three years, in time for the general election that year. Separate legislation removed the Electoral Commission's power to strike prisoners from the electoral roll. The blanket ban on voting for those serving three years or more stayed in place.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 term commitment to act on the Supreme Court's declaration of inconsistency and the Waitangi Tribunal's findings on the prisoner voting ban

promise: Hold a referendum on legalising the personal use of cannabis at, or by, the 2020 general election.
keyNumber: Referendum by the 2020 election -> held 17 Oct 2020, 51.17 per cent no to 48.83 per cent yes
statusReason: The promise was to hold the referendum by the 2020 election, and it was held on time. The outcome was not part of the commitment.
whatHappened: The referendum was held alongside the general election on 17 October 2020. It asked voters whether they supported the proposed Cannabis Legalisation and Control Bill. Voters rejected the proposal: 1,474,635 votes (51.17 per cent) against and 1,406,973 votes (48.83 per cent) in favour. The referendum was non-binding, so Parliament was not required to act on the result. The bill was not proceeded with.
sourceDoc: Labour-Greens Confidence and Supply Agreement 2017

promise: Hold a binding referendum on overturning New Zealand's anti-smacking law.
keyNumber: Binding referendum promised -> dropped in the 2017 coalition negotiation, 0 held
statusReason: The commitment was traded away in the 2017 coalition negotiation, before the government took office.
whatHappened: In the October 2017 coalition negotiations, NZ First agreed to drop its demand for referendums on overturning the anti-smacking law and on abolishing the Māori electorates. That was part of the price of forming a government with Labour. Neither referendum was held during the 2017-2023 government, and the law was not changed.
sourceDoc: NZ First 2017 election campaign commitment to binding referendums, including on the anti-smacking law

promise: Amend the Public Service Act 2020 to clarify the role of the public service, drive performance, and make it accountable for delivering the agenda of the government of the day.
keyNumber: Amend the Public Service Act 2020 -> bill first reading 31 July 2025, not passed as at Aug 2026
statusReason: Term unfinished: the bill was introduced and passed a first reading, but it had not been enacted with under three months of the term remaining.
whatHappened: Public Service Minister Judith Collins announced the overhaul on 1 April 2025. She said the 2020 Act 'added new responsibilities to the core role of chief executives which diminished their responsibility for implementing government policies'. The Public Service Amendment Bill passed its first reading on 31 July 2025. It clarifies the role of the public service, streamlines chief executive responsibilities and reinforces merit-based appointments. It also ends automatic reappointment at the end of a fixed term and strengthens performance management. It removes pay equity, diversity and inclusion provisions on the basis that they are covered elsewhere. The bill had not passed its remaining stages as at 17 August 2026. A separate Plain Language Act Repeal Bill passed its first reading on 1 April 2025.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023

promise: Cut public service spending on consultants and contractors by $400 million over two years to 2024/25.
keyNumber: $400m saved on consultants and contractors over 2 years -> about $800m by June 2025
statusReason: The savings target was met and roughly doubled inside the promised period, on the Government's own published figures.
whatHappened: Public Service Minister Judith Collins announced on 27 March 2025 that savings were on track to reach about $800 million by the end of June. That is double the original $400 million target. Earlier data released on 13 June 2024 showed contractor and consultant spending had fallen to $700.5 million over nine months. That was down 34 per cent on an annualised basis, and the lowest share of total workforce expenditure since 2018. A further release on 9 October 2025 reported contractor spending down by $915 million, while frontline roles increased over two years.
sourceDoc: National 2023 campaign commitment to cut back-office and contractor spending, given effect by the Government's savings target set in Budget 2024

promise: Reduce Core Crown expenditure as a proportion of the overall economy.
keyNumber: Public service FTEs 65,699 (Dec 2023 peak) -> 62,654 (Jun 2025) -> 64,535 (Mar 2026); target 55,000 by July 2029
statusReason: Spending as a share of the economy was forecast to fall, but the reduction sits mostly beyond the end of this term. The public service workforce was also larger in March 2026 than a year earlier.
whatHappened: Public service full-time equivalent staff peaked at 65,699 in the December 2023 quarter. Over the next 18 months they fell 4.6 per cent to 62,654 by June 2025, then rose again to 64,535 by March 2026. Budget 2026 was delivered on 28 May 2026. It forecast core Crown expenses staying stable as a share of GDP for the first two forecast years, then falling to 30.3 per cent of GDP in 2029/30. It also forecast the operating balance returning to a $2.6 billion surplus in 2028/29, and net core Crown debt peaking at 46.1 per cent of GDP in 2027/28. On 19 May 2026 Finance Minister Nicola Willis announced a plan to cut 8,700 public sector jobs and merge departments by mid-2029. It targets 55,000 FTEs by July 2029 and $2.4 billion of savings, with teachers, doctors, nurses, police and defence personnel excluded.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement, signed 24 November 2023

promise: Support a bill providing for a binding referendum on extending the parliamentary term from three years to four.
keyNumber: Binding referendum on a 4-year term -> scrapped 18 Feb 2026, 0 referendums held
statusReason: The referendum the commitment was aimed at was explicitly dropped in February 2026, and the term was not extended.
whatHappened: A four-year term proposal was progressed during the term. But on 18 February 2026 the Government confirmed it had scrapped plans to hold a referendum on extending the parliamentary term at the 2026 general election. No referendum on the parliamentary term was held or scheduled, and the three-year term applied to the 7 November 2026 election.
contestedNote: The commitment was to support a bill to a referendum, not to guarantee a referendum. On that reading the parties met their obligation, and the referendum simply did not survive the parliamentary process. The detail of the bill's progress through the House was not established from the sources available for this run. The status call therefore rests mainly on the February 2026 decision not to hold the referendum.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement, signed 24 November 2023

promise: Conduct a full-scale, wide-ranging, independent public inquiry into the Covid-19 pandemic response, covering matters the existing inquiry did not.
keyNumber: Wider Covid-19 inquiry -> scope expanded 2 Feb 2024, phase two hearings from 7 July 2025, report 10 March 2026
statusReason: A second, expanded inquiry phase covering the promised subject matter was established and reported inside the term.
whatHappened: The Labour government established the Royal Commission of Inquiry into COVID-19 Lessons Learned on 5 December 2022. It launched on 1 February 2023 at an estimated cost of $15 million. On 2 February 2024 Internal Affairs Minister Brooke van Velden announced the scope would be expanded. On 25 June 2024 the Government confirmed a second phase covering vaccine efficacy and safety, the use of vaccine mandates, lockdowns, and the disruption to health, education and business. The phase one report was released on 28 November 2024. Phase two public hearings began on 7 July 2025. The phase two report was released on 10 March 2026 and concluded that the response was effective but late and poorly communicated.
contestedNote: NZ First campaigned for a separate standalone inquiry. The Government instead expanded and re-staged the existing Royal Commission. Supporters say the expanded terms of reference cover everything that was promised. Critics, including some of those who pushed for the inquiry, say reusing the existing commission was not the fresh independent inquiry that was sought. The terms of reference, hearing dates and report dates are agreed.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement, signed 24 November 2023

promise: Pass a Regulatory Standards Act setting principles of responsible regulation, so that all new and existing legislation is tested against those principles.
keyNumber: Regulatory Standards Act -> passed 13 Nov 2025, in force 1 July 2026; about 23,000 submissions, 88 per cent opposed
statusReason: The Act was passed and brought into force inside the term, with the review board established and operating.
whatHappened: Public consultation ran from 19 November 2024 to 13 January 2025 and drew nearly 23,000 submissions. The Ministry estimated 88 per cent opposed the proposal and 0.33 per cent supported it. The bill was introduced on 19 May 2025 and passed its first reading on 23 May 2025 by 68 votes to 55. The Finance and Expenditure Committee heard oral submissions on 7-10 July 2025 and reported back on 10 October 2025. The bill passed its second reading on 4 November 2025 and its third reading on 13 November 2025, on party lines, with royal assent later that month. A Regulatory Standards Board was appointed on 20 April 2026, statutory guidance was issued on 15 May 2026, and the Act took effect on 1 July 2026.
contestedNote: ACT's position is that the Act creates a transparent, non-binding quality check on regulation, protecting property rights and the rule of law. Opponents, including the large majority of submitters, argued it embeds a particular economic philosophy in statute, weakens environmental protection and omits the Treaty of Waitangi. The Waitangi Tribunal heard an urgent claim on 15 May 2025 and issued an interim report on 16 May 2025, urging the Crown to pause for consultation with Māori. David Seymour disputed the submission figures, claiming 99.5 per cent were bot-generated. The legislative dates and vote outcomes are not in dispute.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023

promise: Reduce the size and number of government departments and back-office functions, protecting frontline staff such as teachers, doctors, nurses and police.
keyNumber: Back-office reduction promised -> 4 agencies merged into MCERT from July 2026; 8,700 further cuts scheduled to mid-2029, FTEs 64,535 as at March 2026
statusReason: Real agency mergers and savings were achieved. But the public service was still larger in March 2026 than in mid-2025, and most of the promised reduction is scheduled for after this term.
whatHappened: Finance Minister Nicola Willis asked departments on 26 January 2024 to identify $1.5 billion in annual savings. At least 845 job losses had been signalled by 6 April 2024. On 16 December 2025 the Government announced a merger. The Ministry for the Environment, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development, the Ministry of Transport and the local government functions of the Department of Internal Affairs would become a new Ministry of Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport. The enabling legislation passed on 27 May 2026 and the ministry was to be operational from July 2026. Judith Collins said the merger was 'not intended as a cost-cutting exercise'. On 19 May 2026 the Government announced a further 8,700 job reductions and department mergers by mid-2029, a 14 per cent cut. That targets 55,000 FTEs and $2.4 billion of savings. Budget 2026 cut Te Puni Kōkiri by $23.6 million, the Ministry for Pacific Peoples by $2.8 million and the Ministry for Culture and Heritage by $27 million.
contestedNote: The exact wording of National's 2023 back-office commitment was not verified from a primary manifesto document in this run. The promise text is therefore a summary of the position the Government has consistently described, rather than a word-for-word quotation. The events, dates and figures in the record of what happened all come from Government or Budget sources.
sourceDoc: National 2023 campaign commitment to reduce back-office bureaucracy and the number of government agencies while protecting frontline services

promise: Eliminate the gender pay gap within the public sector.
keyNumber: Eliminate the public sector gender pay gap -> median gap fell from 10.7 per cent (2018) to 5.8 per cent (June 2023); mean gap 7.1 per cent
statusReason: The gap roughly halved over the term, but the agreement promised elimination and it was not eliminated.
whatHappened: The Public Service Commission ran a Gender Pay Gap Action Plan from 2018. It then ran Kia Toipoto, the Public Service Pay Gaps Action Plan 2021-24. That plan extended coverage to Māori, Pacific and ethnic pay gaps, and required every agency to publish an action plan. The public service median gender pay gap fell from 10.7 per cent in 2018 to 5.8 per cent as at 30 June 2023. The mean gap was 7.1 per cent in 2023 ($101,700 average for men against $94,500 for women). The gap narrowed but was not eliminated by the October 2023 handover, and Kia Toipoto ran to 2024.
sourceDoc: Labour-Green Confidence and Supply Agreement 2017, policy goal 12, eliminate the gender pay gap within the public sector

promise: Provide multi-year contestable funding through NZ On Air to fund public interest journalism.
keyNumber: $55m fund promised -> about $64m allocated, 73 projects and 219 roles funded by April 2023
statusReason: The multi-year contestable fund was set up through NZ On Air and fully allocated within the term, as promised.
whatHappened: A $55 million three-year Public Interest Journalism Fund was announced in 2021 and administered by NZ On Air. NZ On Air added a further $9 million, taking the total to about $64 million. The fund ran from July 2021 and completed its final general funding round in April 2023, across seven rounds. It supported 73 projects, 219 journalism roles and 22 industry development initiatives, including regional coverage and Māori journalist training. NZ On Air reported more than 60,000 pieces of funded content and over 134 million views by early April 2023. The fund was time-limited and was not renewed.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 manifesto

promise: Protect the integrity of New Zealand elections and voters' access to the polls, including a review of election financing rules.
keyNumber: Review of financing rules -> disclosure changes legislated Dec 2022; Independent Electoral Review reported 30 Nov 2023, after the term
statusReason: Targeted donation and loan disclosure changes were legislated. But the broader review of financing rules reported only after the term had ended, and produced no legislative change.
whatHappened: Two workstreams followed. The Electoral Amendment Act 2022 passed in December 2022, in time for the 2023 general election. It lowered the threshold at which party donations must be publicly attributed to a named donor, and required disclosure of party loans. Separately, an Independent Electoral Review panel of six was appointed and worked from May 2022 to November 2023. It carried out a full review of the Electoral Act 1993, including party and candidate funding. The panel delivered its final report to the Minister of Justice on 30 November 2023, and the report was published on 16 January 2024. Both fell after the change of government, so no response to the panel's recommendations was possible within the term.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 manifesto

promise: Repeal the Resource Management Act 1991 and replace it with three new laws (a Natural and Built Environments Act, a Spatial Planning Act and a Climate Change Adaptation Act), acting on the recommendations of the Randerson review.
keyNumber: 3 replacement acts promised -> 2 passed (Aug 2023), 0 in operation at handover
statusReason: Two of the three promised statutes were passed inside the term. The third was never introduced, and neither Act had begun operating before the handover.
whatHappened: The independent review panel chaired by retired Court of Appeal judge Tony Randerson reported in 2020 and recommended repealing and replacing the RMA. On 10 February 2021 the Government announced the three-law replacement. An exposure draft of the Natural and Built Environments Bill went to a select committee inquiry in 2021. The Natural and Built Environment Bill and Spatial Planning Bill were introduced together on 14 November 2022. Both passed their third readings on 15 August 2023 by 72 votes to 47 and received royal assent on 23 August 2023, about eight weeks before the general election. The third law, the Climate Change Adaptation Bill, was never introduced. Neither new Act was in operation when the government changed: no natural and built environment plan or regional spatial strategy had been made.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 campaign commitment to repeal and replace the RMA, given effect by the 10 February 2021 Government announcement following the Randerson review

promise: Pass a Climate Change Adaptation Act as the third pillar of the resource management reform, to deal with managed retreat and the funding of climate adaptation.
keyNumber: Climate Change Adaptation Act promised -> bill never introduced
statusReason: The promised third Act was never introduced, let alone passed, in either term.
whatHappened: The Climate Change Adaptation Bill was the only one of the three announced replacement laws never introduced to Parliament. Work was still at the policy stage when the term ended. A cross-party inquiry into community-led retreat and adaptation funding was under way in 2023, and no adaptation statute existed at the October 2023 handover. The two Acts that did pass, the Natural and Built Environment Act 2023 and Spatial Planning Act 2023, were repealed in December 2023.
sourceDoc: Labour-led Government's February 2021 three-law RMA replacement programme (Climate Change Adaptation Act)

promise: Require every region to prepare a long-term regional spatial strategy, agreed between councils, central government and iwi, to co-ordinate land use, infrastructure and development.
keyNumber: Regional spatial strategies legislated Aug 2023 -> 0 completed before repeal Dec 2023
statusReason: The statute promised was enacted within the term, judged as at the October 2023 handover. Its later repeal was the successor government's decision.
whatHappened: The Spatial Planning Bill was introduced on 14 November 2022, and the Spatial Planning Act 2023 received royal assent on 23 August 2023. It required each region to develop a regional spatial strategy through a joint committee of councils, central government agencies and Māori representatives. No regional spatial strategy was completed before the Act was repealed on 23 December 2023, and the country reverted to the RMA 1991.
sourceDoc: Labour-led Government's RMA replacement programme. Spatial Planning Act

promise: Use a National Policy Statement on Urban Development to force councils to allow greater building height and density near city centres and rapid transit. It would also make councils remove minimum car parking requirements from district plans.
keyNumber: 6-storey enablement near centres and rapid transit -> in force Aug 2020, parking minimums gone by Feb 2022
statusReason: The national policy statement was issued, took effect and was implemented through council plan changes within the term. It survived the change of government.
whatHappened: The NPS-UD was gazetted in July 2020 and came into force in August 2020. It required tier 1 councils to enable buildings of at least six storeys within walking distance of city centres, metropolitan centres and rapid transit stops. It also required councils to remove minimum car parking rates from their district plans by February 2022. Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch, Hamilton and Tauranga notified intensification planning instruments giving effect to it from August 2022. The National-led coalition kept the NPS-UD after 2023. It later extended intensification obligations to strategic transport corridors, including key bus routes, and required councils to offset capacity lost to special character areas.
sourceDoc: Labour's urban growth agenda. National Policy Statement on Urban Development 2020

promise: Legislate Medium Density Residential Standards so that up to three homes of up to three storeys can be built on most residential sites in the largest cities without a resource consent.
keyNumber: 3 homes of 3 storeys on most sites -> legislated Dec 2021, applied in tier 1 plans from Aug 2022
statusReason: The density standards were legislated and applied through council plans within the term. Judged at the October 2023 handover the promise was met, and the partial unwinding came afterwards.
whatHappened: The MDRS were agreed with the National Party in October 2021 and legislated in December 2021 by amending the RMA. Tier 1 councils had to put the standards into their plans through intensification planning instruments notified in August 2022, alongside the NPS-UD intensification policies. In most cases the standards took effect immediately on notification. National campaigned in 2023 on giving councils the ability to withdraw from the MDRS. After the change of government the coalition made them optional in policy from July 2024. The Resource Management (Consenting and Other System Changes) Amendment Act, in force from August 2025, gave Auckland and Christchurch a bespoke route out. Other councils could not remove them under the legislation then in force.
sourceDoc: Labour-National bipartisan housing density agreement, October 2021, enacted as the Resource Management (Enabling Housing Supply and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2021

promise: Repeal the Natural and Built Environment Act 2023 and the Spatial Planning Act 2023 by Christmas 2023.
keyNumber: Repeal by Christmas 2023 promised -> passed 19 Dec 2023, assent 23 Dec 2023
statusReason: Both Acts were repealed before Christmas 2023, exactly as the coalition agreement and 100-day plan specified.
whatHappened: The Resource Management (Natural and Built Environment and Spatial Planning Repeal and Interim Fast-track Consenting) Bill was passed under urgency on 19 December 2023. It received royal assent on 23 December 2023, four weeks after the Government was sworn in. Both Labour Acts were repealed and the Resource Management Act 1991 was reinstated as the operative planning statute. An interim fast-track consenting pathway was carried over, pending the Government's own fast-track regime.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023 and National's 100-day plan, repeal the Natural and Built Environment Act 2023 and the Spatial Planning Act 2023 by Christmas

promise: Replace the Resource Management Act 1991 with two new statutes, one for the natural environment and one for planning and development, during this parliamentary term.
keyNumber: 100+ plans -> 17 regional combined plans proposed; bills at select committee Aug 2026
statusReason: The replacement bills were introduced and passed first reading, but they had not been enacted as at August 2026. The new system is not scheduled to operate until 2029, so the term is not finished.
whatHappened: After repealing Labour's replacement laws, the Government confirmed in September 2024 that the RMA would be replaced by two Acts. An expert advisory group reported, and on 24 March 2025 RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop announced a Planning Act and a Natural Environment Act. Detail was released on 9 December 2025. More than 100 existing policy statements and plans would be reduced to 17 regional combined plans. Zoning would be standardised, and national instruments would replace much of the existing national direction. Councils would also have to compensate landowners for some restrictions on property rights. The Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill passed their first readings on 16 December 2025 and were referred to the Environment Committee. Labour supported the bills' progression, and the Green Party and Te Pāti Māori opposed them. The Government's own timetable has the new system taking full effect in 2029, and the RMA 1991 remained the operative statute through the first half of 2026.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023, replace the Resource Management Act 1991 with new resource management laws

promise: Establish a permanent fast-track one-stop-shop consenting and permitting regime for regional and national projects of significance.
keyNumber: One-stop-shop promised -> Act in force 23 Dec 2024 with 149 listed projects
statusReason: A permanent one-stop-shop regime was legislated within the first term and is issuing decisions, although the final Act differs from the introduced Bill in who makes the decision.
whatHappened: The Fast-track Approvals Bill was introduced on 7 March 2024, with a design that gave three ministers the final say on approvals. After more than 27,000 submissions and sustained criticism about executive power, Cabinet agreed on 25 August 2024 to remove ministerial approval and give the decisions to independent expert panels. The change was carried at the select committee stage. On 6 October 2024 the Government listed 149 projects in the Bill: 44 housing, 43 infrastructure, 22 renewable energy, 11 mining and 7 aquaculture or farming projects. The Bill passed its third reading on 17 December 2024 and received royal assent on 23 December 2024. Panels began issuing decisions in 2025-2026. A Southland wind farm of 250-350 MW was referred on 31 July 2025 and approved on 2 April 2026. Trans-Tasman Resources withdrew its South Taranaki seabed mining application on 19 February 2026, after a draft decision to decline it on 5 February 2026. A Fast-track Approvals Amendment Bill adding an express lane for supermarkets was introduced on 3 November 2025 and passed on 11 December 2025. It also extended panel decision timeframes from 60 to 90 days.
contestedNote: Supporters say the regime delivers exactly what was promised, a single consenting pathway with statutory timeframes, and that moving approvals to expert panels strengthened it. Critics say the Government promised, and initially legislated for, ministerial decision-making, and only retreated under public and legal pressure. On that reading the Act that passed is materially different from the one introduced. Others argue the change was a normal select committee improvement rather than a broken promise.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023, establish a fast-track one-stop-shop consenting and permitting process for regional and national projects of significance

promise: Amend the Resource Management Act 1991 to make it easier to consent new infrastructure including renewable energy, to allow farmers to farm, and to enable aquaculture and other primary industries.
keyNumber: Phase one amendments -> 2 Acts passed Aug and Oct 2024
statusReason: The targeted amendments named in the agreement were passed inside the first year of the term.
whatHappened: Phase one amendments were announced on 23 April 2024 and enacted as the Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2024. It received royal assent on 24 October 2024 and commenced the next day. It removed the requirement to give effect to the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy of obligations when deciding consents. It repealed the intensive winter grazing regulations, and removed freshwater farm plan requirements in five regions. It also eased the section 107 test for discharge permits, and blocked councils from notifying new freshwater plans until a replacement national policy statement was issued or 31 December 2025. The Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Act 2024, enacted 27 August 2024, automatically extended existing marine farm coastal permits by 20 years, capped at 2050. Also in March 2024, councils were told the Significant Natural Areas requirements of the indigenous biodiversity national policy statement would be suspended for three years.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023, amend the RMA to make it easier to consent new infrastructure, allow farmers to farm and enable primary industries

promise: Change the consenting system so more houses get built. That includes requiring councils to live-zone at least 30 years of feasible housing capacity instead of three, and removing planning rules such as minimum floor areas, balcony requirements and Auckland's Rural-Urban Boundary.
keyNumber: 3 years of live-zoned housing capacity -> 30 years required, in force Aug 2025
statusReason: The main consenting and zoning changes are law and in force. But parts of the package for councils outside Auckland and Christchurch were still in consultation as at August 2026.
whatHappened: Going for Housing Growth stage one was announced on 4 July 2024. The Resource Management (Consenting and Other System Changes) Amendment Act came into force in August 2025. Tier 1 and 2 councils must now zone for at least 30 years of housing demand, using high growth projections. Minimum floor area and balcony requirements were abolished. The NPS-UD was strengthened to require intensification along strategic transport corridors, including key bus routes, and to offset capacity lost to special character areas. Auckland and Christchurch were given bespoke processes to step away from the Medium Density Residential Standards. Work on the remaining pillar one changes for other councils was still going through submissions from the August 2025 consultation as at 2026. In February 2026 Auckland's intensification target was reduced from capacity for 2 million homes to 1.6 million.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023, amend the RMA to get more houses built; Going for Housing Growth stage one, 4 July 2024

promise: Rewrite the national direction that sits under the resource management system, starting with replacing the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management 2020 and the freshwater national environmental standards.
keyNumber: NPS-FM 2020 replacement promised -> amended NPS-FM gazetted Dec 2025, full package incomplete
statusReason: Some instruments have been amended or replaced, including the freshwater national policy statement in December 2025. But the promised full rewrite of national direction is unfinished, and partly depends on legislation still before Parliament.
whatHappened: Cabinet agreed on 14 December 2023 to replace the NPS-FM, and pushed the council notification deadline out from 31 December 2024 to 31 December 2027. Consultation on a large national direction package covering infrastructure, primary industries, freshwater and housing ran to 27 July 2025, with three options offered for rebalancing Te Mana o te Wai. An amended National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management was gazetted in December 2025. New or amended national environmental standards were issued alongside it, including standards enabling detached minor residential units. The wider rewrite is being folded into the national instruments proposed in the Planning and Natural Environment Bills, so the full replacement set was not complete as at August 2026.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2023, replace the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management 2020 and the National Environmental Standards for Freshwater, and review national direction

promise: Give councils the ability to withdraw from the mandatory Medium Density Residential Standards, while keeping the National Policy Statement on Urban Development and requiring councils to zone for growth.
keyNumber: MDRS optional for all councils promised -> opt-out legislated for Auckland and Christchurch only by Aug 2026
statusReason: Optionality was legislated for two cities and promised for the rest. Most councils still had the standards imposed on them nearly three years into the term.
whatHappened: The Government announced on 4 July 2024 that the MDRS would become optional, subject to a council ratification vote. Councils choosing to step away would have to zone for 30 years of housing capacity instead. The Resource Management (Consenting and Other System Changes) Amendment Act, in force August 2025, delivered this only for Auckland and Christchurch, through bespoke processes. Other councils could not remove the MDRS under the legislation in force as at August 2026. The wider settings were still working through submissions from the August 2025 consultation. The NPS-UD was kept and strengthened, as promised.
sourceDoc: National 2023 housing and planning policy, give councils the ability to withdraw from the MDRS while keeping the NPS-UD

promise: Replace the Resource Management Act 1991 with new resource management laws premised on the enjoyment of property rights as a guiding principle.
keyNumber: RMA replacement premised on property rights -> bills before select committee Aug 2026, system due 2029
statusReason: The property-rights principle has been carried into the drafted replacement bills. But the laws themselves were not passed as at August 2026, and the term is unfinished.
whatHappened: Labour's replacement statutes were repealed in December 2023 and the RMA 1991 was reinstated. The replacement package released on 9 December 2025 adopts the property rights framing. The new system is built around managing effects on other people's use of their property, and standardised zoning. It also puts an obligation on councils to compensate landowners where planning rules restrict the use of their land. The Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill passed first reading on 16 December 2025 and went to the Environment Committee. As at August 2026 no replacement statute had been enacted and the RMA 1991 was still the operative law, with the new system scheduled to take effect in 2029.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023, replace the RMA with new resource management laws premised on the enjoyment of property rights as a guiding principle

promise: Legislate to make the Medium Density Residential Standards optional for councils, requiring councils to ratify any use of the MDRS including in existing zones.
keyNumber: MDRS ratification for all councils -> delivered for 2 of the affected councils by Aug 2026
statusReason: The commitment was legislated for two councils and announced as policy for the rest. The general ratification requirement in the agreement had not been delivered nearly three years in.
whatHappened: The policy decision to make the MDRS optional, subject to a council ratification vote, was announced on 4 July 2024. The legislation that followed was the Resource Management (Consenting and Other System Changes) Amendment Act, in force from August 2025. It provided bespoke opt-out processes for Auckland and Christchurch only. Councils elsewhere could not remove the standards under the legislation in force as at August 2026. The ratification requirement for existing MDRS zones had not been generally legislated, and the remaining changes were still in consultation.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023, legislate to make the MDRS optional for councils, with councils to ratify any use of MDRS including existing zones

promise: Repeal Labour's planning laws and temporarily reinstate the Resource Management Act. Then replace it with legislation modelled on Ireland's Planning and Development Act and England's Town and Country Planning Act, restricting third party appeals and replacing the Environment Court.
keyNumber: Repeal then replace on the Irish/English model -> repeal done Dec 2023, replacement bills unpassed Aug 2026
statusReason: The repeal and temporary reinstatement happened as promised. But the specific replacement model, the appeal restrictions and the replacement of the Environment Court had not been enacted as at August 2026.
whatHappened: The first half was done immediately. The Natural and Built Environment Act and Spatial Planning Act were repealed on 19 December 2023, and the RMA 1991 was reinstated. The replacement was announced in March 2025 and introduced as the Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill on 16 December 2025. It takes a standardised-zoning and national-instruments approach, with compensation for property rights restrictions, rather than adopting the Irish or English statutes wholesale. No legislation replacing the Environment Court had been passed as at August 2026, and the replacement bills were still before the Environment Committee.
sourceDoc: New Zealand First 2023 Policy Manifesto, planning legislation

promise: Stop the co-governance model built into Labour's planning legislation, including the joint council and iwi planning committees created under the new system.
statusReason: The specific committee structures the party objected to were abolished with the repeal, though iwi involvement in the planning system continues in other forms.
whatHappened: The Natural and Built Environment Act and Spatial Planning Act were repealed on 19 December 2023. That removed the regional planning committees and the joint spatial planning committees that included mana whenua representation. The replacement system released on 9 December 2025 keeps a role for iwi in developing national instruments, and retains Treaty settlement protections. It does not restore the joint planning committee structure. Treaty settlement land, protected customary rights areas and iwi aquaculture settlement areas were also expressly excluded from the fast-track regime.
contestedNote: NZ First and its supporters describe the repeal as ending co-governance in planning. Critics, including Te Pāti Māori and the Green Party, say iwi and hapū participation rights under Treaty settlements and section 8 of the RMA were never removed. On their reading the change was to the committee structure rather than to the underlying obligations, so how much was undone is disputed.
sourceDoc: New Zealand First 2023 Policy Manifesto, opposition to 50:50 council/iwi planning committees

promise: Build light rail in Auckland from the city centre down Dominion Road to Mt Roskill within four years, then extend the line to Auckland Airport.
keyNumber: Light rail to Mt Roskill within 4 years (by 2021) -> 0 metres of track and approx $228m spent by Oct 2023
statusReason: Six years and about $228m of planning produced no construction and no track.
whatHappened: No construction started in the first term. A NZ Super Fund consortium proposal was run against a Waka Kotahi bid in a twin-track procurement, and the Super Fund proposal was blocked before the 2020 election. The project was reset in 2021 under a new establishment unit. Work stopped in November 2023 and the project was formally cancelled on 14 January 2024. Auckland Light Rail Ltd spent about $228 million on planning over six years, without a metre of track being laid.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 campaign transport policy (Auckland light rail)

promise: Re-commit to light rail from Auckland's city centre to Mangere and the airport, and settle the route and mode in the 2020-23 term.
keyNumber: $14.6b tunnelled line chosen in 2022 -> advice of up to $29.2b, cancelled Jan 2024 with no construction
statusReason: A route and mode were chosen, but nothing was built and no funded delivery plan existed at the end of the term.
whatHappened: In January 2022 Cabinet chose a partly tunnelled light rail line to Mangere, estimated at about $14.6 billion. Later official advice put the possible cost at up to $29.2 billion. The detailed business case was still incomplete when the Government changed. Work was halted in November 2023 and the project was cancelled on 14 January 2024, with no construction ever begun.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 campaign re-commitment to Auckland light rail (city centre to Mangere/airport)

promise: Deliver $6.8 billion of transport projects under the $12b New Zealand Upgrade Programme, including Penlink (open late 2025), Mill Road (complete 2027/28), Papakura to Drury South (complete late 2025), Drury rail stations (complete late 2024) and the Northern Pathway (complete 2023/24).
keyNumber: $6.8b transport package with completion dates 2023-2029 -> Drury/Paerata stations promised late 2024 opened Aug 2026
statusReason: A large programme was funded and parts were built, but the published completion dates were widely missed and the package was rescoped.
whatHappened: The transport component was $6.8b: about $5.3b for roads, $1.1b for rail and $360m for walking and cycling. Costs rose and the programme was rescoped. Several projects were deferred or dropped, and others slipped years behind their announced dates. The Drury and Paerata stations, announced for completion in late 2024, did not open until 1 August 2026. Otaki to north of Levin, announced to start in 2025, was still under construction in 2026.
sourceDoc: New Zealand Upgrade Programme, announced 29 January 2020 (major government/campaign fiscal announcement)

promise: Reprioritise National Land Transport Fund spending away from new state highways and towards rail infrastructure in cities and regions, public transport, and walking and cycling.
statusReason: The funding rebalance and the new rail funding architecture happened. But walking and cycling stayed a minor share, and it was reversed within months of the handover.
whatHappened: The Government Policy Statement on land transport 2018 and GPS 2021 shifted the funding ranges towards public transport, rail, safety and road maintenance, and away from new state highway capacity. The Land Transport (Rail) Legislation Act 2020 brought rail network funding into the National Land Transport Fund and created the Rail Network Investment Programme, first published in 2021. Walking and cycling remained a small activity class throughout. The incoming Government's GPS 2024 reversed the rebalancing.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First coalition agreement 2017 and Labour-Greens confidence & supply agreement 2017 (transport clauses)

promise: Deliver the Let's Get Wellington Moving programme (mass rapid transit, a second Mt Victoria tunnel, Basin Reserve improvements and the Golden Mile), jointly funded by the Crown (60 per cent) and Wellington councils (40 per cent).
keyNumber: Multi-billion-dollar Wellington package agreed 2019 -> no major project built; programme ended 17 Dec 2023
statusReason: Four and a half years of programme work produced no major built project before the programme was disestablished.
whatHappened: LGWM stayed in the detailed investigation and development stage from May 2019 until it was wound up, and delivered no major infrastructure. Its mass rapid transit business case was still incomplete in 2023. On 17 December 2023 the incoming Government, the Wellington Mayor and the Greater Wellington Regional Council chair agreed to end LGWM. The Crown took the Mt Victoria tunnel and Basin Reserve projects, and the city council took the Golden Mile.
sourceDoc: Let's Get Wellington Moving Recommended Programme of Investment agreed by the Labour-led Government (Oct 2018; package announced May 2019)

promise: Work will begin on light rail from the city to the airport in Auckland.
keyNumber: Work to begin on city-to-airport light rail -> planning only, approx $228m spent, cancelled Jan 2024
statusReason: Planning work did begin, as the clause required, but no line was built and the project was cancelled.
whatHappened: Planning work did begin. A procurement process ran from 2018 to 2020, an establishment unit reported in 2021, and Cabinet selected a partly tunnelled route to Mangere in January 2022. No construction was ever started. Work was halted in November 2023 and the project was cancelled on 14 January 2024, after about $228 million of planning spend over six years.
contestedNote: Read literally, the commitment was that work 'will begin', and design, procurement and route selection all happened, so it was met. Read against the outcome the Greens were seeking, a light rail line to the airport, nothing was delivered and the project was cancelled.
sourceDoc: Labour-Greens confidence & supply agreement 2017

promise: Auckland's East-West motorway link will not proceed as currently proposed.
statusReason: The project as proposed did not proceed at any point in the 2017-2023 period, which is what the clause committed to.
whatHappened: The consented East-West Link was shelved in 2018 and did not proceed during either Labour-led term. The incoming Government revived it as one of the 15 Roads of National Significance in GPS 2024. By July 2026 NZTA had placed the East-West Link in the slowest delivery phase, with route protection work only and no construction timeline.
sourceDoc: Labour-Greens confidence & supply agreement 2017

promise: Create a $1.5 billion Cycle Super Highway fund for protected cycleways in major cities, plus more than $400 million for local walking and cycling improvements, within a $13.6 billion decade-long transport plan.
keyNumber: $1.5b cycle super highway fund promised -> no such fund created; walking and cycling class set at $70m-$110m a year in GPS 2024
statusReason: The specific $1.5b fund was never created, and cycling funding stayed an order of magnitude smaller.
whatHappened: No dedicated Cycle Super Highway fund was established in the 2020-23 term. Walking and cycling remained a small activity class inside the National Land Transport Fund, rather than a separate multi-billion-dollar programme.
