The incoming Government's GPS 2024 then reduced the walking and cycling activity class to a range of $70-110 million a year from 2025/26. It directed that 25 per cent of new improvement spending go to footpaths.
sourceDoc: Green Party 2020 transport policy

promise: Commission a feasibility study on the options for moving the Ports of Auckland, with Northport at Whangarei given serious consideration.
keyNumber: Feasibility study on moving Ports of Auckland -> study delivered, relocation costed at $10.3b, no decision by Oct 2023
statusReason: The study NZ First bargained for was delivered, but the relocation it was meant to enable never got a decision.
whatHappened: The Upper North Island Supply Chain Strategy working group was established in 2018. Its 2019 report recommended closing Auckland's freight port and shifting capacity to Northport, with an EY analysis putting the cost at about $10.3 billion. On 9 December 2019 Cabinet agreed the Ports of Auckland was not viable as the upper North Island's key import port in the long term. It did not decide where or when freight would move. No relocation decision was taken and nothing moved before the October 2023 handover.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First coalition agreement 2017

promise: Cancel the Auckland Light Rail project as part of the Government's 100-day plan.
keyNumber: Cancel Auckland light rail -> cancelled 14 Jan 2024; approx $228m already spent
statusReason: The cancellation was completed inside the 100-day window.
whatHappened: Stop-work notices were issued in November 2023, and the project was formally cancelled on 14 January 2024, with Auckland Light Rail Ltd instructed to cease work and wind down. The Transport Minister said the project would have cost $15 billion, with advice showing up to $29.2 billion. The Minister also said about $228 million had been spent in six years without a metre of track. Cabinet papers later released showed the disestablishment itself would cost millions more over about six months.
sourceDoc: Coalition Government 100-day plan (2023)

promise: Introduce legislation in the first 100 days to repeal the Auckland Regional Fuel Tax.
keyNumber: Repeal Auckland regional fuel tax -> tax ended 30 June 2024, six years after it began
statusReason: The tax was repealed on the announced date.
whatHappened: Legislation was introduced within the 100 days and passed, and the Auckland Regional Fuel Tax ended on 30 June 2024. The tax was 10 cents a litre plus GST, and the previous Government had introduced it on 1 July 2018. Remaining collected funds were redirected by agreement with Auckland Council to the Eastern Busway, electric trains and stabling for the City Rail Link, and road corridor improvements.
sourceDoc: Coalition Government 100-day plan (2023)

promise: Build 13 new Roads of National Significance, including four-laning State Highway 1 from Whangarei to Tauranga, Mill Road, a second Mt Victoria Tunnel, the Hope Bypass, the Woodend Bypass, Hamilton Southern Links and Petone to Grenada, as part of a transport plan costed at about $24 billion.
keyNumber: 13-15 Roads of National Significance -> 4 under construction and 6 expected by early 2027; 5 shifted to no construction timeline (July 2026)
statusReason: The programme was reinstated and construction started on several roads. But a third of the projects have no construction timeline, and delivery of most is well beyond this term.
whatHappened: GPS 2024, issued in March 2024, reinstated the programme with 15 Roads of National Significance. NZTA's Major Transport Projects Pipeline of 9 July 2026 showed four under construction: Otaki to north of Levin, Hawke's Bay Expressway, Takitimu North Link Stage 1 and SH29 Tauriko West. Northland Expressway Stage 1 and Cambridge to Piarere were moving into construction, giving six under construction by early 2027. Five were placed on a slower track with no construction timeline: Hope Bypass Stage 2, Northland Expressway Stages 2 and 3, the Auckland East-West Link, Mill Road Alfriston to Drury, and Petone to Grenada. The Transport Minister said fuel excise duty had fallen 21 per cent in real terms since 2020, while construction costs had risen sharply. The Government acknowledged the 2023 promises had been very ambitious. The next Government Policy Statement, due before the 2026 election, was delayed until after it.
contestedNote: The Government argues these are 10-year projects, and that route protection, design and property acquisition must come before construction, so phasing is normal delivery rather than retreat. Critics point out that specific roads promised in 2023 now have no construction date at all, and that the funding gap in the National Land Transport Fund is the binding constraint.
sourceDoc: National 2023 policy: Transport for the Future

promise: Rewrite the Government Policy Statement on land transport within the first six months to prioritise roads and maintenance, including dedicated pothole prevention funding, and move to a ten-year investment horizon.
keyNumber: New GPS within 6 months -> issued March 2024 with over $22b for 2024/25-2026/27 and new pothole prevention classes
statusReason: The GPS was rewritten within the promised timeframe, with the promised reprioritisation.
whatHappened: GPS 2024 was issued in March 2024, about four months after the election. It set National Land Transport Fund expenditure of over $22 billion for 2024/25-2026/27 ($6.4b, $6.85b and $6.85b a year). It created two new activity classes: State Highway Pothole Prevention ($420-700m a year) and Local Road Pothole Prevention ($570-780m a year). It added $640 million to maintenance relative to the draft, reinstated 15 Roads of National Significance, and cut the walking and cycling range to $70-110m a year from 2025/26. It also relied on a $3.1 billion Crown loan facility for NZTA across the 2024-27 period, plus a further $1.795b of smaller facilities. The following GPS, covering 2027 onwards, was delayed until after the 2026 election, breaking a near two-decade pattern.
sourceDoc: National 2023 policy commitment to rewrite the Government Policy Statement within six months; GPS on land transport 2024 (issued March 2024)

promise: Scrap Let's Get Wellington Moving, and have central government fully fund and build a second Mt Victoria tunnel and the Basin Reserve upgrade.
keyNumber: Scrap LGWM and build second Mt Vic tunnel -> LGWM ended 17 Dec 2023; tunnel at route protection only as at Aug 2026
statusReason: The disestablishment happened immediately, but nearly three years later the tunnel it was meant to unblock still has no construction date.
whatHappened: LGWM was ended by agreement on 17 December 2023, between the Transport and Infrastructure Ministers, the Wellington Mayor and the Greater Wellington Regional Council chair. The Crown took full funding responsibility for the second Mt Victoria Tunnel and the Basin Reserve upgrade, removing the 40 per cent council share. Wellington City Council took over the Golden Mile. By NZTA's July 2026 pipeline the SH1 Wellington improvements, which include the second tunnel, were still only at route protection stage with no construction date. Petone to Grenada had been moved to the slowest delivery phase.
sourceDoc: National 2023 campaign commitment to scrap Let's Get Wellington Moving and build a second Mt Victoria tunnel

promise: Establish a National Infrastructure Agency as the shopfront for investors in public infrastructure and to build public-private partnership capability, and publish a 30-year National Infrastructure Plan.
keyNumber: National Infrastructure Agency and 30-year plan -> agency operating 1 Dec 2024, plan published 17 Feb 2026
statusReason: Both institutions were created on time, and the first major PPP under the new arrangements reached financial close.
whatHappened: National Infrastructure Funding and Financing Ltd began operating on 1 December 2024, replacing Crown Infrastructure Partners, with a board chaired by Mark Binns. Te Waihanga published the final 30-year National Infrastructure Plan on 17 February 2026. It contains 16 system recommendations and 10 priorities for the next decade, against annual infrastructure investment of over $20 billion. The PPP pipeline produced a result on 30 July 2026, when the Crown reached financial close with the Northway consortium on the Warkworth to Te Hana expressway. That 26km four-lane road has a net present value of $3.649 billion, against a $3.9b public sector comparator. It is supported by a $1.6b ten-year Crown loan, and was described as the largest PPP in New Zealand's history. The road is due to open in 2033.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First coalition agreement 2023 and the Government's Q4 2024 Action Plan

promise: End the road user charge exemption for light electric vehicles from 1 April 2024, and over time move all 3.5 million light vehicles off fuel excise duty and onto distance and weight-based electronic road user charges.
keyNumber: EV RUC exemption ended 1 April 2024 -> full transition of 3.5m light vehicles still undated at Aug 2026
statusReason: The EV element was delivered on time, but the full transition of light vehicles is still undated and no congestion charging scheme is running.
whatHappened: The exemption ended on 1 April 2024 under the Road User Charges (Light Electric RUC Vehicles) Amendment Act 2024. On 6 August 2025 the Transport Minister set out the wider transition, described as the biggest change to road funding in 50 years. Legislation is to pass in 2026, and the RUC system is to be 'open for business' to third-party providers in 2027. There is no fixed date for shifting petrol vehicles off the roughly 70 cents a litre fuel excise. A bill expanding road user charges was introduced in 2025. Separately, the Land Transport Management (Time of Use Charging) Amendment Bill passed its first reading in March 2025 to enable congestion charging. As at 2026 Auckland Transport had no approved scheme and no start date.
sourceDoc: Coalition Government 100-day plan (EV road user charges) and the Government's road pricing programme announced 6 August 2025

promise: Reverse the blanket speed limit reductions made under the previous government, where it is safe to do so.
keyNumber: Reverse blanket speed limit reductions -> 38 state highway sections reverted automatically, 49 more consulted; completed by 1 July 2025
statusReason: The rule was made and the reversals were completed on the stated deadline.
whatHappened: The Setting of Speed Limits Rule 2024 required reversals. From 29 January 2025, 38 sections of state highway automatically reverted to their previous limits, starting with SH2 between Featherston and Masterton. A further 49 sections went to public consultation. Councils had to advise on local road changes by 1 May 2025, and state highway reversals had to be complete by 1 July 2025. NZTA reported more than 65 per cent of consultation submitters supported the reversals.
sourceDoc: National-ACT coalition agreement 2023

promise: Run a public tipline so people can report excessive road cone use, and cut over-the-top temporary traffic management.
keyNumber: Road cone tipline -> 1,100+ reports in 5 months, excessive cones at 6 per cent of sites, pilot ended early; NZTA traffic management spend down approx $46m
statusReason: The tipline ran and the wider traffic management reform produced measurable savings, but the tipline itself was wound up early after finding limited over-coning.
whatHappened: WorkSafe's digital road cone tipline opened on 3 June 2025 and received over 1,100 valid notifications to 31 October 2025, falling to about 15 a week by late October. Inspections found 77 per cent of sites complied with their approved traffic management plans, and excessive cone use at 6 per cent of sites visited, which were addressed. The pilot cost $148,545 excluding GST to 30 September 2025, against a $395,000 twelve-month budget. WorkSafe recommended discontinuing it by 19 December 2025, and it was ended early. Separately, NZTA moved to risk-based temporary traffic management, and its spend on it fell by about $46 million between 2023/24 and 2024/25. Nine councils had adopted the approach by July 2026.
sourceDoc: Government action plan commitment delivered by the ACT Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety. WorkSafe road cone tipline, announced June 2025

promise: Deliver a four-lane expressway from Auckland to Whangarei, including a four-lane alternative route over or around the Brynderwyn Hills.
keyNumber: Four-lane Auckland to Whangarei -> Stage 1 (26km) contracted July 2026 opening 2033; Stages 2 and 3 have no construction timeline
statusReason: One of three stages is contracted and starting; the two stages that reach Whangarei have no construction date.
whatHappened: On 23 April 2025 NZTA announced an emerging preferred corridor from Te Hana to Whangarei in three stages. It selected a 'near east' alignment close to SH1 over the Brynderwyns, after reassessing western options. Stage 1, Warkworth to Te Hana, is the 26km section that includes Dome Valley. It reached financial close as a PPP on 30 July 2026, with a net present value of $3.649 billion. Early works began in August 2026, main construction starts in November 2027, and the road is due to open in 2033. Stages 2 and 3, Te Hana to Port Marsden and Port Marsden to Whangarei, were placed in the slowest delivery phase in July 2026 with no construction timeline.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First coalition agreement 2023 (Northland roading, four-lane alternative to the Brynderwyns)

promise: After cancelling iReX, deliver two new rail-enabled Cook Strait ferries in service by Christmas 2029. Each would be about 200m long and carry 1,500 passengers and 40 rail wagons. This would reuse Wellington's existing marine infrastructure and build a new dual-level wharf at Picton, at a cost far below the cancelled programme.
keyNumber: Two rail-enabled ferries by Christmas 2029 -> contracts let and ships named in 2026, delivery still scheduled 2029; iReX wind-down cost approx $671m
statusReason: Ships, operator and port contracts are settled and the 2029 date still stands, but no vessel has been built and the term is not finished.
whatHappened: The Finance Minister cancelled the iReX programme in December 2023. KiwiRail later disclosed about $500 million had already been spent, and the wind-down and settlement cost roughly $671 million in total. Ferry Holdings was established to procure the replacements. In July 2026 the two ships were named Kupe and Cook, and KiwiRail was confirmed as operator on a 30-year contract from 2029 with a 2039 review point. Construction was set to begin in 2027 at Guangzhou Shipyard International for 2029 delivery, about three years later than iReX would have delivered. The Crown contribution is capped at $1.7 billion with total project cost under $2 billion. That includes $373m of marine infrastructure via Ferry Holdings, $100m at CentrePort and $110m at Port Marlborough.
contestedNote: The Government says the revised package saves about $2.3 billion against iReX and avoids a gold-plated port rebuild. Critics note the ferries arrive around three years later than iReX would have, and that roughly $671 million was spent on a cancelled programme. They also say the full cost was not disclosed at the time of the 2025 announcement.
sourceDoc: Cabinet decision on Cook Strait ferry replacement announced by Rail Minister Winston Peters, 31 March 2025

promise: Decarbonise public transport. The government target is that only zero-emission public transport buses be purchased from 2025, and that the entire public transport bus fleet be decarbonised by 2035.
keyNumber: Only zero-emission buses purchased from 2025 and fleet decarbonised by 2035 -> targets set and co-investment fund opened 2023; both dates fall after the term
statusReason: Targets were set and a funding mechanism established, but only a small share of the fleet had been converted by the handover.
whatHappened: The targets were adopted as government policy and carried into the Emissions Reduction Plan: no new fossil-fuel buses purchased from 2025, and a fully decarbonised bus fleet by 2035. Waka Kotahi opened a public transport decarbonisation co-investment fund in 2023 to help councils buy zero-emission buses and build depot charging, with first-round results due September 2023. Uptake was concentrated in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch. At the October 2023 handover, zero-emission buses were a small minority of the national fleet. Both target dates fall after the end of the term, so neither had come due.
contestedNote: One reading is that this cannot be scored against Labour's term, because the target dates are 2025 and 2035. The other is that the commitment was to decarbonise public transport during the term of the agreement. On the fleet conversion rate achieved by 2023, the 2035 date would require a step change no government had funded.
sourceDoc: Labour-Greens Cooperation Agreement 2020, achieving the purpose and goals of the Zero Carbon Act through decarbonising public transport

promise: Establish an independent Māori Health Authority with its own commissioning powers, as a Treaty partnership body inside the reformed health system.
keyNumber: Independent Māori health authority promised -> Te Aka Whai Ora operating from 1 July 2022, $188m in Budget 2022
statusReason: The authority was legislated and operating well before the end of the term, in the form promised.
whatHappened: Health Minister Andrew Little announced the authority on 21 April 2021. It was created by the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022, which passed its third reading on 7 June 2022. Te Aka Whai Ora began operating on 1 July 2022 with Riana Manuel as chief executive. Budget 2022 allocated $188 million for commissioning and iwi partnership work. It was still operating at the October 2023 handover, and the incoming government disestablished it on 30 June 2024.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 term commitment, following the Health and Disability System Review, to establish an independent Māori health authority

promise: Remove the provisions of the Local Electoral Act that let five per cent of electors force a binding poll. Those polls could overturn a council decision to establish Māori wards or constituencies.
keyNumber: Poll veto removed Feb 2021 -> Māori constituencies in 6 of 11 regional councils and wards in 29 of 67 territorial authorities by 2022
statusReason: The poll provisions were repealed within four months of the promise being acted on, and the intended effect followed: councils established wards without a referendum.
whatHappened: The Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2021 passed its third reading on 25 February 2021 under urgency, removing the mechanism for petition-triggered referendums. Councils then adopted wards in large numbers. By the 2022 local elections, six of eleven regional councils (54.5 per cent) had Māori constituencies and 29 of 67 territorial authorities (43.3 per cent) had Māori wards. The next government reinstated the provisions in July 2024.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 term commitment to remove the binding-poll provisions of the Local Electoral Act, announced by Local Government Minister Nanaia Mahuta in February 2021

promise: Create a new public holiday for Matariki, the first public holiday recognising te ao Māori, to take effect from 2022.
keyNumber: New Matariki public holiday from 2022 -> first observed 24 June 2022, dates set to 2051
statusReason: The holiday was legislated and first observed in 2022, exactly on the promised timetable.
whatHappened: The Te Kahui o Matariki Public Holiday Bill was introduced on 30 September 2021. It passed its third reading on 7 April 2022 and received royal assent on 11 April 2022. The first Matariki public holiday was observed on 24 June 2022, marked by a pre-dawn hautapu ceremony. The date is set by a lunar calculation rather than a fixed calendar date, and dates were published through to 2051. The holiday remained in place through the change of government.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 election campaign pledge announced by Jacinda Ardern on 7 September 2020

promise: Establish water services entities governed by regional representative groups made up of equal numbers of council and mana whenua representatives, with a Te Mana o te Wai statement mechanism for mana whenua.
keyNumber: 50-50 council and mana whenua governance legislated Dec 2022 -> 0 entities and 0 representative groups operating at the Oct 2023 handover
statusReason: The co-governance structure was legislated but never came into operation before the term ended, and the wider programme was rescoped and delayed.
whatHappened: The 50-50 council and mana whenua regional representative group model was announced in October 2021. It was legislated in the Water Services Entities Act, passed in December 2022 with only Labour's votes. In April 2023 the programme was rebranded and expanded from four entities to ten, with the start date pushed back to 1 July 2026. No entity ever began operating, so no regional representative group was ever constituted. The legislation was repealed on 14 February 2024.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 term commitment to the Three Waters reform programme (Cabinet decisions announced October 2021)

promise: Hold a binding referendum on whether the separate Māori electorates should be abolished.
keyNumber: Binding referendum on 7 Māori electorates promised -> dropped in the 2017 coalition negotiation, 0 referendums held
statusReason: The commitment was traded away in the 2017 coalition negotiation, before the government took office, and was never pursued in the term.
whatHappened: During the post-election coalition negotiations in October 2017, Peters signalled he would consider dropping the referendum call. NZ First agreed to drop the demand as part of forming a government with Labour. No referendum was held, and the seven Māori electorates were retained throughout the 2017-2023 government. NZ First returned to campaigning on a referendum on the future of the Māori electorates, announced on 12 February 2026.
sourceDoc: NZ First 2017 election campaign commitment, announced by Winston Peters, to hold a binding referendum on the Māori electorates

promise: Introduce a Treaty Principles Bill based on existing ACT policy, and support it to a Select Committee as soon as practicable.
keyNumber: Support to select committee promised -> introduced, first reading 68-54 on 14 Nov 2024, defeated 112-11 on 10 Apr 2025
statusReason: The agreement required introduction and support only to select committee, and both happened. National and NZ First never undertook to support it further.
whatHappened: David Seymour introduced the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill. It set out three proposed principles: that the Government has the right to govern all New Zealanders; that the Government will honour all New Zealanders in the chieftainship of their land and property; and that all New Zealanders are equal under the law with the same rights and duties. It passed its first reading on 14 November 2024 by 68 votes to 54 and was referred to the Justice Committee. The committee received over 200,000 online and 12,000 handwritten submissions, with about 90 per cent opposed and 8 per cent in support. A nationwide hikoi that began on 11 November 2024 brought tens of thousands to Parliament on 19 November. The bill was defeated at its second reading on 10 April 2025 by 112 votes to 11, with National and NZ First voting against as their agreements provided.
contestedNote: One reading is that the commitment was met in full, because the agreement only ever required support to select committee and the bill got there. The other is that the exercise did not change the law and consumed a very large amount of parliamentary and public process, with roughly 90 per cent of submissions opposed. The facts of the votes and the wording of the agreement are not in dispute; what the commitment was worth is.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023

promise: Hold a binding referendum on the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi at the 2026 general election.
keyNumber: Binding referendum at the 2026 election sought -> not agreed in coalition, 0 referendums held
statusReason: The 2023 coalition negotiation dropped the referendum. It was replaced with a commitment that went no further than a select committee.
whatHappened: Seymour announced the referendum plan in March 2022 and raised it as a condition in coalition negotiations. It was not agreed. The National-ACT agreement committed only to introducing a Treaty Principles Bill and supporting it to select committee. No referendum was legislated for or held. The bill itself was defeated at second reading on 10 April 2025.
sourceDoc: ACT policy announced by David Seymour in March 2022 and carried into the 2023 campaign

promise: Conduct a comprehensive review of all legislation that includes 'the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi', except where it relates to full and final Treaty settlements. Replace all such references with specific words about the relevance and application of the Treaty, or repeal the references.
keyNumber: 28 Acts in scope -> 19 reviewed, 7 references to be repealed, 2 made specific, 10 capped at 'take into account'; 0 enacted by Aug 2026
statusReason: Term unfinished. The review was completed and decisions taken, but the statutory changes had not been introduced and passed by August 2026.
whatHappened: Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith announced the outcome of the review on 15 May 2026. Twenty-eight Acts were originally in scope, narrowed to 19 for review. Existing Treaty settlements were excluded and several Acts were handled through separate processes. Cabinet agreed to make two references more specific and to repeal seven references outright. It capped the remaining ten at a 'take into account' standard. Future provisions would refer to both 'the Treaty of Waitangi' and 'te Tiriti o Waitangi'. Iwi consultation was under way and a full select committee process was still to follow. No amending legislation had been enacted as at 17 August 2026.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement, signed 24 November 2023

promise: Amend the Waitangi Tribunal legislation to refocus the scope, purpose, and nature of its inquiries back to the original intent of that legislation.
keyNumber: Amend Waitangi Tribunal legislation -> advisory group announced 9 May 2025, 0 amending Acts passed by Aug 2026
statusReason: A review process and membership changes have happened. But the promised amendment to the Tribunal's governing legislation had not been made, with under three months of the term remaining.
whatHappened: On 17 January 2025 Minister for Māori Development Tama Potaka announced a membership overhaul. Eight new members were appointed and six warrants renewed. Ten members were not reappointed, including Linda Tuhiwai Smith, Rawinia Higgins and Monty Soutar. On 9 May 2025 Potaka announced an independent technical advisory group to review the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975. Further Tribunal appointments were confirmed on 28 July 2026. No amending legislation had been introduced or passed as at 17 August 2026.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement, signed 24 November 2023

promise: Amend section 58 of the Marine and Coastal Area Act to make clear Parliament's original intent, following the Court of Appeal decision in Re Edwards.
keyNumber: Amend s58 test -> Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Act passed 22 Oct 2025
statusReason: The section 58 test was amended by Act of Parliament inside the term, as the agreement required.
whatHappened: The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Act 2025 passed on 22 October 2025. It tightened the statutory threshold that applicants must meet to be awarded customary marine title.
contestedNote: The Government says the amendment restores the threshold Parliament intended in 2011, which applied before the Court of Appeal's Re Edwards judgment. Māori applicants and opposition parties argued that it raises the bar above what the courts had found the 2011 Act to mean. They said it will defeat claims that would otherwise have succeeded. The text of the amendment and the date of passage are agreed. Its practical effect on future title applications was not yet tested as at August 2026.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement, signed 24 November 2023

promise: Restore the right to a local referendum on setting up or continuing to use Māori wards. This includes requiring a referendum at the next local body elections on any wards established without one.
keyNumber: Binding referendums restored -> Act passed 30 July 2024, 42 polls held in 2025, 24 councils voted to remove wards and 18 to retain
statusReason: Legislation restored the referendum right within nine months, and the binding polls were held at the 2025 local elections exactly as promised.
whatHappened: Local Government Minister Simeon Brown announced on 4 April 2024 that councils which had introduced Māori wards without a poll would have to hold referendums or disestablish the wards. The Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2024 passed on 30 July 2024. It required affected councils either to disestablish their wards by 6 September 2024 or hold binding polls alongside the 2025 local elections. Those polls went ahead, with 24 councils voting to remove their Māori wards and 18 voting to retain them. The results take effect from the 2028 local elections.
sourceDoc: National-ACT and National-NZ First Coalition Agreements 2023

promise: Repeal section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989.
keyNumber: Repeal s7AA -> Oranga Tamariki (Repeal of Section 7AA) Amendment Act, royal assent 3 April 2025
statusReason: Section 7AA was repealed by Act of Parliament inside the term, as promised.
whatHappened: Section 7AA had been added on 1 July 2019 by the Sixth Labour Government. It required the chief executive to reduce disparities for Māori children, to take whakapapa and whānau links into account when children were removed, and to develop strategic partnerships with iwi and Māori organisations. The Oranga Tamariki (Repeal of Section 7AA) Amendment Act 2025 received royal assent on 3 April 2025. The replacement provisions kept a duty on the chief executive to develop strategic relationships with Māori and iwi organisations and to report on the wellbeing of Māori children.
contestedNote: The Government says section 7AA created a duty that could be read as competing with the child's safety as the paramount consideration. It says the replacement provisions keep the practical iwi partnership and reporting obligations. Iwi organisations, the Children's Commissioner's successor bodies and opposition parties argued the repeal removed the only explicit statutory recognition of whakapapa in care decisions. Both sides agree on what the repeal Act does and when it passed.
sourceDoc: 2023 coalition commitments on constitution and rights, compiled from the National-ACT and National-NZ First agreements

promise: Remove co-governance from the delivery of public services.
keyNumber: Co-governance removed from public service delivery -> Māori Health Authority, Three Waters representative groups and s7AA all repealed between Feb 2024 and Apr 2025
statusReason: The named co-governance arrangements in health, water and care of children were all removed. Co-governance arrangements in conservation, Treaty settlement bodies and some council structures continued.
whatHappened: Three of the main co-governance structures in public service delivery were removed. Urgent legislation passed on 28 February 2024 disestablished Te Aka Whai Ora, the Māori Health Authority, which ceased to exist on 30 June 2024. Iwi-Māori partnership boards were retained inside the health system. Parliament repealed the Water Services Entities Act on 14 February 2024. That Act had provided for regional representative groups with equal council and mana whenua membership. Section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act was repealed with effect from 3 April 2025. The Waitangi Tribunal found in its Hautupua report of 29 November 2024 that the Crown had breached Treaty principles in disestablishing Te Aka Whai Ora.
contestedNote: The Government describes these bodies as duplicative structures that gave a non-elected group decision rights over universal services, and says need-based delivery replaces them. The Waitangi Tribunal found in Hautupua that the Crown did not act in good faith over Te Aka Whai Ora, did not consult Māori, and acted on political ideology rather than evidence. It also found the authority was integral to equitable health delivery. The legislative facts are not disputed. What is disputed is how to characterise what was removed.
sourceDoc: National-ACT and National-NZ First Coalition Agreements 2023 (the commitment appears in both)

promise: The Coalition Government will honour the undertakings made by the Crown through past Treaty of Waitangi settlements.
keyNumber: Honour past settlements -> at least 8 settlement bills or deeds progressed between May 2024 and May 2026; settlements excluded from the Treaty clauses review
statusReason: Settlement legislation continued to pass throughout the term, and past settlements were expressly excluded from the Treaty principles review.
whatHappened: Settlements continued to be signed and legislated through the term. The Whakatohea claims settlement passed on 28 May 2024 after three decades of negotiation. Ngāti Ranginui settled on 15 May 2025 after 17 years. Ngāti Paoa's settlement passed its final reading on 5 November 2025 after 14 years. Legislation returning Kororipo Pa to Ngapuhi passed on 17 December 2025. The Ngāti Haua settlement passed its final reading on 29 January 2026, with $19 million of financial redress, the return of 64 culturally significant sites and posthumous pardons. A deed was signed with Ngāti Ruapani on 25 February 2026. Three Hauraki iwi settlement bills, for Ngāti Rahiri Tumutumu, Ngāti Tara Tokanui and Ngāti Hei, passed their final reading on 13 May 2026. Existing settlements were also expressly carved out of the review of Treaty principles clauses announced on 15 May 2026.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement, signed 24 November 2023

promise: Stop all work on He Puapua. Confirm that the Government does not recognise the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples as having any binding legal effect on New Zealand.
statusReason: There is no evidence of continuing work on He Puapua or a Declaration Plan after the change of government. But no published document confirming the work programme was formally closed was located.
whatHappened: He Puapua was a 2019 report commissioned through Te Puni Kōkiri by a Declaration Working Group set up in August 2019 and chaired by Claire Charters. It set out a path to implement UNDRIP by 2040. It was completed in December 2019 but was not released publicly at the time, and was never adopted as government policy. No Declaration Plan was ever formally adopted. The incoming government adopted NZ First's position of halting all work related to the report. No Declaration Plan work programme has been identified as running after November 2023.
contestedNote: Evidence for this entry is limited. The commitment is documented, and so is the fact that the Government adopted the policy of halting work. But the sources available for this run contained no primary document formally recording the closure of the Declaration Plan work programme, and no statement of the Government's position on UNDRIP's legal effect. The status should be treated as provisional.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement, signed 24 November 2023

promise: Ensure all public service departments have their primary name in English, except for those specifically related to Māori. Require public service departments and Crown entities to communicate primarily in English.
statusReason: English-first naming and communication came through ministerial direction at individual agencies rather than across the board, and no statutory name changes were made.
whatHappened: The change was applied agency by agency rather than through a single instrument. On 8 December 2023 the Transport Minister directed Waka Kotahi to prioritise its English name, NZ Transport Agency. Similar direction followed at other agencies. Agencies with a specifically Māori remit, such as Te Puni Kōkiri and Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori, kept their Māori names. No legislation was passed changing the statutory names of departments. Māori names remained in use alongside English ones in many agencies.
contestedNote: Evidence for how complete this change was is limited. The direction to NZ Transport Agency in December 2023 is documented, and so is the coalition commitment. But the sources available for this run contained no consolidated public record of which departments changed their primary name, and when.
sourceDoc: National-ACT Coalition Agreement 2023 (a related commitment on communicating primarily in English appears in the National-NZ First agreement)

promise: Legislate to make English an official language of New Zealand.
keyNumber: Legislate English as an official language -> 0 Acts passed; official languages remain te reo Māori (1987) and NZ Sign Language (2006)
statusReason: English still had no statutory official language status with under three months of the term remaining.
whatHappened: New Zealand has two statutory official languages: te reo Māori under the Māori Language Act 1987, and New Zealand Sign Language under the New Zealand Sign Language Act 2006. English remains a de facto official language that is not recognised in statute. Clayton Mitchell introduced a NZ First member's bill in February 2018 to recognise English in statute, and it did not become law. In the sources reviewed, no Act recognising English as an official language had been passed as at August 2026.
contestedNote: The evidence here is the absence of any recorded legislation, rather than a positive statement that the commitment was abandoned. A bill may have been introduced late in the term that the sources available for this run do not capture, so the status should be treated as provisional.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First Coalition Agreement, signed 24 November 2023

promise: Provide further support for Whānau Ora, the whānau-centred commissioning model delivered through independent Māori and Pacific commissioning agencies.
keyNumber: Further support for Whānau Ora -> $80m over four years in Budget 2019, plus $3m in-year in Jan 2020; agency allocation approx $87m for 2019/20
statusReason: Funding was increased repeatedly as promised, but the commissioning model was not broadened in the way the 2018 review pointed to.
whatHappened: Labour commissioned a review of Whānau Ora in 2018. It reported that other government agencies were not buying into the model enough. Budget 2019 allocated $80 million over four years. Close to two-thirds went directly to the three commissioning agencies, and $20 million was set aside to test localised commissioning in the North Island. On 23 January 2020 a further $3 million was redirected to the three existing agencies in-year, taking their combined allocation for that year to about $87 million. More Whānau Ora funding flowed through the COVID-19 response. The commissioning model itself was not restructured or expanded to new agencies during the term. The Auditor-General reported on Whānau Ora commissioning in 2023.
sourceDoc: Labour Māori manifesto: 'further support for Whānau Ora'

promise: Integrate te reo Māori into education in early learning services and schools by 2025, so that te reo Māori is part of every student's education. Do not make it a compulsory core curriculum subject.
keyNumber: Te reo integrated into all early learning and schools by 2025 -> teacher programme scaled from 685 educators in 2019; no curriculum requirement in place at Oct 2023
statusReason: Real workforce investment was made. But te reo was not integrated across all schools, and the enabling programme was ended before the 2025 date.
whatHappened: Labour rejected compulsion and pursued integration by building teacher capability instead. Te Ahu o te Reo Māori, a $12 million teacher language programme, was piloted in 2019 with 685 educators enrolled across four regions, and was then scaled up nationally. The Maihi Karauna Crown strategy for te reo Māori revitalisation was adopted in 2018, with a 2040 goal of one million New Zealanders speaking basic te reo. At the October 2023 handover te reo Māori had not been made a core curriculum subject, and the 2025 integration date had not arrived. The incoming government discontinued Te Ahu o te Reo Māori funding in 2024.
contestedNote: One reading is that the target date of 2025 fell outside Labour's term, so the goal could not fairly be marked failed at the October 2023 handover. The other is that the 2025 date was never going to be met on the trajectory set. There was no curriculum change, no entitlement, and after six years the workforce programme still reached only a fraction of teachers.
sourceDoc: Labour te reo Māori education policy, integrate te reo Māori into education in early learning and schools by 2025

promise: Make te reo Māori a core curriculum subject in all state primary and secondary schools by 2025, alongside additional resourcing for kaupapa Māori education.
keyNumber: Te reo a core subject in all schools by 2025 -> no curriculum change made by Oct 2023
statusReason: The core-curriculum requirement the Greens promised was never adopted while they were in government arrangements.
whatHappened: The Greens carried this policy into the 2017 confidence and supply arrangement and the 2020 cooperation agreement, but it was not adopted as government policy. Labour declined to make te reo compulsory, citing insufficient teacher supply, and pursued integration through the Te Ahu o te Reo Māori workforce programme instead. Green MPs continued to advocate the position publicly through the term. No legislation or National Curriculum change making te reo a core subject was made before the October 2023 handover.
sourceDoc: Green Party 2017 te reo Māori policy, te reo Māori a core curriculum subject in all schools by 2025

promise: Progress the settlement of historical Treaty of Waitangi claims through Te Arawhiti, prioritising durable settlements over speed. This includes advancing negotiations with Ngapuhi, the largest iwi grouping.
keyNumber: 13 settlements worth approx $690m over six years -> vs 46 settlements worth approx $1.23b over the previous nine years; 2030 completion target dropped
statusReason: Settlements continued and Te Arawhiti was established. But the rate was roughly a quarter of the previous one, the completion target was removed, and the largest outstanding claim did not advance to settlement.
whatHappened: Labour established Te Arawhiti, the Office for Māori Crown Relations, in January 2019. Over Andrew Little's five-plus years as Treaty Negotiations Minister the Crown completed 13 settlements worth about $690 million. That compares with 46 settlements worth about $1.23 billion over the previous government's nine years. Labour dropped the previous target of completing all willing historical settlements by 2030, with Little arguing that durable settlements mattered more than a deadline. The Ngapuhi settlement was not achieved. By early 2023 the Crown was negotiating with roughly eight separate Ngapuhi groupings rather than a single mandate.
contestedNote: Critics read the drop in settlement numbers as a delivery failure. The Crown and several iwi argue the remaining claims are the most complex and contested ones. They say the earlier pace reflected easier settlements being done first, and that a 2030 deadline would have pressured groups into settlements they did not accept.
sourceDoc: Labour Māori manifesto, commitment to Te Tiriti o Waitangi and to Te Arawhiti, the Office for Māori Crown Relations, to progress settlements

promise: Bring into force statutory Treaty duties on the chief executive of Oranga Tamariki. These require the agency to reduce disparities for tamariki Māori, to have regard to mana tamaiti, whakapapa and whanaungatanga, to develop strategic partnerships with iwi and Māori organisations, and to report publicly each year.
keyNumber: Section 7AA in force 1 July 2019 -> operated until repeal took effect 7 April 2025
statusReason: The statutory duties came into force on time and operated for the rest of the term, with partnerships signed and annual reporting published.
whatHappened: Section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 came into force on 1 July 2019 under the Labour government. It required the chief executive to set measurable outcomes for reducing disparities for Māori children, to have regard to mana tamaiti, whakapapa and whanaungatanga, to seek strategic partnerships with iwi and Māori organisations, and to report annually and publicly. Strategic partnerships with iwi and Māori organisations were signed, and section 7AA reports were published each year. The provision remained in force at the October 2023 handover. The incoming government repealed it, with the repeal taking effect on 7 April 2025.
contestedNote: The drafting provenance is disputed. Section 7AA was inserted by the Children, Young Persons, and Their Families (Oranga Tamariki) Legislation Act 2017, which passed under the previous National government. But its commencement on 1 July 2019, the strategic partnership programme built under it, and the response to the 2021 Waitangi Tribunal urgent inquiry all sat with Labour. Some critics also note that Labour declined the Tribunal's central recommendation for an independent Māori transition authority.
sourceDoc: Labour Māori manifesto, ensure Oranga Tamariki partners with iwi, hapū and Māori organisations to find the best solutions

promise: Fund Māori-led housing through Whai Kāinga Whai Oranga. The four-year $730 million programme, announced in October 2021, was to build over 1,000 new Māori homes, repair 700 existing whānau-owned homes, and provide infrastructure for papakāinga sites.
keyNumber: 1,000 new homes and 700 repairs from $730m -> up to 959 new builds and 331 repairs approved as at late 2022; completions not reported
statusReason: Funding approvals came close to the new-build target, but repairs ran well behind. Throughout the term the programme reported approvals rather than completed homes.
whatHappened: Budget 2021 provided $380 million for Whai Kāinga Whai Oranga plus $350 million for a Māori infrastructure fund, a combined $730 million over four years. Applications opened on 20 October 2021, with no completion deadline set. By December 2021, 24 further projects had been approved covering over 140 new houses, and $15 million had gone to repairs on 242 whānau-owned homes. A progress update from late 2022 recorded funding approved for up to 959 of the 1,000 new-build homes, up to 331 of the 700 repairs, and infrastructure enabled for up to 1,356 of 2,700 identified sites. No consolidated count of completed homes was published by the October 2023 handover. The programme ended in May 2025.
sourceDoc: Labour Māori manifesto, strengthen Māori housing through collaborative partnerships, home-ownership models and papakāinga provision

promise: Strengthen Māori housing through collaborative partnerships, home-ownership models and papakāinga provision, set out in a new national Māori housing strategy developed with Māori.
keyNumber: New national Māori housing strategy -> MAIHI Ka Ora published 2021 with six priority areas
statusReason: The new national strategy was written, published and given an implementation plan and funding vehicle within the term.
whatHappened: The government published MAIHI Ka Ora, the National Māori Housing Strategy, in 2021. It became the operative national Māori housing strategy in place of He Whare Āhuru He Oranga Tangata, the strategy issued in July 2014 under the previous government. MAIHI Ka Ora does not itself describe the earlier document as revoked, and presents itself as building on the MAIHI framework. It set six priority areas: Māori Crown partnerships, Māori-led local solutions, Māori housing supply, Māori housing support, the Māori housing system, and Māori housing sustainability. It came with an implementation plan and progress reporting through Te Tūāpapa Kura Kāinga and Te Puni Kōkiri. The strategy is not set in statute and has no binding numeric targets. Its main funding vehicle was Whai Kāinga Whai Oranga.
sourceDoc: Labour Māori manifesto, continued work with iwi to build more papakāinga and improve Māori home ownership rates

promise: Make New Zealand history, including the Treaty of Waitangi and Māori history, a core part of the curriculum in all schools and kura by 2022.
keyNumber: Core curriculum in all schools by 2022 -> curriculum launched March 2022, compulsory from the 2023 school year
statusReason: The curriculum was written and made compulsory as promised, but a year later than the stated 2022 date.
whatHappened: The government announced in September 2019 that New Zealand history would be taught in all schools and kura. A draft curriculum went out for consultation in 2021 and drew substantial criticism from historians. In January 2022 the Ministry of Education deferred implementation by a year. Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern launched Aotearoa New Zealand's Histories on 17 March 2022. It became a compulsory part of the curriculum for years 1 to 10 from the start of the 2023 school year, one year later than the manifesto date.
sourceDoc: Labour Māori manifesto. New Zealand history a core curriculum subject in all schools and kura by 2022

promise: Introduce a progressive procurement policy setting a target for the share of government contracts awarded to Māori businesses.
keyNumber: 5 per cent of contracts to Māori businesses -> 6 per cent achieved in 2021/22 (3,200+ contracts, approx $930m); target raised to 8 per cent in 2023
statusReason: The policy and a numeric target were introduced, the target was met, and it was then raised within the term.
whatHappened: A progressive procurement policy took effect from 2020. It required departments to award at least 5 per cent of their contracts by number to Māori businesses. In the 2021/22 financial year Māori businesses accounted for 6 per cent of government procurement contracts, more than 3,200 contracts worth about $930 million across the public sector. On 23 March 2023 the government raised the target to 8 per cent, with a review set for 2024.
sourceDoc: Labour Māori manifesto, a progressive procurement policy that would set a target for Māori business procurement

promise: Invest $20 million into a fund to upgrade New Zealand's four Māori boarding schools. Te Aute College, St Joseph's Māori Girls' College, Hukarere Girls' College and Hato Paora College.
keyNumber: $20m fund for four Māori boarding schools -> approx $17.2m allocated by August 2022
statusReason: The fund was created and most of it was allocated to the four named schools. But allocation ran two years behind the announcement, and the full $20 million was not publicly accounted for.
whatHappened: The commitment was announced on 26 September 2020 during the election campaign and funded in Budget 2021. About $2.337 million was paid out in 2021/22 for urgent works at Hato Paora and St Joseph's. On 16 August 2022 the remaining $14.9 million was allocated: $6.2 million to St Joseph's Māori Girls' College, $5.0 million to Te Aute College, $2.7 million to Hato Paora College and $981,300 to Hukarere Girls' College. That accounts for about $17.2 million of the $20 million. The balance was not separately reported by the October 2023 handover.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 campaign policy, $20 million fund to support Māori boarding schools

promise: Use the Provincial Growth Fund to unlock the productive potential of Māori-owned land. Its special legal status creates particular barriers to commercial finance.
keyNumber: Up to $100m of the Provincial Growth Fund ring-fenced for Māori land development -> announced 3 February 2019
statusReason: The dedicated $100 million allocation was made, and a loans and grants programme for Māori landowners operated for the rest of the term.
whatHappened: On 3 February 2019 Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern and Regional Economic Development Minister Shane Jones made an announcement at Otamatea Marae. Up to $100 million of the Provincial Growth Fund would be set aside for projects increasing the productivity of Māori-owned land, delivered as loans and grants under the Whenua Māori programme. Funded projects included horticulture conversions, such as an 18.2 hectare blueberry orchard at Te Teko. No full outcome reporting on jobs created and hectares brought into production was published. The PGF as a whole drew Auditor-General scrutiny over its assessment processes.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, $1 billion per annum Provincial Growth Fund, administered by NZ First's Regional Economic Development Minister

promise: Honour te Tiriti o Waitangi, as one of the twenty policy goals in the 2017 Labour-Green confidence and supply agreement.
statusReason: Treaty measures the Greens supported did pass, but the commitment as written specified nothing that could be delivered or missed.
whatHappened: Unlike most of the other nineteen goals, this commitment carried no named policy, number or date. Across the two terms Green ministers held Conservation, Climate Change, Associate Environment, Land Information, Prevention of Family and Sexual Violence and Associate Housing. None of these were Māori Crown relations portfolios. Labour ministers led the Government's Treaty measures in this period: the Māori Health Authority, removal of the Māori wards poll provisions, the Matariki public holiday and the New Zealand histories curriculum. Cabinet halted work on a plan to implement the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples in December 2022, without a plan being produced. The Greens supported these measures in the House, but the agreement goal itself was never given a deliverable to measure.
contestedNote: The Greens argue the goal was honoured through support for the Māori Health Authority, Māori wards changes and the histories curriculum. Critics of the scorecard note that scoring an undefined aspiration either way is arbitrary. They also note that the one concrete Treaty workstream of the period, the UNDRIP implementation plan, was stopped without a Green minister holding the portfolio to prevent it.
sourceDoc: Labour-Green Confidence and Supply Agreement 2017, policy goal 17, honour te Tiriti o Waitangi

promise: Within the first six months of Government, issue a Cabinet Office circular to all central government organisations. It is to state the Government's expectation that public services should be prioritised on the basis of need, not race.
keyNumber: Circular due within 6 months (by late May 2024) -> issued 13 September 2024
statusReason: The circular was issued in the form promised, but about four months after the six-month deadline written into the agreement.
whatHappened: Cabinet Office Circular CO (24) 5, Needs-based Service Provision, was issued on 13 September 2024. That was about nine and a half months after the Government was formed, and roughly four months after the six-month deadline. It states that the targeting, commissioning and design of public services should be based on the needs of all New Zealanders. It applies to public service agencies and their chief executives, and asks Crown entities and state-owned enterprises to comply so far as is consistent with their legal obligations. A supporting Cabinet paper, Ensuring Public Services are Based on Need and Contracts are Awarded on Value, was released at the same time. An identically worded commitment appears in the National-NZ First coalition agreement, without the six-month deadline.
contestedNote: The Government says the circular directs agencies to allocate services by assessed need rather than ethnicity, and does not stop agencies from taking ethnicity into account where it is itself evidence of need. Critics, including public health researchers publishing in the NZ Herald and in academic journals, argue that ethnicity is an established marker of need. They say removing ethnic targeting reduces the reach of services to Māori and Pacific populations, and that the circular sits uneasily with Treaty obligations. The dispute is about the circular's effect, not about whether it was issued.
sourceDoc: National. ACT Coalition Agreement, 24 November 2023

promise: Establish an independent national drinking water regulator with oversight of drinking water, wastewater and stormwater networks.
keyNumber: New water regulator promised -> Taumata Arowai established 1 March 2021
statusReason: The regulator was legislated, established and operational within the term, and has been retained by the successor government.
whatHappened: The Taumata Arowai, the Water Services Regulator Bill was introduced in December 2019 and enacted in 2020. Taumata Arowai was established as a Crown entity on 1 March 2021 and became fully operational in November 2021. Its regulatory powers are set out in the Water Services Act 2021. It regulates drinking water safety and has an oversight role for wastewater and stormwater networks, supported by a Māori Advisory Group. The regulator survived the change of government and was renamed the Water Services Authority (Taumata Arowai) in August 2025.
sourceDoc: Labour commitment to a dedicated drinking water regulator following the 2017 Havelock North Inquiry

promise: Move drinking water, wastewater and stormwater services from 67 councils into four large publicly owned water services entities, operating from 1 July 2024.
keyNumber: 4 entities operating by 1 July 2024 -> rescoped to 10 entities from 1 July 2026, none ever operational
statusReason: The legislation was passed, but the promised structural change was rescoped and delayed during the term, and no entity was operating at the October 2023 handover.
whatHappened: The mandatory four-entity model was announced in October 2021. It had council and mana whenua co-governance at the regional representative group level, and a 75 per cent parliamentary supermajority safeguard against privatisation. The Water Services Entities Act passed in December 2022 with only Labour's votes. In April 2023 the programme was rebranded the Water Services Reform Programme, expanded from four entities to ten on regional boundaries, and pushed back to 1 July 2026. That change became law on 16 August 2023. No entity ever took over water services. The legislation was repealed on 14 February 2024, before the new bodies began operating.
sourceDoc: Labour 2020 term commitment to the Three Waters reform programme (Cabinet decisions announced October 2021)

promise: Introduce a royalty on commercial users of water, including irrigators and water bottlers.
keyNumber: Royalty on commercial water use -> dropped in coalition negotiation; no charge legislated by Oct 2023
statusReason: The policy was dropped in the 2017 coalition negotiation with NZ First, before the government took office.
whatHappened: Labour dropped its proposed water tax on farmers as part of the coalition arrangement with NZ First after the 2017 election. The only surviving element in the coalition agreement was a narrower tax on exports of bottled water, and that was never introduced either. No royalty or charge on commercial water take was legislated in the 2017-2023 term.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 campaign policy, royalty on commercial water use

promise: Introduce a tax on exports of bottled water.
keyNumber: Bottled water export tax -> never introduced
statusReason: This was an explicit coalition agreement commitment with a specific tax base, and it was never legislated over two full terms.
whatHappened: The bottled water export tax was the narrowed remnant of Labour's broader water royalty policy, after NZ First refused to accept a charge on farm irrigation. Neither the wider royalty nor the bottled water export tax was introduced during the 2017-2023 term. No bottled water export tax was in force at the October 2023 handover.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement, 24 October 2017 (tax section)

promise: Repeal Labour's Three Waters legislation in the Government's first 100 days and restore council ownership and control of water assets.
keyNumber: Repeal within 100 days -> Water Services Acts Repeal Act passed 14 February 2024
statusReason: The repeal was passed inside the promised 100-day window, exactly as committed.
whatHappened: Cabinet agreed on 14 December 2023 to introduce and pass repeal legislation early in 2024. The Water Services Acts Repeal Act passed under urgency and became law on 14 February 2024, within the 100-day window. It disestablished the entity model before any entity began operating. Local Government Minister Simeon Brown said two further bills would follow. The first was to be enacted by mid-2024, and the second introduced in December 2024 and enacted by mid-2025.
sourceDoc: Coalition Government 100-day plan / 2023 coalition agreements, repeal Three Waters

promise: Replace the centralised Three Waters entity model with locally owned and controlled water services, allowing councils to voluntarily form water services groupings.
keyNumber: Voluntary council-owned model -> 44 councils chose CCOs, 23 in-house; 19 water CCOs established
statusReason: Council ownership was retained, and the voluntary grouping model was legislated and is operating.
whatHappened: Local Water Done Well kept water assets in council ownership and made grouping voluntary. Of 67 mainland councils, 44 chose to transfer services to a council-controlled organisation (CCO) and 23 kept them in-house. In all, 19 water CCOs were established, seven standalone and 12 multi-council. Five were operating by 1 July 2026, including IAWAI, Waikato Waters, Tiaki Wai in Wellington, a Kaikoura-Hurunui joint organisation and Selwyn Water. Another 13 were due within a year. The CCO model will serve about 76 per cent of New Zealanders.
sourceDoc: National-NZ First coalition agreement 2023 (water commitments, also in the National-ACT agreement)

promise: Pass transitional legislation by mid-2024 and a second, substantive Local Water Done Well Act by mid-2025. Require every council to produce a Water Services Delivery Plan showing financially sustainable, ring-fenced water services.
keyNumber: Second Act by mid-2025 -> passed 19 August 2025; all mainland councils had approved plans by 1 July 2026
statusReason: The framework, plans and approvals were all delivered, but both bills passed later than the dates the Government set itself.
whatHappened: The Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Act was passed on 28 August 2024, slightly after the mid-2024 target. The substantive Local Government (Water Services) Act 2025 and its companion Repeals and Amendments Act were passed on 19 August 2025, about two months after the mid-2025 target. Councils submitted Water Services Delivery Plans in September 2025. All had been assessed by 11 December 2025, and every mainland council had an approved plan by 1 July 2026, covering 46 councils forming new water organisations. The plans set out $47.9 billion of water investment over ten years, nearly $9 billion more than councils' previous long-term plan estimates. They imply around 9,000 additional water industry jobs.
sourceDoc: Local Water Done Well implementation plan, announced 5 April 2024

promise: Reach an agreement with Auckland Council that keeps Watercare in local ownership while separating its balance sheet, so Auckland can fund water infrastructure without steep water price rises.
keyNumber: Avoid Watercare's proposed price path -> 25.8% increases avoided; approx $899m saving over four years
statusReason: The agreement was reached, endorsed by the council, confirmed by the ratings agency and legislated within the first year of the term.
whatHappened: On 5 May 2024 the Government and Auckland Council agreed a financial arrangement, which the council's governing body endorsed unanimously. It allows Watercare to borrow more and spread repayment over a longer period. S&P Global Ratings confirmed Watercare's borrowing would be assessed separately from Auckland Council for credit rating purposes. The Government said Aucklanders would avoid the 25.8 per cent water price increases Watercare had previously proposed. The arrangement was legislated through the transitional water services bill. The Government later reported a $899 million saving for Aucklanders over four years from the Watercare financial solution.
sourceDoc: Local Water Done Well. Auckland financial arrangement

promise: Establish economic regulation of water services by the Commerce Commission by late 2025 and ring-fence water revenue. Let the Local Government Funding Agency lend to water CCOs at up to 500 per cent of operating revenue.
keyNumber: LGFA lending to water CCOs -> up to 500% of operating revenue, approx double council limits
statusReason: Borrowing capacity and ring-fencing were delivered on time and the Commerce Commission regime is legislated. But economic regulation is being introduced in stages rather than fully operating from late 2025.
whatHappened: The LGFA moved immediately to lend to council-supported water CCOs at up to 500 per cent of operating revenues, roughly double normal council limits. Work continued on lending to standalone CCOs and on a 350 per cent limit for high-growth councils. Water revenues must be ring-fenced for water services. The Local Government (Water Services) Act 2025, passed on 19 August 2025, put Commerce Commission oversight in place through an information disclosure regime. The fuller regulatory framework is being phased in.
sourceDoc: Local Water Done Well, new water service delivery models, announced 8 August 2024

promise: Set national wastewater environmental performance standards to cut the cost and delay of consenting wastewater treatment plants.
keyNumber: National wastewater standards -> in force Dec 2025, covering 330+ plants, up to $830m savings over 35 years
statusReason: The standards were consulted on, finalised and in force within the term.
whatHappened: The standards were announced on 28 November 2025 and took effect in December 2025, after more than 150 submissions from councils, industry, iwi and hapū and the public. They cover more than 330 publicly owned treatment plants. They set rules for discharges to land and water, biosolids reuse, and monitoring of overflows and bypasses on a risk-based approach. The Government estimated savings of up to $830 million over 35 years, cutting per-plant consenting costs by up to 40 per cent (up to 60 per cent for smaller plants). About 60 per cent of plants need new consents within a decade.
sourceDoc: Local Water Done Well, national wastewater environmental performance standards

promise: Refocus councils on core services by removing the four wellbeings from the purpose provisions of the Local Government Act. Introduce published performance benchmarks for councils.
keyNumber: Four wellbeings removed from the Local Government Act -> Bill still before Parliament at Aug 2026
statusReason: The policy was announced and legislation introduced, but the Local Government (System Improvements) Bill had not passed as at August 2026 and the term is unfinished.
whatHappened: The reform was announced on 21 August 2024, against a backdrop of average rates rises of about 15 per cent, which the Minister described as more than four times inflation. The changes were put into the Local Government (System Improvements) Bill. As at June 2026 that Bill was still before Parliament. Further amendments were being added to it, including restricting voting rights at council committee meetings to elected members, with councils to be given six months after passage to review delegations. Separately, on 25 November 2025 the Government proposed replacing elected regional councillors with Combined Territories Boards, consulting until 20 February 2026. On 5 May 2026 it invited councils to submit local reorganisation proposals within three months, with final decisions expected in 2027, ahead of the 2028 local elections.
sourceDoc: 'Back to basics for local government' reform programme, announced 21 August 2024

promise: Investigate and introduce a cap on council rates increases to stop spending on non-core projects.
keyNumber: Rates cap -> proposed 2-4% per capita a year, transition from 1 Jan 2027, full model 1 July 2029
statusReason: Policy settings were announced and consulted on, but no cap was in force as at August 2026, with full operation scheduled for 2029.
whatHappened: On 1 December 2025 Local Government Minister Simon Watts announced that the Government had agreed to progress a rates cap. It would limit annual increases to a target range of 2 to 4 per cent per capita, with a maximum of 4 per cent. It would apply to general rates, targeted rates and uniform annual charges, but exclude water charges and non-rates fees. Councils exceeding the upper limit would need regulator approval, granted only in extreme circumstances such as natural disasters. Stakeholder consultation ran to February 2026 and legislation was planned for enactment during 2026. A transition period with financial reporting starts on 1 January 2027, and the full regulatory model is not due to be operating until 1 July 2029.
sourceDoc: 'Back to basics for local government', exploring council revenue capping, announced 21 August 2024

promise: Establish a City and Regional Deals framework, invite up to five regions to submit proposals, and finalise New Zealand's first Regional Deal in 2025.
keyNumber: First deal in 2025 and up to 5 regions -> first deal signed 10 April 2026; 2 deals signed by Aug 2026
statusReason: The framework was delivered on time and two deals were signed. But the first deal came roughly a year after the promised 2025 date, and fewer than five regions had deals by August 2026.
whatHappened: The Regional Deals Strategic Framework was published on 22 August 2024, and up to five regions were invited to propose deals. The deals focused on economic growth, resilient infrastructure and housing supply. No deal was signed in 2025. The first, the Auckland City Deal, was signed on 10 April 2026. It covers a 30-year transport plan, Crown uplift funding and asset recycling, and growth areas at Drury, Maungawhau-Kingsland-Morningside and the city centre. A Western Bay of Plenty deal followed on 14 May 2026, targeting about 12,000 greenfield and 3,000 infill homes over a decade. A third deal was signalled for later in 2026.
sourceDoc: National-ACT coalition agreement 2023. City and Regional Deals; framework announced 22 August 2024

promise: Share a portion of the GST collected on new residential construction with local councils, so councils benefit financially from consenting new housing.
keyNumber: Share of GST on new builds -> $400m Incentives for Growth Fund over 4 years, first payments 1 April 2027
statusReason: The underlying objective, paying councils for enabling housing growth, was delivered. But it came through a capped appropriation rather than the promised share of GST revenue, and payments start after the term ends.
whatHappened: GST sharing itself was not adopted. Instead, Budget 2026 created an Incentives for Growth Fund of up to $400 million over four years from 2026/27, announced on 28 May 2026 by Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour. Payments to councils begin on 1 April 2027, based on residential building consents issued in the year to 31 January 2027. The scale is tiered: 0.25 per cent of the national average consent value per home for growth up to 1 per cent, 0.5 per cent for 1-2 per cent growth, and 1.25 per cent beyond 2 per cent. Funding can be used for infrastructure capital and operating costs, but not for water infrastructure or developer-chargeable costs.
sourceDoc: National-ACT coalition agreement 2023, share a portion of GST on new residential construction with councils

promise: Cancel National's legislated April 2018 tax threshold cuts and replace them with a Families Package. It included a Best Start payment of $60 a week for every child under one, extended to age three for low and middle income families and reaching nearly 60,000 families a year, a higher Family Tax Credit, and Working for Families extended to 30,000 more families.
keyNumber: Best Start $60 a week per child under three -> legislated Dec 2017, first payments 1 July 2018
statusReason: Legislated within weeks of taking office and paid at the promised rates and dates.
whatHappened: The Families Package (Income Tax and Benefits) Act passed in December 2017. Accommodation Supplement and Accommodation Benefit changes took effect on 1 April 2018. The Winter Energy Payment, Best Start payment and the Working for Families changes started on 1 July 2018. Best Start was paid at $60 a week per child, not income tested in the child's first year and income tested for years two and three. MSD's own material put the package's direct reach at about 1.025 million people from the Winter Energy Payment alone: 275,000 beneficiaries plus 750,000 superannuitants and veterans. Working for Families was simplified to two rates, $101.98 and $91.25 a week.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 Families Package campaign policy factsheet

promise: Pay a Winter Energy Payment of $450 a year to single superannuitants and beneficiaries and $700 a year to couples and people with dependent children, automatically and without application, reaching about one million New Zealanders.
keyNumber: $450 single / $700 couples, about 1 million people -> paid from 1 July 2018, $1.81b over four years
statusReason: Paid at the promised rates, to the promised group, from the promised date, and still in place.
whatHappened: The payment began on 1 July 2018 for a 13 week winter period, then ran for 22 weeks from 1 May in later years. The rates were as promised: $450 for single people with no dependent children and $700 for couples or single people with dependants. It is paid automatically with New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran's Pension and main benefits, at a budgeted cost of $1.81 billion over four years. It has been paid every winter since, and the next government retained it.
sourceDoc: Labour 2017 Winter Energy Payment factsheet

promise: Overhaul the welfare system, ensure access to entitlements, remove excessive sanctions and review Working for Families. The aim is that everyone has a standard of living and income that enables them to live in dignity and participate in their communities, and that lifts children and their families out of poverty.
keyNumber: Remove excessive sanctions -> sanctions applied fell from 60,588 in 2017 to 25,329 in 2023
statusReason: Sanctions fell and indexation was made more generous. But the promised system overhaul and Working for Families rewrite did not happen within the two terms.
whatHappened: Sanction use fell sharply across the two terms. The incoming coalition later cited 60,588 sanctions applied in 2017 against 25,329 in 2023. From 1 April 2020 main benefits were indexed to net average wage growth rather than to prices, a change the next government reversed in February 2024. No comprehensive replacement of the welfare system was legislated. Labour was still offering Working for Families settings as an unfulfilled election promise in 2023. Over the same period the number of people on Jobseeker Support rose by roughly 70,000, on the figures used by the incoming government.
sourceDoc: Labour-Green Confidence and Supply Agreement 2017

promise: Keep the age of eligibility for New Zealand Superannuation at 65.
keyNumber: Superannuation age 65 -> unchanged at 65 across both terms
statusReason: The age stayed at 65 for the whole term, which is exactly what the commitment required.
whatHappened: The eligibility age was not changed at any point in the 2017-2023 period, and no legislation to raise it was introduced. Independent tracking of the 2017 coalition agreement records the superannuation age commitment as fully implemented as at July 2020. NZ First then secured the identical commitment in writing again from National in 2023. The National-NZ First coalition agreement states 'Keep the superannuation age at 65'.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, superannuation eligibility age

promise: Introduce a SuperGold smartcard with expanded discounts and concessions for cardholders.
keyNumber: SuperGold smartcard -> website and app launched Oct 2019 covering about 5,500 businesses
statusReason: The discount network and digital platform were delivered, but the smartcard itself did not eventuate within the term.
whatHappened: A new SuperGold website and app were launched in October 2019, offering discounts and concessions from about 5,500 businesses. Independent tracking of the coalition agreement records the commitment as fully implemented. The card itself was not converted into a chipped smartcard during the term. That step was announced only in May 2026 under the following government, with rollout expected from October 2028.
sourceDoc: Labour-NZ First Coalition Agreement 2017, SuperGold smartcard

promise: Raise the Working for Families in-work tax credit by $25 a week from 1 April 2024, and lift the Working for Families abatement threshold to $50,000 from 1 April 2026.
keyNumber: In-work tax credit +$25 a week from 1 April 2024 -> not delivered by Labour; legislated by National from 31 July 2024
statusReason: The promising party left office before implementing any part of it, though its successor later legislated the in-work tax credit component.
whatHappened: Labour lost the October 2023 election and never introduced the policy. The incoming National government legislated the same $25 a week increase to the in-work tax credit in Budget 2024, lifting it from $72.50 to $97.50 a week from 31 July 2024. The abatement threshold was not raised to $50,000. The next government adjusted Working for Families income thresholds, but not to the level Labour promised.
sourceDoc: Labour 2023 campaign policy announcement, 13 August 2023

promise: Index main benefit increases to the consumer price index rather than to net average wage growth.
keyNumber: CPI indexation restored -> legislated Feb 2024, $669.5m saved across the forecast period to 2027/28
statusReason: Legislated under urgency within three months of taking office and applied from the first annual adjustment.
whatHappened: A bill restoring CPI indexation of main benefits was introduced under urgency on 14 February 2024. It reversed the previous government's 2019 decision to index to net average wage growth. The government put the saving at $669.5 million across the forecast period to 2027/28. The first adjustment under the restored basis took effect on 1 April 2024. It lifted New Zealand Superannuation by $71.08 a fortnight for couples and $46.20 for singles, Jobseeker Support for couples with children by $56.48, and sole parent rates by $44.02. It affected about 1.4 million people, including 909,000 superannuitants and veterans and 371,000 working-age beneficiaries.
sourceDoc: National 2023 welfare policy, as summarised in RNZ's guide to party policy
